They combine these with responsible-innovation ideas (anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, responsiveness) and systems thinking. The result is SMACTR, five stages that each leave documents in a 'transparency trail'. In Scoping, auditors read the product requirements and the organisation's AI principles, run an ethical review of the use case with diverse voices, and write a social impact assessment that rates severity. In Mapping, they list stakeholders, map the development lifecycle and system components, interview engineers in a light ethnographic study, and start the FMEA. In Artifact Collection, they check that required documentation exists with a design checklist and collect datasheets and model cards; in the smile example the CelebA datasheet shows skewed age and skin-type distributions. In Testing, they run tests chosen by FMEA priority, mainly adversarial and counterfactual inputs and subgroup tests, then build an ethical risk analysis chart that labels each risk high, mid or low from likelihood and severity. In Reflection, auditors and engineers update the FMEA, write a remediation plan, assemble an algorithmic design history file and a summary report used for the go or no-go decision. To adapt this for a clinical multi-agent system, a PhD student can run SMACTR with Sri Lankan neurosurgeons and radiologists, use FMEA to rank failure modes such as missed lesions or wrong grade, test subgroup and adversarial cases, and define explicit risk thresholds that trigger deferral to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Conceptual framework paper with hypothetical case illustrations. Authors from Partnership on AI and Google (USA). No real data collection, no participants, not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset analysed. The smile-detector example refers to CelebA via a hypothetical datasheet built from prior studies: binary gender labels 58.1% female, 42% male; age 77.8% 0-45 years, 22.1% over 46; skin type 14.2% lighter-skinned, 85.8% darker-skinned (figures as printed in the paper). Image counts are not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: SMACTR stages and artifacts: (1) Scoping - inputs: statement of AI principles and Product Requirements Document; outputs: ethical review of system use case (with diverse viewpoints and an internal ethics review board) and social impact assessment (severity of risk plus identification of social, economic and cultural impacts). (2) Mapping - stakeholder map and collaborator list, system map of the development lifecycle, engineering system overview, design history file review, ethnographic field study with semi-structured interviews; FMEA begins and risks are prioritised. (3) Artifact Collection - design checklist (inventory of expected documentation; avoid yes/no questions), datasheets for datasets and model cards. (4) Testing - tests based on FMEA risk priority; adversarial testing with tailored, intersectional, non-statistical inputs; ethical risk analysis chart combining failure likelihood (from testing) and severity (from earlier stages), each risk labelled high, mid or low. (5) Reflection - use-related risk analysis and updated FMEA (designer vs user mental models, distribution drift, foreseeable misuse), remediation and risk mitigation plan (jointly by auditors and engineers), algorithmic design history file, and algorithmic audit summary report comparing results to stated ethical objectives. Example company principles: Transparency; Justice, Fairness and Non-Discrimination; Safety and Non-Maleficence; Responsibility and Accountability; Privacy.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: No empirical evaluation. The framework is illustrated by walking through two hypothetical audits (child-abuse screening tool; Happy-Go-Lucky smile-triggered photo booth) and a supplementary end-to-end worked example with document templates for the smile case.
papers.baselines: Not applicable. The paper compares conceptually with audit practice in aerospace, medicine/medical devices (FDA design controls), finance and safety engineering.
papers.results: No quantitative results. Qualitative outcome of the illustration: the smile detector could be approved after retraining on more diverse data, opt-in use, a default-off trigger and a privacy disclaimer; the child-abuse screening project might be stalled or cancelled because of high-severity risks (false positives separating families; false negatives leaving children at risk).
papers.statistics: Not reported
papers.availability: Supplementary worked example and templates are mentioned as an online resource; exact link not given in the text read. No code.

papers.title: Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI (AMIE)
papers.authors: Tu T, Palepu A, Schaekermann M, Saab K, Freyberg J, et al., Natarajan V
papers.aim: To build an LLM that can take a medical history and give a diagnosis through conversation.
papers.method: Self-play training in a simulated environment with automatic feedback. Tested in a blinded OSCE-style study with patient actors against primary care doctors.
papers.result: Higher diagnostic accuracy than the doctors and rated better on most quality axes by specialists and by patient actors.
papers.tools: PaLM-2 based LLM, self-play, simulated dialogue
papers.gap: Text chat only, which is not how real consultations happen. Not tested in real practice.
papers.relation: Relevant to our patient-intake agent. Their OSCE-style blinded evaluation can be adapted for O4.
papers.limitations: Chat setting unfair to doctors, no images. Future: real-world studies.
papers.methodologyDetail: AMIE starts from PaLM 2. The team built a training mixture of static data: MedQA (11,450 train questions plus 191 with expert reasoning), 64 expert long-form answers, 65 clinician summaries of MIMIC-III notes, and 98,919 real US clinic transcripts, cleaned of nurse turns and paraverbal tags and split 90/10 (89,027 train, 9,892 validation) by condition and visit reason. Because real dialogues are noisy and cover limited conditions, they added a self-play multi-agent environment. For each condition, 60 web passages (20 on demographics, 20 on symptoms, 20 on management) were retrieved, filtered by PaLM-2, and turned into patient vignettes by AMIE using a one-shot format. Then AMIE played three roles: a patient agent answering from the vignette, a doctor agent asking at most two questions per turn, and a moderator deciding when the conversation had ended. A fourth critic agent, which knew the true diagnosis, gave feedback on empathy, question count and diagnostic coverage; the doctor agent replayed the dialogue with this feedback, twice. Each iteration produced 11,686 dialogues from 5,230 conditions (4 per common condition from 613; 2 per less common condition from 4,617). These refined dialogues were added to the next fine-tuning round (outer loop). Training predicted the next turn, sampling about 3 target turns per role per dialogue. At inference AMIE used three calls: analyse the case (symptoms, differential, missing information, confidence and urgency), draft a reply with questions or escalation, and refine for factual accuracy and empathy. Validation was a randomised blinded crossover OSCE: 149 scenario packs, 20 patient actors, 20 PCPs, text chat up to 20 minutes, ranked DDx of 3-10 items, and ratings by 23 matched specialists and the actors. Statistics used 10,000-sample bootstrap and Wilcoxon tests with FDR correction. A PhD student can reuse the critic loop, the confidence step and the OSCE-style blinded crossover design, adding a calibrated deferral rule that AMIE lacks.
papers.studyDesign: Model development plus prospective randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover simulation study (remote OSCE). Google Research and Google DeepMind with OSCE laboratories in Canada and India; scenario packs from Canada, India and the UK.
papers.datasets: Training: (1) MedQA (USMLE-style, 4-5 options): 11,450 training and 1,273 test questions, plus 191 training questions with expert step-by-step reasoning. (2) Long-form medical QA: expert responses to 64 questions from HealthSearchQA, LiveQA and MedicationQA (MultiMedBench). (3) Medical summarisation: 65 clinician-written summaries of MIMIC-III notes (MIMIC-III has about 2 million notes across 13 types; 5 notes per category selected, minimum total length 400 tokens, at least one nursing note per patient). (4) Real-world dialogue: 98,919 de-identified audio transcripts of in-person US clinic visits from over 1,000 clinicians over 10 years, 51 specialties and 168 conditions/visit reasons; mean 149.8 turns (P25 = 75.0, P75 = 196.0); only doctor-patient dialogues kept. (5) Simulated dialogues: 11,686 per fine-tuning iteration from 5,230 conditions, drawn from Health QA (613 common conditions), MalaCards (18,455 less common) and MedicineNet (4,617 less common); mean 21.28 turns (P25 = 19.0, P75 = 25.0). Evaluation: 149 OSCE scenario packs (India 75, Canada 60, UK 14) covering cardiovascular 29, respiratory 30, gastroenterology 31, neurology 30, urology/obstetrics/gynaecology 15, internal medicine 14; 149 simulated patients (Canada 67, India 82). Excluded: pediatrics, psychiatry, intensive care and inpatient management.
papers.preprocessing: Real-world dialogues: removed non doctor/patient roles (for example nurses) and paraverbal annotations such as [LAUGHING] and [INAUDIBLE]; stratified split by condition category and visit reason into 90% training (89,027 conversations) and 10% validation (9,892). Target turns: on average 3 turns per role sampled per dialogue, from turns of at least 30 characters. Vignettes: 60 passages retrieved per condition (20 each on demographics, symptoms, management), filtered by PaLM-2 with a Yes/No relevance prompt. Few-shot (1-5) exemplars added for all tasks except dialogue and long-form generation.
papers.modelDetails: Base: PaLM 2, instruction fine-tuned with task-specific instructions (doctor role, patient role, QA/reasoning, EHR summarisation). Self-play environment: (1) Vignette generator: web search for the condition, PaLM-2 passage filtering, AMIE generates 2 vignettes per prompt with a one-shot format example. (2) Simulated dialogue generator with three agents played by AMIE: patient agent (answers honestly from vignette), doctor agent (empathetic clinician, no more than two questions per turn), moderator (decides Yes/No whether the conversation has ended: diagnosis and plan given and no patient questions left, or a goodbye). Dialogue starts with 'Doctor: So, how can I help you today?'. (3) Self-play critic: a fourth AMIE agent that knows the ground-truth diagnosis gives in-context feedback on empathy and professionalism, at most one or two questions per response, not revealing it is AI, and asking enough to identify at least two likely differentials; the doctor agent redoes the dialogue from scratch with its previous history; repeated twice per fine-tuning iteration (inner loop). Outer loop: refined dialogues added to the next fine-tuning round. Inference chain-of-reasoning (three sequential calls): (1) analyse patient information - summarise positive and negative symptoms and history, produce current differential, note missing information, assess confidence in the differential and its urgency; (2) formulate response and action - answer, ask questions to fill gaps, recommend immediate action such as emergency visit if needed, present differential if confident; (3) refine response for factuality, no repetition, empathy and clear format. No explicit numeric confidence threshold or deferral rule is reported.
papers.training: Iterative instruction fine-tuning: first round on static datasets only; later rounds also on self-play simulated dialogues (11,686 per iteration). Dialogue training predicts the next turn given previous turns. Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, number of steps or iterations, hardware and training time are not reported.
papers.evaluation: Randomised, blinded crossover remote OSCE: each of 149 simulated patients had two text consultations, one with a PCP and one with AMIE, in random order, maximum 20 minutes, agents told not to reveal identity. 20 board-certified PCPs (10 India, 10 Canada; 3-25 years post-residency, median 7) and 20 patient actors (10 India, 10 Canada). After each consultation the agent gave a ranked DDx (3 to 10 conditions) and recommendations on escalation, investigations, treatment, management and follow-up. Patient actors rated GMCPQ, PACES (Managing Patient Concerns, Maintaining Patient Welfare) and PCCBP 'Fostering the Relationship' items. 23 specialist physicians (India 14, North America 6, UK 3; 1-36 years post-residency, median 5), matched by specialty and region, rated both agents per case in random blinded order on DDx accuracy, appropriateness and comprehensiveness, management items, PACES, PCCBP and confabulations. Top-k accuracy = percentage of cases where the ground-truth (or accepted) diagnosis is in the top k, a match being exact, very close or closely related as judged by the specialist. Auto-evaluation: Med-PaLM 2 Y/N matcher for DDx; AMIE self-CoT 5-shot rater for four PACES criteria, validated by rank-order agreement on 149 dialogue pairs and against a second specialist on 139 pairs. Ablations: DDx by specialty, by location (67 Canada, 82 India; 40 shared scenarios), AMIE DDx from PCP transcripts, accuracy vs number of turns, and self-play vs baseline on 1,142 simulated dialogues.
papers.baselines: 20 board-certified primary care physicians (PCPs) in the same text-chat setting. For auto-evaluation prompting: 0-shot, 5-shot and shuffled 5-shot self-CoT; random guessing according to specialist preference distribution; second specialist (inter-specialist agreement). For self-play: baseline simulated dialogues without critic revision.
papers.results: DDx (specialist-rated, 149 cases): AMIE higher top-k accuracy than PCPs for all k from 1 to 10, against both ground truth and accepted differential, p < 0.05 after FDR; exact percentages shown only in Figure 3. PCP DDx length min 3, mean 5.39. Auto-evaluated DDx: AMIE better for k > 2 (ground truth) and k > 4 (accepted differential). AMIE DDx from PCP transcripts vs own transcripts: no significant difference, both better than PCP DDx. By specialty: AMIE matched or exceeded PCPs in all six, largest gains in respiratory and cardiovascular; both weaker in obstetrics/gynaecology and internal medicine. By location: higher accuracy in Canada (significant at all k) than India (not significant); on 40 shared scenarios performance equivalent. Turns: top-3 accuracy plateaued within 10 turns. Conversation quality: patient actors rated AMIE better on 24 of 26 axes (no difference for Respecting Patient's Privacy, N = 108, and Acknowledging Mistakes, N = 41); specialists rated AMIE better on 28 of 32 axes (no difference for escalation recommendation, treatment inappropriate avoided, follow-up recommendation, confabulation absent; N = 149). Self-play vs baseline (auto-evaluation, four PACES criteria): self-play preferred 0.24 to 0.33, baseline preferred 0.18 to 0.22, tie 0.46 to 0.58. Auto-evaluator rank-order agreement was above chance and about equal to inter-specialist agreement (values shown only in figures).
papers.statistics: DDx accuracy: bootstrap tests with 10,000 samples and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction across all k. Patient actor and specialist ratings: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with FDR correction; 'Cannot rate / Does not apply' cases excluded. Significance levels reported as p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001. Inter-rater: rank-order agreement between auto-evaluation and specialists, and between two specialists on 139 pairs (values in figures). Confidence intervals not given in text.
papers.availability: Not available. Model, code and the licensed real-world dialogue dataset are not released; a model card is given in Table A.5. Public data used: MedQA, MultiMedBench, MIMIC-III (credentialed access).

papers.title: Enhancing diagnostic capability with multi-agents conversational large language models
papers.authors: Chen X, Yi H, You M, Liu W, Wang L, Li H, Zhang X, Guo Y, Fan L, Chen G, Lao Q, Fu W, Li K, Li J
papers.aim: To build a Multi-Agent Conversation (MAC) framework that copies a clinical Multi-Disciplinary Team (MDT) discussion, and to test whether it diagnoses rare diseases better than single GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models.
papers.method: The authors built MAC on Microsoft AutoGen with one admin agent, several doctor agents and one supervisor agent that discuss a case until consensus or a maximum of 13 rounds. They tested it on 302 rare-disease case reports (Orphanet diseases, Medline reports), each turned into a primary consultation and a follow-up consultation. Outputs were scored by GPT-4o against the correct answer, and GPT-4o scoring was checked against a blinded three-physician panel.
papers.result: With GPT-4 and 4 doctor agents, MAC reached 34.11% most-likely-diagnosis accuracy, 48.12% possible-diagnosis accuracy and 78.26% helpful-test rate in primary consultation, versus 19.65%, 34.55% and 58.17% for GPT-4 alone. In follow-up consultation MAC reached 53.86% and 67.88% versus 37.86% and 59.71% for GPT-4 alone. Four doctor agents plus a supervisor was the best setting. Cost with GPT-4 was USD 0.12 per primary case and USD 0.17 per follow-up case. MAC also beat Chain-of-Thought, Self-Refine and Self-Consistency.
papers.tools: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini (generalisability test), GPT-4o (automatic evaluator); Microsoft AutoGen multi-agent framework; Orphanet database; Medline/PubMed; SPSS version 25; GraphPad Prism version 8. Hardware not reported (models used through API).
papers.gap: Uses text-only rare-disease case reports from the literature, not real prospective patients or images. There is no uncertainty estimate or deferral rule; consensus is decided by an LLM supervisor. Assigning specialist roles did not help, so true domain specialisation of agents is still open.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration) this paper gives a tested template for a supervisor-led team of LLM agents: an admin agent feeds the case, doctor agents debate, and a supervisor drives consensus and stops the talk. It shows that a coordinating supervisor adds accuracy (34.11% vs 32.67% without it) and that 3-4 agents is a good team size, which can guide the number and roles of agents in the brain-tumour pathway orchestrator. It lacks calibrated deferral and imaging agents, which our PhD must add. Its GPT-4o-as-judge plus blinded physician-panel check is a low-cost evaluation design that could be adapted for clinician validation in Sri Lanka.
papers.limitations: Sample is small compared with the 7000+ rare diseases (302 cases). Primary-consultation text was extracted manually by clinicians, which is subjective. Data are published case reports. Explanations in the agent dialogue may not reflect the true model reasoning. The authors state MAC is a support tool, not a replacement for clinicians. Future work: larger samples, more diseases, real clinical implementation.
papers.methodologyDetail: Step 1, disease sampling: the team took the Orphanet database (over 7000 rare diseases in 33 categories) and drew 302 diseases with normalised weighted random sampling, where category weights were based on disease counts moderated by a natural log, giving 1 to 9 diseases per category. Step 2, case collection: for each disease they searched Medline for case reports published after January 2022. Two specialist doctors screened them against clear criteria (complete real-patient picture, English; exclude missing data, animal studies, factual errors, wrong disease). If no report fitted, a new disease from the same category was sampled. Step 3, extraction and curation: one investigator extracted demographics, presentation, history, examination, test results and final diagnosis; a specialist checked it. Each case became two text prompts: a primary consultation with only first-visit information, and a follow-up consultation with all test results. Step 4, the MAC system: using AutoGen, an admin agent posts the case and task; doctor agents (2-5) reason, critique each other and revise; a supervisor agent challenges, points out gaps, drives consensus and ends the chat, with a hard stop at 13 rounds. Primary output is one most likely diagnosis, a list of possible diagnoses and further tests; follow-up output drops the tests. Step 5, comparisons: single GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, CoT, Self-Consistency (10 paths, temperature 0.7) and Self-Refine (4 rounds, temperature 0.7, 0-50 self-score), plus ablations on base model, agent count, supervisor removal, dynamic specialist roles, and GPT-4o-mini. Step 6, scoring: over 35,000 outputs were graded by GPT-4o given the correct answer (exact-match accuracy plus 0-5 rating scales). A blinded three-physician panel scored all 302 cases by consensus, and agreement with GPT-4o was high (kappa 0.859-0.958). Step 7, statistics: chi-square for accuracy, ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis for scores, Fleiss' kappa across three repeated runs. The best setting, GPT-4 with four doctor agents and a supervisor, gave 34.11% top-1 accuracy in primary and 53.86% in follow-up consultation, at about USD 0.12-0.17 per case. To adapt it, one could replace text cases with brain-tumour MDT summaries and add an imaging agent and an uncertainty-based deferral step.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, simulation-based evaluation study using published case reports; no human participants (ethics approval waived). Institutions: West China Hospital and Sichuan University (Chengdu), Zhejiang University, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Shanghai AI Laboratory. Country: China.
papers.datasets: (1) Orphanet rare-disease database: pool of over 7000 rare diseases in 33 categories; 302 diseases sampled across all 33 categories (1 to 9 diseases per category) by normalised weighted random sampling with natural-log-moderated weights. (2) Medline/PubMed clinical case reports published after January 2022: one eligible report per disease, so 302 cases. Modality: text only (demographics, presentation, history, physical examination, test results such as genetic tests, biopsies and radiographic examinations, and final diagnosis). Inclusion: complete clinical picture of a real patient with the rare disease; published in English. Exclusion: missing information needed for diagnosis, not English, animal studies, factual errors affecting the diagnosis, a disease other than the one searched. If no eligible report was found, another disease from the same category was re-sampled. Dataset released on GitHub for non-commercial use.
papers.preprocessing: Search done by one investigator and reviewed by a second. Two specialist doctors screened reports independently; disagreements were resolved by group discussion. One investigator extracted data from each report and a specialist doctor checked it. Each case was curated into two text scenarios: primary consultation (limited first-visit information, as in primary care) and follow-up consultation (complete information including all test results). Final and differential diagnoses from the original text were kept as reference answers. No train/validation/test split, because no model was trained (all 302 cases are test cases). No image preprocessing (text only).
papers.modelDetails: MAC is built on AutoGen. Agents: (1) admin agent presents patient information and the task; (2) doctor agents (3 in the core design; 2 to 5 tested; 4 was best) give diagnostic reasoning and recommendations, comment on other agents' opinions with reasons, and revise their own output; (3) supervisor agent oversees and evaluates suggestions, challenges diagnoses and tests, points out missed issues, facilitates discussion, drives consensus on diagnosis and tests only, and ends the conversation when consensus is reached. No fixed speaking order (consensual framework). Stopping rule: consensus or a maximum of 13 conversation rounds (13 and 25 forced rounds also tested in the token-scaling study). Primary consultation output: one most likely diagnosis, several possible diagnoses and further diagnostic tests; follow-up output: one most likely diagnosis and several possible diagnoses; no limit on the number of items. Knowledge task: generate definition, epidemiology, clinical description, aetiology, diagnostic methods, differential diagnosis, antenatal diagnosis, genetic counselling, management and treatment, and prognosis. Subgroup variants: base model GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4; 2-5 doctor agents; with vs without supervisor; dynamic specialty assignment (GPT-4 picks the 4 most relevant specialties per case and prompts each doctor agent to act as that specialist). No uncertainty estimate, confidence threshold or deferral rule is used.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning; all models were used through prompting. Self-Consistency comparator: 10 reasoning paths, temperature 0.7 (5, 10 and 20 paths tested). Self-Refine comparator: 4 refinement rounds, temperature 0.7, self-feedback score 0-50, best-scoring version kept (2, 4 and 10 rounds tested). Temperature for MAC: Not reported. Hardware and run time: Not reported. Cost with GPT-4 as base: USD 0.12 per primary consultation case and USD 0.17 per follow-up case.
papers.evaluation: All 302 cases in both scenarios. Knowledge scored on 5 Likert aspects (1-5): inaccurate or inappropriate content, omission, likelihood of harm, extent of harm, bias. Diagnosis accuracy: correct if the exact correct diagnosis is included (most likely diagnosis; possible diagnoses). Test recommendation accuracy: correct if helpful for reaching the correct diagnosis. Rating scales: diagnosis scored 5/4/3/2/0 (Bond et al. scale); tests scored 1-5 Likert. Because over 35,000 outputs were produced, GPT-4o scored them with the correct answer supplied. Human evaluation on 302 cases by a panel of three physicians, blinded to model condition and reviewing in random order, reaching consensus scores; human-LLM agreement was measured. Reliability: 3 repeated runs in 6 settings, Fleiss' kappa. Error analysis: diagnosis errors in 4 categories, test errors in 3 levels. Cost analysis. Generalisability test with GPT-4o-mini. Output-token scaling analysis across methods.
papers.baselines: Single-agent GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (input/output prompting); Chain-of-Thought prompting; Self-Consistency; Self-Refine; GPT-4o-mini with and without MAC; MAC ablations (no supervisor, specialty assignment, 2-5 doctor agents, GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 base).
papers.results: Primary consultation (most likely / possible / helpful tests): GPT-3.5 = 16.23% / 27.92% / 47.68%; GPT-4 = 19.65% / 34.55% / 58.17%. MAC with GPT-3.5, 2/3/4/5 agents = 23.18/36.09/73.84; 24.17/35.43/79.14; 24.28/36.64/77.59; 22.85/36.09/79.47 (%). MAC with GPT-4, 2/3/4/5 agents = 31.13/45.03/73.51; 32.45/46.36/76.82; 34.11/48.12/78.26; 31.79/46.36/81.46 (%). No supervisor (4 agents): GPT-3.5 = 24.50/36.20/74.28; GPT-4 = 32.67/45.47/78.04. Specialty assignment (4 agents): GPT-3.5 = 24.84/36.64/78.03; GPT-4 = 34.32/48.23/80.02. Follow-up consultation (most likely / possible): GPT-3.5 = 29.36% / 46.91%; GPT-4 = 37.86% / 59.71%; MAC GPT-3.5 with 2 agents = 41.06/56.62 and 3 agents = 42.83/57.29 (4-5 agents not feasible due to token limits); MAC GPT-4 with 2/3/4/5 agents = 51.99/65.56; 53.31/67.88; 53.86/67.88; 50.99/66.56. No supervisor: GPT-3.5 (3 agents) = 41.72/54.75; GPT-4 (4 agents) = 51.66/65.78. Specialty assignment: GPT-3.5 (3) = 43.59/58.61; GPT-4 (4) = 53.75/67.88. Knowledge: all three systems averaged above 4 on all 5 aspects. Rating scores, GPT-4o vs human: most likely 3.03 +/- 1.78 vs 2.99 +/- 1.75; possible 3.35 +/- 1.84 vs 3.32 +/- 1.82; tests 3.64 +/- 1.22 vs 3.60 +/- 1.20. MAC beat CoT, Self-Refine and Self-Consistency on all metrics (exact values in Supplementary Table 12, not in the main text). Raising MAC to 13 and 25 forced rounds increased tokens without significant gain. Confidence intervals: Not reported.
papers.statistics: SPSS 25 and GraphPad Prism 8. Shapiro-Wilk normality test, then ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis for continuous scores (mean +/- SD); chi-square test for accuracy rates. Fleiss' kappa for run-to-run reliability: moderate (>0.4) in 23 of 28 evaluations and fair (0.35-0.4) in the other 5; GPT-4o-mini within MAC 0.3-0.6. Agreement between GPT-4o and human evaluation (Fleiss' kappa): most likely diagnosis 0.859, possible diagnoses 0.958, further tests 0.952. Exact p-values are in supplementary tables, not in the main text.
papers.availability: Code and dataset: https://github.com/geteff1/Multi-agent-conversation-for-disease-diagnosis (non-commercial use).

papers.title: Orchestrator multi-agent clinical decision support system for secondary headache diagnosis in primary care
papers.authors: Wu X, Zhang H, Garduno-Rapp NE, Rousseau JF, Thakkallapally M, Ji Y, Visweswaran S, Peng Y, Wang Y
papers.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (JAMIA), ocag111 (preprint arXiv:2512.04207)
papers.aim: To build and test an LLM-based multi-agent clinical decision support system, with a central orchestrator and 7 red-flag specialist agents, that detects secondary-headache red flags from free-text vignettes in an interpretable way.
papers.method: Seven red flags were derived from 10 clinical guidelines. A LangGraph orchestrator reads each vignette, outputs a JSON routing decision, and sends the case to the relevant specialist agents, each giving a yes/no answer with evidence; a manual fan-out step calls any agent the orchestrator missed, and results are aggregated. Four set-ups (single LLM vs multi-agent, question prompt vs guideline prompt) were compared on 90 expert-labelled cases with 5 local open-source LLMs, using per-case multi-label precision, recall and F1.
papers.result: Multi-agent with guideline prompting (GPrompt) gave the best F1 for every model: Qwen-30b 0.605 (vs 0.542 single-LLM QPrompt), GPT-OSS-20b 0.568 (vs 0.474), Qwen-14b 0.603 (vs 0.568 in table), Qwen-8b 0.594 (vs 0.557), Llama-3.1-8b 0.519 (vs 0.530 single-LLM QPrompt, but above 0.508 single-LLM GPrompt). Gains were larger for small and medium models. Multi-agent with a plain question prompt did not reliably help, except for Qwen-30b.
papers.tools: LangGraph (graph-based agent orchestration with shared state); Ollama for local model serving (MERLIN prototype); open-source LLMs Qwen-30b (Qwen-30B-A3B), GPT-OSS-20b, Qwen-14b, Qwen-8b, Llama-3.1-8b; PMC-Patients dataset; Docker (MERLIN web application). Hardware not reported.
papers.gap: Best F1 of 0.605 is too low for clinical use. Tested only on curated published case reports, not real primary-care notes, and only 7 red flags. No calibrated confidence, uncertainty estimate or deferral rule; the system outputs binary yes/no per agent. Orchestrator misrouting can cascade, and routing is not learned.
papers.relation: For O1 this is the closest design template: a central orchestrator that outputs a structured JSON routing decision (next agents, reason, evidence quotes), domain-specialist agents run in parallel, a deterministic fan-out safety net that calls missed agents, a shared auditable state, and a full execution trace. The same pattern maps onto a brain-tumour pathway (e.g. imaging, pathology, surgical-planning agents). It shows that guideline-grounded prompts plus decomposition help small local models (8B-30B), which suits low-resource Sri Lankan hospitals and local, privacy-preserving deployment (MERLIN runs fully locally via Ollama). Our PhD must add what it lacks: calibrated per-agent confidence and a selective-deferral rule to clinicians, imaging inputs, and prospective clinician validation.
papers.limitations: F1 0.605 is not enough for real decision support; recall is reasonable, so the authors suggest use as a screening aid. Data are curated case reports, not prospective primary-care documentation, so generalisability is uncertain. Only 7 red-flag domains. Multi-agent design adds cascading-error risks (misrouting, inconsistent agents). Future work: larger or clinical LLMs, reinforcement learning (multi-agent RL, RLHF) to learn routing and decision boundaries, cross-agent consistency checks, dynamic stopping, negotiation between agents, testing on noisy notes and structured EHR data, prospective deployment, more red flags and urgency levels, passive EHR-integrated flagging for human review.
papers.methodologyDetail: Step 1, define the clinical targets: the team reviewed 10 US and North American guidelines on secondary headache and pulled out 141 features from decision trees, algorithms and text. They kept only the features that many guidelines agreed on, giving 7 red flags: temporal arteritis, meningismus, systemic illness, papilledema, thunderclap onset, focal neurological deficit, and worst-ever headache at age 40 or older. Synonyms were merged into one concept per flag. Step 2, build the test set: a red-flag title search in PMC-Patients (167,000 summaries) gave 97 candidates; two headache specialists chose 70 adult cases, and added 20 cases from news and journal reports, for 90 vignettes. One specialist labelled each case with one or more flags; a second reviewed, and disagreements were settled by consensus. Thunderclap (22) and meningismus (20) were most common; focal deficits (4) least. Step 3, build the system in LangGraph: an orchestrator LLM reads the vignette and must return only JSON with the next agents, a reason of up to 30 words, and verbatim evidence quotes. Chosen specialist agents run in parallel and each answer yes or no with reasons. A deterministic fan-out function then checks for agents that should have run but did not, and calls them. All outputs, evidence and a full trace are stored in a shared state and aggregated. Seven robustness tricks (JSON repair, per-agent error isolation, logging and others) keep small models from crashing the pipeline. Step 4, prompts: QPrompt is one plain question; GPrompt adds a guideline definition, indicator phrases and a decision rule. Step 5, experiments: 5 local open-source LLMs (8B-30B) at temperature 0 and top-p 1, each in 4 set-ups (single vs multi-agent, QPrompt vs GPrompt). Step 6, scoring: per-case precision, recall and F1 between predicted and expert label sets, averaged over 90 cases. Multi-agent GPrompt was best for all models (top F1 0.605 with Qwen-30b). For a brain-tumour pathway, one could reuse the JSON router, fan-out safety net and trace, and add calibrated confidence and deferral to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, in-silico evaluation study on published case vignettes; no prospective patients. Institutions: University of Pittsburgh, UT Southwestern Medical Center (Dallas), Weill Cornell Medicine (New York). Country: USA.
papers.datasets: Gold-standard set of 90 adult secondary-headache cases (free-text vignettes). Sources: (1) 70 cases from PMC-Patients (a dataset of 167,000 patient summaries from PubMed Central case reports); a title search for red-flag terms returned 97 candidate cases; (2) 20 cases from publicly available online articles and peer-reviewed publications (PubMed, BMJ, AJNR, Elsevier). Two headache specialists selected cases. Labels (multi-label, one or more per case, plus 'none of the above' option): thunderclap headache 22 cases (24.4%), meningismus 20 (22.2%), systemic illness 18 (20.0%), papilledema 9 (10.0%), temporal arteritis 8 (8.9%), first/worst headache (age 40 or older) 8 (8.9%), focal neurologic deficits 4 (4.4%). Red-flag definitions came from 10 US/North American guidelines, from which 141 distinct features were extracted and reduced to 7 consistently flagged red flags. Explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond 'adult secondary headache case': Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Red flags built by manual review of 10 guidelines: 141 features extracted from decision trees, algorithms and narrative text, overlaps analysed, synonyms merged (e.g. 'neck stiffness', 'meningeal signs' as meningismus). Annotation: one headache specialist labelled every vignette; a second specialist reviewed all labels; disagreements resolved by consensus. No text normalisation or train/validation/test split reported, because no model was trained; all 90 cases are test cases.
papers.modelDetails: Built with LangGraph. Step 1, orchestrator agent: reads the vignette, extracts salient features, and outputs strict JSON {next: [agent list], why: reason of 30 words or fewer, evidence: [direct quotes from the note]}; valid agent names are thunderclap, meningismus, papilledema, temporal_arteritis, systemic_illness, focal_deficits, first_worst_headache; if none apply it returns an empty list. Unrelated agents are skipped. Step 2, routed specialist agents run in parallel; each returns a yes/no answer with an evidence-based explanation. Step 3, manual fan-out function checks which agents should have run and calls any non-executed agents (fixes routing and tool-call errors in light models). Step 4, aggregation into a structured output with per-agent classification, evidence, rationale and full execution trace. LangGraph state holds the patient note, message history, pending and completed agent lists, orchestrator JSON decisions, and a dictionary of agent outputs. Seven robustness strategies: manual fan-out; tracking pending vs completed calls; multi-strategy JSON parsing for malformed output; per-agent error isolation; multi-source extraction of agent outputs; fallback chain for file encodings; per-case trace logging of stdout. Prompting: QPrompt asks one direct question (e.g. 'Does this patient have papilledema? Answer Yes or No and explain why'); GPrompt adds guideline-based definition, list of key indicator phrases and an explicit decision rule (e.g. thunderclap = sudden severe headache peaking within 1 hour). Shared template asks agents to use only vignette information and cite text spans. The same LLM serves as orchestrator and specialists in each run. Single-LLM baseline classifies all 7 red flags in one step. No confidence score, uncertainty measure or deferral threshold.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning. Inference settings: temperature 0, top-p 1 for all models. Models: Qwen-30b, GPT-OSS-20b, Qwen-14b, Qwen-8b, Llama-3.1-8b, deployed locally. Hardware, run time and cost: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: 4 configurations x 5 LLMs: Single-LLM QPrompt, Single-LLM GPrompt, Multi-agent QPrompt, Multi-agent GPrompt. Each system outputs yes/no for all 7 red flags per case. Per-case multi-label comparison of predicted positive labels with expert labels gives TP, FP and FN; per-case precision, recall and F1 are computed and then averaged over the 90 cases (macro over cases, equal weight per case). Qualitative error example comparing Llama-3.1-8b and Qwen-30b outputs. No cross-validation, external validation or clinician reader study of system outputs.
papers.baselines: Single-LLM with question-based prompting (QPrompt); single-LLM with guideline-based prompting (GPrompt); multi-agent with QPrompt; each across 5 open-source LLMs.
papers.results: Precision / recall / F1. Qwen-30b: single QPrompt 0.498/0.806/0.542; single GPrompt 0.492/0.700/0.495; multi-agent QPrompt 0.559/0.717/0.563; multi-agent GPrompt 0.600/0.796/0.605 (best overall F1). GPT-OSS-20b: 0.420/0.606/0.474; 0.447/0.528/0.459; 0.441/0.674/0.469; multi-agent GPrompt 0.549/0.735/0.568. Qwen-14b: 0.534/0.689/0.568; 0.554/0.622/0.556; 0.543/0.672/0.530; multi-agent GPrompt 0.613/0.726/0.603 (text says the single-LLM QPrompt F1 was 0.558, table says 0.568). Qwen-8b: 0.543/0.644/0.557; 0.498/0.606/0.520; 0.380/0.528/0.376; multi-agent GPrompt 0.600/0.717/0.594. Llama-3.1-8b: 0.474/0.689/0.530; 0.451/0.667/0.508; 0.420/0.604/0.408; multi-agent GPrompt 0.550/0.704/0.519. Multi-agent GPrompt beat single-LLM GPrompt for all 5 models. Confidence intervals: Not reported.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals; inter-annotator agreement not reported, labels adjudicated by consensus of two specialists).
papers.availability: Test cases and gold-standard labels: https://github.com/PittNAIL/Jamia-Headache-Paper-Gold-Standard-Data-and-Result. MERLIN prototype app (Docker): https://hub.docker.com/r/yanshanwang/merlin.

papers.title: Large Language Model Based Multi-agents: A Survey of Progress and Challenges
papers.authors: Guo T, Chen X, Wang Y, Chang R, Pei S, Chawla NV, Wiest O, Zhang X
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Thirty-Third International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-24), Survey Track, pp. 8048-8057
papers.aim: To give a structured overview of LLM-based multi-agent (LLM-MA) systems: where they are used, how agents are profiled and communicate, how they gain skills, which tools and benchmarks exist, and what challenges remain.
papers.method: A narrative (non-systematic) survey. The authors propose a schema with four dimensions (agents-environment interface, agent profiling, agent communication, agent capability acquisition) and use it to classify 33 representative LLM-MA works in two application streams: problem solving and world simulation. They also list open-source frameworks, common datasets/benchmarks, and open challenges.
papers.result: No experiments. Main outputs are taxonomies: interface types (Sandbox, Physical, None); profiling methods (Pre-defined, Model-Generated, Data-Derived); communication paradigms (Cooperative, Debate, Competitive); communication structures (Layered, Decentralized, Centralized, Shared Message Pool); feedback sources (Environment, Agent interaction, Human, None); adjustment strategies (Memory, Self-Evolution, Dynamic Generation). Table 1 classifies 33 works; Table 2 lists about 30 datasets/benchmarks (e.g. MedQA, PubMedQA, MMLU used by MedAgents). Six challenges are named, including multi-modality, hallucination cascades, collective intelligence, scaling/orchestration, and evaluation.
papers.tools: Frameworks reviewed: MetaGPT, CAMEL, AutoGen (named as the three most popular open-source frameworks), plus dynamic collaboration frameworks (e.g. AgentVerse-type work). Benchmarks listed include HumanEval, MBPP, SoftwareDev, RoCoBench, MMLU, MedQA, PubMedQA, GSM8K, StrategyQA, MovieLens-1M. A maintained paper list on GitHub. No hardware (no experiments).
papers.gap: Most LLM-MA work is text-only; multi-modal agents (images, audio, video) are rare. Hallucination by one agent can spread to others, and controlling information flow between agents is unsolved. Joint adjustment of many agents for collective intelligence is open. Orchestration, scaling and resource use need new methods. Benchmarks test single agents in narrow tasks and miss emergent multi-agent behaviour. The survey does not cover uncertainty calibration, deferral to humans, privacy or clinical safety.
papers.relation: For O1 this survey gives the vocabulary and design space for the orchestration layer of the brain-tumour system. Our design can be described in its terms: pre-defined agent profiles (radiology, pathology, surgical-planning agents), a centralized structure with an orchestrator, cooperative plus debate paradigms, and human feedback from clinicians as the capability-acquisition route. Its stated challenges map directly to our thesis: the multi-modal gap supports adding an MRI imaging agent; the hallucination-cascade problem supports calibrated, selective deferral at each hand-off; and the lack of multi-agent benchmarks supports building a clinician-validated evaluation in Sri Lanka. It also points to MedAgents (MedQA, PubMedQA) as the main medical example.
papers.limitations: Narrative survey with no stated search strategy, inclusion criteria, number of screened papers or quality appraisal. Covers mostly 2023 work, so it is quickly outdated. Medical coverage is thin (one main medical work). No quantitative comparison across methods. Future directions given by the authors: multi-modal environments, hallucination control, collective intelligence and joint agent adjustment, scaling laws and orchestration, better benchmarks for emergent behaviour, links to cognitive science, symbolic AI, cybernetics and complex systems.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative survey, so the method is a classification scheme rather than an experiment. Step 1, background: the authors first describe what a single LLM agent can do (decision-making thought such as task decomposition and reflection, tool use, and short- and long-term memory) and contrast it with multi-agent systems, which add varied agent profiles, interaction between agents and collective decisions. Step 2, schema: they define four dimensions for dissecting any LLM-MA system. The agents-environment interface (sandbox, physical, or none) says what agents act on. Agent profiling (pre-defined, model-generated, data-derived) says how roles are written. Agent communication covers the paradigm (cooperative, debate, competitive), the structure (layered, decentralized, centralized, shared message pool) and the content (usually text). Capability acquisition covers feedback sources (environment, other agents, humans, none) and adjustment methods (memory retrieval, self-evolution, dynamic generation of new agents). Step 3, mapping: they place 33 representative works into Table 1 under two motivations, problem solving (software development, embodied robots, science experiments, science debate including medical diagnosis) and world simulation (society, gaming, psychology, economy, recommender systems, policy, disease spread), coding each work on all four dimensions. Step 4, resources: they name MetaGPT, CAMEL and AutoGen as the main open-source frameworks and list about 30 benchmarks in Table 2, including MedQA and PubMedQA for medical debate. Step 5, challenges: multi-modal settings, hallucination that cascades across agents, collective intelligence, scaling and orchestration, and evaluation of emergent behaviour. No search protocol or numbers of screened papers are given. For the PhD, the schema can be used as a checklist to describe and justify each design choice of the brain-tumour orchestrator: pre-defined clinical roles, a centralized orchestrator, cooperative-debate communication, clinician feedback, and explicit controls on information flow so that one agent's error does not cascade, which is where calibrated deferral fits.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative literature survey (IJCAI-24 Survey Track). Institutions: University of Notre Dame (USA), King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (Saudi Arabia), Southern University of Science and Technology (China), University of Massachusetts Boston (USA), independent researcher. No patients or prospective data.
papers.datasets: No primary data. The survey reviews 33 representative LLM-MA works in Table 1 (problem solving: software development, embodied agents, science experiments, science debate; world simulation: society, gaming, psychology, economy, recommender systems, policy making, disease propagation). Table 2 lists datasets/benchmarks by domain: software (HumanEval, MBPP, SoftwareDev), embodied AI (RoCoBench, Watch-And-Help, ThreeDWorld Transport, HM3D v0.2), science debate (MMLU, MedQA, PubMedQA, GSM8K, StrategyQA, Chess Move Validity), society (SOTOPIA, Gender Discrimination, Nuclear Energy), gaming (Werewolf, Avalon, Welfare Diplomacy, Overcooked-AI, Chameleon, Undercover), psychology (Ultimatum Game TE, Garden Path TE, Wisdom of Crowds TE), recommender (MovieLens-1M, Amazon review), policy (Board Connectivity). Search method and number of screened papers: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (survey). No search strings, databases, date range or screening counts are reported. Works were grouped every 3 months by topic to plot the rising trend of LLM-MA papers (Figure 1).
papers.modelDetails: Analytical schema, not a model. (1) Agents-environment interface: Sandbox (simulated, e.g. code interpreter, game rules), Physical (real robots), None (pure debate). (2) Agent profiling: Pre-defined by designers, Model-Generated by an LLM, Data-Derived from datasets. (3) Communication: paradigms Cooperative, Debate (agents argue to reach consensus), Competitive; structures Layered (hierarchical), Decentralized (peer-to-peer), Centralized (central agent coordinates, others talk through it), Shared Message Pool (MetaGPT publish-subscribe); content mostly text. (4) Capability acquisition: feedback from Environment, Agent interaction, Human (human-in-the-loop), or None; adjustment by Memory retrieval, Self-Evolution (changing goals/strategies, e.g. ProAgent, Learning through Communication), and Dynamic Generation of new agents on the fly. Example medical entry: MedAgents (Tang et al. 2023), interface None, pre-defined profiles (e.g. cardiology, surgery), Debate and Cooperative paradigms, Centralized and Decentralized structure, agent-interaction feedback, memory. Agent orchestration is named as a key challenge as agent numbers grow. No uncertainty, deferral or threshold rules discussed.
papers.training: Not applicable (survey; no training).
papers.evaluation: Not applicable. The survey discusses evaluation only as a challenge: current studies evaluate individual agents in narrow scenarios and lack comprehensive benchmarks for emergent multi-agent behaviour and for domains such as science teams and economic modelling.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (survey). Single-agent LLM systems are contrasted conceptually with multi-agent systems (decision-making thought, tool use, memory).
papers.results: Not applicable (no quantitative results). Key descriptive outputs: 33 works classified in Table 1 across 4 dimensions; about 30 datasets/benchmarks in Table 2; MetaGPT, CAMEL and AutoGen identified as the three most popular open-source frameworks; 6 challenge areas identified.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no statistical analysis).
papers.availability: Maintained paper list: https://github.com/taichengguo/LLM_MultiAgents_Survey_Papers. Preprint: arXiv:2402.01680.

papers.title: MAM: Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Modal Medical Diagnosis via Role-Specialized Collaboration
papers.authors: Zhou Y, Song L, Shen J
papers.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025, pages 25319-25333
papers.aim: To build a modular multi-agent LLM framework that splits multimodal medical diagnosis into specialised roles, so knowledge can be updated per module instead of retraining one unified model.
papers.method: Five LLM-based roles (General Practitioner, Specialist Team, Radiologist, Medical Assistant, Director) work in a fixed workflow: triage and referral, problem decomposition and anonymisation, web retrieval and summary, opinion generation and discussion, Director synthesis, and unanimous yes/no voting with up to 3 discussion rounds. It is a zero-shot, prompt-based pipeline built on existing open medical LLMs and evaluated on 10 public text, image, audio and video datasets.
papers.result: MAM beat modality-specific baselines on all datasets, with gains of 18% to 365% over baselines. Brain Tumor MRI accuracy was 97.9% vs 80.2% for HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B. NIH Chest X-ray 58.6% vs 12.6%; DeepLesion 35.1% vs 11.1%; PubMedQA 84.0% vs 48.5%; MedQA 40.0% vs 30.8%; Heartbeat 64.0% vs 34.9%; MedVidQA 74.3% vs 55.3%.
papers.tools: Medichat-Llama3-8B (text), HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B (image), Qwen-Audio-Chat (audio), VideoLLaMA2-7B (video); Google API for retrieval; prompt templates in Appendix B; code at https://github.com/yczhou001/MAM. Hardware not reported.
papers.gap: No real clinical validation. Retrieval recall is low (12.1% to 34.0%). There is no calibrated uncertainty or deferral to clinicians; consensus is only unanimous voting. More roles (5) reduced accuracy, so the best team design is unclear.
papers.relation: For O1, MAM is a close template for a role-specialised brain-tumour pathway: a triage agent, a radiologist agent, specialist agents and a director that synthesises. It already reports 97.9% on a public brain-tumour MRI dataset (Bhuvaji 2020). Our framework can reuse its triage-referral-discussion-vote loop, but must add calibrated confidence, a deferral rule to clinicians, local (non-Google) retrieval for privacy, and clinician validation in Sri Lanka.
papers.limitations: Performance is limited by the base LLMs; their biases and knowledge gaps can pass through the system. No real-world clinical validation because of cost and expert effort. Small evaluation subsets (200 to 461 cases per dataset). Retrieval from the open web, not a hospital database. Future work: better knowledge retrieval and evaluation in real clinical settings.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first ran a pilot study. They used open models per modality: Medichat-Llama3-8B for text, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B for images, Qwen-Audio-Chat for audio and VideoLLaMA2-7B for video. On 10 public datasets (200 to 461 cases each) they compared a plain prompt with a prompt that gives the model a physician role. Role prompts raised accuracy on every dataset, for example Brain Tumor MRI from 80.2% to 98.2%. They then generated three diagnoses per case and showed that the model picks the right one more often than chance (PathVQA 91.7% vs 50.0%). Based on this, they built MAM. A General Practitioner agent classifies the input with short single-word prompts (for images: MRI, CT, X-Ray, pathology; and body part such as brain). A role-generation prompt then creates a Specialist Team for that disease type. The specialists split the question into sub-problems and remove identifying details. A Medical Assistant agent sends these sub-problems to the Google API and summarises the results. Each specialist writes assessment steps, three possible answers with reasons and a conclusion; a Radiologist agent reads the image. A Director agent writes a summary of agreements and disagreements. Each specialist then votes yes or no. Only a unanimous vote ends the loop; otherwise discussion repeats, up to 3 rounds. The Director gives the final answer. There is no training. Evaluation is plain accuracy on fixed test subsets (for example 394 Brain Tumor test cases), compared with 15 baseline models. An ablation adds roles, discussion and retrieval in turn (Brain Tumor 80.2, 92.4, 97.0, 97.9). The authors also vary rounds (best at 2 to 3) and number of roles (best at 3; 5 is worse) and measure retrieval recall (12.1% to 34.0%). To adapt this, a PhD student could keep the triage, specialist, radiologist and director roles, replace Google search with a local guideline store, and replace unanimous voting with a calibrated confidence score that triggers deferral to a neurosurgeon or radiologist.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark study of a zero-shot multi-agent LLM framework on public datasets. Includes an empirical pilot study (role assignment and diagnostic discernment), main comparison, ablation, consistency, discussion-round and role-number sensitivity, retrieval recall, and a case study. Institution: SKL-IOTSC, CIS, University of Macau, China (Macau SAR). No patients recruited.
papers.datasets: Text: MedQA (200 English four-option multiple-choice questions); PubMedQA (200 question-answer pairs). Image: Brain Tumor MRI classification (Bhuvaji et al., 2020; test set, 394 cases); DeepLesion CT (225 cases from 9 categories); NIH Chest X-rays (215 cases); PathVQA (200 cases); PMC-VQA (200 pairs). Audio: Heartbeat / PASCAL Classifying Heart Sounds Challenge 2011 (461 instances, clinical trial data); SoundDr respiratory sounds (240 instances). Video: MedVidQA Temporal Segment Prediction test set (284 data points). Class counts per dataset are not reported. Inclusion/exclusion: subsets selected by the authors; selection rules not reported. For the discernment pilot (Table 2) data were filtered to instances where at least one of three generated diagnoses was correct.
papers.preprocessing: No training, so no train/validation/test split; only evaluation subsets are used. MedVidQA was converted into yes/no questions using original and alternative video segments. The Specialist Team decomposes each question into sub-problems and anonymises them before retrieval. A multimodal description prompt asks the model to describe the input in 100 words. Image resolution, normalisation and augmentation are not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Input M = {m1..mk} modalities. Step 1: General Practitioner G classifies disease type d = CG(M) with single-word prompts (image type: X-Ray, CT, MRI, Pathology, Biomedical; body part: brain, bone, abdomen, mediastinum, liver, lung, kidney, soft tissue, pelvis; audio: Cardiovascular, Respiratory; video: Sports, Rehabilitation, Emergency; text: 21 subject types such as Anaesthesia, Radiology, Surgery, Unknown) and refers to a Specialist Team S = RG(d) generated by a role-generation prompt. Step 2: Specialists decompose and anonymise the problem P = DS(M). Step 3: Medical Assistant retrieves information Ir from Google API using P and summarises it to Is. Step 4: each specialist gives opinion Osi = Diag(M, Is) with three possible answers plus reasoning and a conclusion; the Radiologist gives ORad = Diag(M). Step 5: the Director synthesises report Rp from all opinions and Is (summary lists answers, agreements, disagreements, conclusions). Step 6: each specialist votes vi in {0,1}; consensus only if V = n (unanimous). If not, discussion repeats, up to a maximum of 3 rounds. A review prompt checks for reasoning errors, redundancy or invalid outputs (yes/no). Step 7: the Director gives the final diagnosis Dfinal = Diagnosis(Rp). The case study uses 3 expert roles. No numeric confidence, calibration or deferral threshold is used.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning; zero-shot prompting of existing models. Optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size, decoding temperature, hardware and run time are not reported.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on each dataset subset compared with modality-matched baselines. Ablation adds functions step by step: Direct, +Roles, +Discussion, +Retrieval (full MAM). Consistency = percentage of instances where MAM's final prediction matches a correct Direct prediction. Sensitivity to discussion rounds (1 to 3) and number of roles (1 to 5) shown in figures. Retrieval recall = proportion of instances where retrieved content contains the correct answer; Answer Correct = accuracy when retrieved content contains the answer. No external validation, no cross-validation, no reader study.
papers.baselines: Text: LLaMA-7B, DAPT-7B, MedAlpaca-7B, AdaptLLM-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, Medichat-Llama3-8B. Image: LLaVA-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, LLaVA-Med-7B, Qilin-Med-VL-13B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B. Audio: Qwen-Audio-Chat. Video: LLaVA-Next-Video-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, VideoLLaMA2-7B.
papers.results: Pilot (Direct vs Assigned Roles): Brain Tumor 80.2 vs 98.2; NIH 12.6 vs 50.7; PubMedQA 48.5 vs 87.0; gains 5.0 (PMC-VQA) to 38.5 (PubMedQA). Discernment (Expectation vs Reasoning): PathVQA 50.0 vs 91.7; Brain Tumor 55.1 vs 73.9. Text: MedQA MAM 40.0 vs Medichat-Llama3-8B 30.8 (best other AdaptLLM-7B 30.5); PubMedQA 84.0 vs 48.5 (AdaptLLM 56.8). Image (MAM vs HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B): PathVQA 47.6 vs 40.1; PMC-VQA 32.5 vs 24.0; DeepLesion 35.1 vs 11.1; NIH 58.6 vs 12.6; Brain Tumor 97.9 vs 80.2 (Qilin-Med-VL-13B 80.6). Audio: Heartbeat 64.0 vs 34.9; SoundDr 47.9 vs 25.0. Video: MedVidQA 74.3 vs 55.3. Ablation Brain Tumor: Direct 80.2, +Roles 92.4, +Discussion 97.0, +Retrieval 97.9; NIH 12.6, 36.0, 38.6, 58.6. Consistency Brain Tumor 97.5. Retrieval recall: DeepLesion 31.7, Heartbeat 34.0, NIH 12.1; Answer Correct 53.4, 58.8, 46.2. Best number of roles was 3; 5 roles reduced performance. No confidence intervals.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests, no confidence intervals, single run reported).
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/yczhou001/MAM. Data: public datasets (MedQA, PubMedQA, Brain Tumor MRI on Kaggle by Bhuvaji et al., DeepLesion, NIH ChestX-ray, PathVQA, PMC-VQA, PASCAL Heartbeat, SoundDr, MedVidQA). Exact subset IDs not reported in the paper.

papers.title: MedChat: A Multi-Agent Framework for Multimodal Diagnosis with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Liu PR, Bansal S, Dinh J, Pawar A, Satishkumar R, Desai S, Gupta N, Wang X, Hu S
papers.venue: IEEE MIPR 2025 (8th International Conference on Multimedia Information Processing and Retrieval)
papers.aim: To build a multi-agent system that turns retinal fundus images into clinical glaucoma reports. Several role-specific LLM agents write sub-reports and a director agent merges them, to reduce hallucination compared with a single generalist LLM.
papers.method: A pretrained SwinV2 classifier gives a glaucoma probability, which is mapped to four verbal grades, and a pretrained SegFormer segments optic disc and cup to compute the cup-to-disc ratio. These outputs plus optional clinician notes form a shared prompt. GPT-4.1 picks clinical roles, one GPT-4.1 agent per role writes a sub-report, and a GPT-4.1 director agent writes the final report. A web platform adds PDF export and follow-up chat.
papers.result: No quantitative results are reported. The paper shows one qualitative case from Harvard-FairVision with four agents (ophthalmologist, optometrist, pharmacist, glaucoma specialist) and a director report. Formal evaluation of diagnostic quality, coherence and clinical accuracy is left to future work.
papers.tools: Pretrained SwinV2-tiny glaucoma classifier (Hugging Face pamixsun/swinv2_tiny_for_glaucoma_classification); pretrained SegFormer optic disc/cup segmentation (pamixsun/segformer_for_optic_disc_cup_segmentation); OpenAI GPT-4.1 via API for role selection, role agents, director agent and chatbot; Python backend with RESTful API and session IDs; JavaScript/HTML frontend; PDF report export. Compute support from NAIRR Pilot and TACC Lonestar6.
papers.gap: No quantitative evaluation, no clinician reader study, no uncertainty handling or deferral, no clinician feedback loop, agents are not fine-tuned, and all agents share one prompt, so their views are very similar.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), MedChat is a simple pattern for passing results from imaging models to text agents. Vision outputs are turned into words (probability to grade, mask to ratio), role agents work on them, and a director merges the sub-reports. This can be adapted for brain-tumour MRI: classifier and segmentation outputs feed role agents such as neuroradiologist, neurosurgeon and oncologist. The thresholded verbal grades (p<0.2, 0.2-0.5, 0.5-0.9, >=0.9) are a basic way to express confidence. But the paper has no calibration, no deferral to clinicians and no evaluation. Our PhD must add these parts.
papers.limitations: Authors list: LLM agents are general models without domain fine-tuning; no feedback loop for clinician corrections; shared prompt leads to high consensus and low diversity of reasoning; without clinical notes the reports are generic. Future work: fine-tune agents on glaucoma case reports and guidelines; human-in-the-loop refinement; reinforcement learning such as Group Relative Policy Optimization; role-specific prompt subsets; more CAD modules (e.g. blood vessel segmentor). Additional: only a single demonstration case and no metrics.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedChat is a pipeline that links image models to several LLM agents. The input is one retinal fundus image and an optional clinical note. First, a pretrained SwinV2-tiny classifier (from Hugging Face) outputs a glaucoma probability p. The authors do not use p directly. They map it to words with fixed thresholds: below 0.2 is 'no glaucoma', 0.2 to 0.5 is 'possible glaucoma', 0.5 to 0.9 is 'likely glaucoma', and 0.9 or more is 'glaucoma detected'. Second, a pretrained SegFormer model labels each pixel as optic disc, optic cup or background. From the two binary masks they compute the cup-to-disc ratio as the square root of cup pixels divided by cup plus disc pixels, and write it as a sentence (for example 'approximately 0.62'). Third, they build a core prompt. The classifier is called Network A and the segmentor Network B, as in ChatCAD. The clinical note (history, medicines, exam findings) is appended when it exists. Fourth, GPT-4.1 is asked which clinical roles fit the case. In the example it chose ophthalmologist, optometrist, pharmacist and glaucoma specialist. A separate GPT-4.1 agent is created for each role. Each gets the same core prompt plus an instruction to stay within its specialty, avoid repetition, not mention Network A or B, and write as part of a formal report. Fifth, a director GPT-4.1 agent receives all sub-reports. It is told to summarise findings, give reasoning and recommendations, fix small contradictions and not cite the sub-reports. Finally, a Python REST backend with session IDs and a JavaScript web frontend show the report. Users can chat with a GPT-4.1 bot about it and download a PDF with the segmentation overlay. Evaluation is one qualitative case from the Harvard-FairVision dataset only. To adapt this for brain tumours, swap in an MRI tumour classifier and segmentor, verbalise calibrated probabilities and tumour volumes, and add a deferral rule and a clinician evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: System design and demonstration paper (engineering prototype). Purdue University and University at Albany, USA. Retrospective use of one public dataset image for demonstration. No prospective or clinical study.
papers.datasets: Harvard-FairVision dataset (public; retinal fundus images with clinical notes) used only for the example fundus image and clinical note in Figures 1 and 6. Number of images used for evaluation: Not reported (a single demonstration case is shown). Classes, counts and inclusion/exclusion criteria: Not reported. The pretrained classifier and segmentor training data: Not reported in this paper.
papers.preprocessing: Fundus image is passed to the pretrained classifier and segmentor; resizing and normalisation: Not reported. Classifier probability p is discretised into four verbal grades. Segmentation map is split into binary optic cup and optic disc masks. Train/validation/test split: Not applicable (no model training; pretrained models used). Augmentation: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: SwinV2 classifier C(X) outputs glaucoma probability p. Grade mapping: p<0.2 no glaucoma; 0.2<=p<0.5 possible glaucoma; 0.5<=p<0.9 likely glaucoma; p>=0.9 glaucoma detected. Step 2: SegFormer S(X) labels each pixel optic disc, optic cup or background. CDR = sqrt(|M_cup| / (|M_cup| + |M_disc|)), with pixel counts of the masks; verbalised as e.g. 'optic-cup-to-disc ratio is approximately 0.62'. Step 3: core prompt = 'Network A suggests ...' (classifier) + 'Network B estimates ...' (segmentor) + optional clinician notes (history, medication, exam findings), following ChatCAD naming. Step 4: GPT-4.1 is asked to identify clinically relevant roles (e.g. ophthalmologist, optometrist, pharmacist, glaucoma specialist); one GPT-4.1 agent per role gets the core prompt plus instructions to only cover its specialty, avoid overlap, not mention Network A or B, and write in professional report style. Agents run independently. Step 5: director agent (GPT-4.1) gets concatenated sub-reports and is told to summarise key findings, give diagnostic reasoning and recommendations, resolve minor contradictions, and not mention sources or sub-reports. Step 6: GPT-4.1 chatbot with retained conversation history answers follow-up questions. No uncertainty-based deferral rule.
papers.training: No training. Pretrained classifier and segmentor are used as-is; LLM agents are general GPT-4.1 without fine-tuning. Temperature, token limits and hardware for inference: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative demonstration only: one fundus image and clinical note from Harvard-FairVision are run through the pipeline and the sub-reports and final report are shown (Fig. 6). No metrics, no reader study, no cross-validation, no external validation.
papers.baselines: None compared experimentally. Related systems discussed: ChatCAD, ChatCAD+, OphthUS-GPT, Med-MLLM, MDLM, ViGPT2.
papers.results: No quantitative results. Qualitative: ophthalmologist agent noted structural damage and suggested surgery for left eye; optometrist stressed follow-up testing and imaging; pharmacist reviewed medications and side-effect risks; glaucoma specialist gave severity assessment and multi-step plan. Director report emphasised advanced glaucoma in left eye, escalation of treatment and possible surgery.
papers.statistics: Not reported
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/Purdue-M2/MedChat. Models: Hugging Face pamixsun/swinv2_tiny_for_glaucoma_classification and pamixsun/segformer_for_optic_disc_cup_segmentation. Data: Harvard-FairVision (public).

papers.title: MedAgent-Pro: Towards Evidence-based Multi-modal Medical Diagnosis via Reasoning Agentic Workflow
papers.authors: Wang Z, Wu J, Cai L, Low CH, Yang X, Li Q, Jin Y
papers.aim: To make multimodal medical diagnosis by vision-language models evidence-based and step by step, instead of one-hop question answering. The workflow uses retrieved guidelines to plan, specialist tools to measure indicators, and a check of each step before continuing.
papers.method: A hierarchical agentic workflow with GPT-4o as the core VLM. At disease level, a RAG agent retrieves guideline text from a MedlinePlus knowledge base and the VLM turns it into a JSON diagnostic plan of tool-calling steps. At patient level, the VLM selects runnable steps, calls segmentation and coding tools for quantitative indicators, checks the reliability of each step (Continue/Terminate/Complete), and combines indicators with guideline-based weights into a risk score compared with a threshold.
papers.result: Glaucoma (REFUGE2): bAcc 90.4%, F1 76.4%, AUC 95.1% vs GPT-4o bAcc 56.4%, F1 21.1%. Heart disease (MITEA): bAcc 77.8%, F1 72.3% vs GPT-4o 56.8%, 28.1%. NEJM overall accuracy 81.7% vs MDAgent 73.8% and GPT-4o 70.9%. MIMIC chest X-ray average bAcc 72.0% vs GPT-4o 58.3%. Clinicians rated it higher than other VLMs on five quality dimensions.
papers.tools: GPT-4o (core VLM; also used by baseline agent systems); LangChain for the RAG agent; vector database over MedlinePlus (1,000+ diseases, 4,000+ articles); tools: Medical SAM Adapter, MedSAM, Cellpose (segmentation), Maira-2 (grounding), LLM coding tools such as Copilot; plan stored as JSON with predefined Python functions. VisionUnite used in ablation. Hardware: Not reported.
papers.gap: Depends on the availability of visual tools for each domain; qualitative steps still rely on a hallucination-prone VLM; the step reliability check is a VLM judgement, not a calibrated uncertainty; no deferral to clinicians; no confidence intervals or statistical tests; human evaluation details are thin.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this is a strong template for traceable, multi-step diagnostic orchestration. A guideline-retrieved plan is stored as JSON steps (object, tool, result). Tools are called step by step, and each step can stop the pipeline when its output is judged unreliable (Terminate). The final decision is a weighted risk score against a threshold. For brain tumours, the plan could come from WHO CNS 2021 and NCCN guidance. The tools could be MRI tumour segmentation, volume and midline-shift measurement. Our project should replace the VLM-based Terminate check with calibrated uncertainty that sends the case to a clinician.
papers.limitations: Authors: framework depends on visual tools, which are limited in some domains; qualitative analysis relies on VLMs that are inconsistent and hallucinate. Additional: zero-shot GPT-4o only (closed API, privacy concern for patient data); MITEA baselines needed 3D-to-2D slice sampling; number of clinicians and cases in human evaluation not reported; no statistical testing.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedAgent-Pro uses GPT-4o as its main reasoning model and does not train anything. It runs in two levels. At the disease level, the authors built a knowledge base from MedlinePlus, with over 1,000 diseases and over 4,000 expert-reviewed articles. Each document was cut into chunks and stored in a vector database built with LangChain. Each document also got a one-sentence summary used as an index. For a disease query, the RAG agent first removes unrelated documents by keyword search on the summaries. It then takes the top 5 chunks by vector search. GPT-4o summarises these chunks into a procedural guideline and a list of clinical indicators. Next, GPT-4o reads short text descriptions of the available tools (segmentation models such as MedSAM and Medical SAM Adapter, Cellpose, Maira-2 for grounding, and a coding tool). It writes a plan as a JSON list of steps, each with input type, tool and output type. At the patient level, GPT-4o keeps only the steps whose input data is present. It then runs them in order, for example optic cup and disc segmentation, then code that computes vertical cup-to-disc ratio (0.624 in the example) and rim thickness. After every step, GPT-4o judges if the output is reliable. If not, the chain stops (Terminate). If yes, the output feeds the next step (Continue). An output that is a final indicator is marked Complete. GPT-4o then gives guideline-based weights to the indicators, for example 0.3, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.2. It sums weight times value into a risk score and compares it with a threshold, for example 0.65 against 0.4. Evaluation was zero-shot on REFUGE2 (glaucoma), MITEA (3D echo heart disease), 442 MIMIC chest X-ray cases from 100 patients (12 findings) and 992 NEJM cases. Metrics were bAcc, F1, accuracy and AUC. There were also an additive ablation and clinician ratings on a 1-5 scale. MedAgent-Pro reached 90.4% bAcc on glaucoma against 56.4% for GPT-4o.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark study on public datasets plus clinician rating of outputs. Institutions: National University of Singapore, University of Oxford, Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), National University of Defense Technology, Second Affiliated Hospital Zhejiang University School of Medicine (Singapore, UK, China).
papers.datasets: (1) REFUGE2: retinal fundus images for glaucoma diagnosis (binary); test size Not reported. (2) MITEA: 3D echocardiography for heart disease diagnosis (e.g. dilated cardiomyopathy, amyloidosis); size Not reported. (3) MIMIC (chest X-ray): 442 cases from 100 patients sampled; each case has up to 12 thoracic findings (atelectasis, cardiomegaly, consolidation, edema, enlarged cardiomediastinum, fracture, lung lesion, lung opacity, pleural effusion, pneumonia, pneumothorax, support devices). (4) NEJM image challenge database: 992 real diagnostic cases, multiple-choice, over 10 anatomical regions, 10 imaging modalities and 50 diseases; sub-groups cell imaging, chest X-ray, CT and MRI, ophthalmology imaging. Knowledge base: MedlinePlus, over 1,000 diseases and conditions and over 4,000 expert-reviewed articles. Inclusion/exclusion criteria: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Knowledge base: each MedlinePlus document is split into chunks and indexed in a vector database; a one-sentence summary per document is pre-generated as an index. For baseline VLMs on 3D MITEA echocardiography, three random slices are given as input, repeated 10 times and averaged. No model training, so no train/validation/test split (zero-shot evaluation). Image resizing and normalisation: Not reported. Simulated noisy segmentation masks were used in an ablation.
papers.modelDetails: Disease level: (1) RAG agent R receives a disease query, filters documents by keyword search over summaries, then vector retrieval gives the top-5 chunks. (2) The VLM summarises them into a guideline G = V(R(K)) and lists clinical indicators I = {I1..Im}. (3) With tool descriptions A (one per tool in toolset T, e.g. 'This model segments the optic cup in a fundus image'), the VLM writes a plan P = {P1..Pn}; each step is a key-value triple (input data property ko, tool t as a predefined Python function, output data property kr), stored as JSON. Patient level: (4) Orchestration: the VLM keeps only steps whose input type exists in the patient data D (e.g. skip OCT or visual field if only a fundus image is given). (5) Quantitative analysis: tools such as segmentation of optic cup and disc, then a coding tool computes vertical cup-to-disc ratio (example 0.624) and rim thickness against the ISNT rule. (6) Evidence-based reasoning: after each step the status s is Complete if the output is an indicator, Terminate if it is not an indicator and the VLM state function phi judges it unreliable, or Continue if it is reliable (output becomes input to the next step). (7) Decision: the VLM gives guideline-based weights W to the completed indicators; risk score rho = sum of w_i times v_i; diagnosis if rho exceeds threshold theta. Example: weights for vCDR, rim thickness, peripapillary atrophy and disc haemorrhage = [0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2], score 0.65 > threshold 0.4 means glaucoma.
papers.training: No training; zero-shot use of GPT-4o and pretrained tools. Optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size, hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Zero-shot evaluation on four datasets. Metrics: balanced accuracy (bAcc) and F1 for REFUGE2, MITEA and MIMIC (per sub-task bAcc for 12 MIMIC findings); accuracy for NEJM multiple-choice; AUC for comparison with REFUGE2 challenge leaderboard. Ablations: adding planning, quantitative analysis, and evidence-based reasoning in turn; replacing GPT-4o qualitative analysis with VisionUnite; simulated noisy segmentation masks; structured fusion vs flat fusion for decision. Human evaluation: (a) count of plan steps for 12 chest X-ray tasks compared with thoracic clinicians' ranking of difficulty from 1 to 12; (b) clinical experts rated outputs for glaucoma and chest X-ray on relevance, comprehensiveness, clinical reliability, reasoning coherence and language clarity on a 1-5 scale. Number of raters and cases: Not reported.
papers.baselines: General VLMs: GPT-4o, Janus-Pro-7B, LLaVA-Med, BioMedCLIP, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Medical agent systems (all using GPT-4o): MedAgents (ACL 2024), MMedAgent (EMNLP 2024), MDAgents (NeurIPS 2024). Task-specific: REFUGE2 winners VUNO EYE TEAM (AUC 88.3) and MIG (AUC 87.6); RetiZero, VisionUnite (ophthalmology); Maira-2, CheXagent (chest X-ray).
papers.results: Glaucoma (REFUGE2) bAcc/F1: MedAgent-Pro 90.4/76.4; GPT-4o 56.4/21.1; Janus-Pro 53.4/13.3; LLaVA-Med 50.0/0.0; BioMedCLIP 58.1/21.3; Qwen2.5-VL 54.3/16.3; InternVL2.5 51.8/13.8; MedAgents 52.1/8.9; MMedAgent 52.4/16.3; MDAgents 56.8/22.2; VisionUnite 85.8/73.1; RetiZero 50.8/18.4. AUC: MedAgent-Pro 95.1 vs VUNO 88.3, MIG 87.6. Heart disease (MITEA) bAcc/F1: MedAgent-Pro 77.8/72.3; GPT-4o 56.8/28.1; MDAgents 57.2/30.3; MMedAgent 55.0/26.7. NEJM accuracy (all/cell/chest X-ray/CT and MRI/ophthalmology): MedAgent-Pro 81.7/90.5/69.1/72.7/89.7; MDAgents 73.8/79.6/52.9/67.3/73.0; MMedAgent 71.7/73.8/56.4/65.3/70.5; GPT-4o 70.9/74.6/54.5/63.4/70.5. MIMIC average bAcc: MedAgent-Pro 72.0 vs GPT-4o 58.3, BioMedCLIP 57.9, Qwen 55.2, CheXagent 69.1, Maira-2 64.1; e.g. atelectasis 85.5, support devices 89.2. Ablation (glaucoma bAcc/F1; heart bAcc/F1): none 56.4/21.1, 56.8/28.1; +planning 75.9/36.5, 63.3/45.9; +quantitative 88.5/71.0, 73.4/66.6; +evidence reasoning 90.4/76.4, 77.8/72.3. VisionUnite for qualitative steps: 92.9/79.1. Structured fusion beat flat fusion at all indicator counts (figure only). Clinician ratings higher than other VLMs on all five dimensions (figure only).
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals; MITEA baseline results are the mean over 10 random slice samplings).
