Tool training data (from cited works): CheXinstruct 8.5M samples (CheXagent), 600K PMC-15M pairs plus 60K instructions (LLaVA-Med), 1,570,263 image-mask pairs (MedSAM), ChestX-Det 3,578 NIH images with 13 classes, 223K CheXpert Plus reports, NIH/CheXpert/MIMIC-CXR/PadChest for the 18-class DenseNet-121.
papers.preprocessing: Eurorad cases were preprocessed (with help acknowledged) and filtered to cases with chest X-rays and complete clinical documentation. Questions were made by prompting GPT-4o per case and per question type (five types: detailed finding analysis, pattern recognition and relations, spatial understanding, clinical decision making, diagnostic characterization) to write a six-choice question verifiable from the case findings and discussion. GPT-4o then checked each question for six-choice structure with one correct answer, grounding in the case, and verifiability; failing questions were removed, plus a further quality check removing ungrounded or incomplete questions. Image resolution and normalisation for tools: Not reported (tools used with official configurations). No training, so no train/validation/test split; all benchmarks used as test sets.
papers.modelDetails: Algorithm 1 (ReAct): inputs are user query Q, CXR images I, tool set T, memory M and maximum time tmax. Step 0: record start time and observe Q, I and M. Loop while time is below tmax: (1) LLM reasons over state and memory; (2) if more user input is needed, return a prompt to the user; (3) if an answer can be given, return it; (4) otherwise select tools, run independent tools in parallel, add (thoughts, tools, results) to memory and observe again. If time runs out, return a timeout response. Tool calls are structured JSON with arguments such as image path and text prompt. Tool errors are returned as tool messages so the LLM can try another tool, ask the user or state limits. Memory caches tool outputs to avoid repeat work. Tools can be quantized and placed on CPU or GPU. New tools need only a class definition of input/output and capability; no retraining. Implemented as a LangGraph state machine with reasoning and action nodes and conditional edges. Value of tmax: Not reported. No confidence threshold or uncertainty-based deferral.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning of MedRAX; all tools are pre-trained models used off the shelf. Deployed on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU with GPT-4o as backbone. Answer parsing by regex to extract the letter choice; unclear responses, errors or timeouts retried up to 3 times; still-invalid answers counted wrong. Temperature, runtime per query and cost: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Four benchmarks. (1) ChestAgentBench: accuracy over 2,500 six-choice questions, reported per category and overall. (2) CheXbench: accuracy on 238 VQA (Rad-Restruct, SLAKE) and 380 OpenI fine-grained image-text reasoning questions. (3) MIMIC-CXR report generation on 3,858 test images: CheXbert-based micro F1 and macro F1 for 14 observations (mF1-14, MF1-14) and 5 key findings (cardiomegaly, edema, consolidation, atelectasis, pleural effusion; mF1-5, MF1-5). (4) SLAKE VQA on 114 CXR samples: exact-match accuracy and recall of ground-truth words. Baselines run with official implementations; literature baselines for benchmarks 3 and 4 taken from the M4CXR paper. Two qualitative case studies (Eurorad cases 17576 and 16703). No external clinical validation or radiologist comparison.
papers.baselines: Run by authors: LLaVA-Med (LLaVA-13B), CheXagent (Vicuna-13B based), GPT-4o, Llama-3.2-90B Vision. From literature (M4CXR paper): RadFM, MAIRA-1, LLaVA-Rad, Med-PaLM M 84B, M4CXR, CheXagent.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no confidence intervals, significance tests or inter-rater agreement).
papers.availability: Code and data: https://github.com/bowang-lab/MedRAX. ChestAgentBench released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

papers.title: CXRAgent: Director-Orchestrated Multi-Stage Reasoning for Chest X-Ray Interpretation
papers.authors: Lou J, Yang Y, Yu Z, Fu Z, Han W, Huang Q, Yu J
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (accepted version read: arXiv:2510.21324v2)
papers.aim: To build a chest X-ray (CXR) agent in which a central director LLM calls many CXR tools, checks each tool output against visual evidence, and then forms a virtual expert team, so that conflicting tool outputs are resolved and the final answer is evidence-backed.
papers.method: A multimodal LLM director (GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-Max) runs three stages: ReAct tool invocation with an Evidence-driven Validator (EDV) that lists supporting and refuting image evidence and rates each tool claim High, Medium or Low confidence; diagnostic planning that picks one of four collaboration modes (Skip, Relay, Dispatch, Probe); and collaborative decision-making where a recruited team of role agents answers sub-tasks before the director synthesises a final answer from team output and memory. It was tested on CheXbench, Medical-CXR-VQA and MIMIC-CXR report generation, with ablations and a blinded radiologist study.
papers.result: CXRAgent (Qwen) reached 67.0% overall accuracy on CheXbench and 75.6% on Medical-CXR-VQA; CXRAgent (GPT-4o) reached 66.3% and 71.7%. On MIMIC-CXR report generation (GPT-4o director) it got RaTEScore 0.569, GREEN 0.359, RadGraph 0.251 and LLMScore 3.267. EDV raised accuracy by 1.9 to 5.7 points under simulated 3:1 conflicting tool outputs. Five radiologists preferred CXRAgent reports on average 65.8% (completeness), 67.2% (accuracy) and 69.6% (clinical usability) of pairwise comparisons.
papers.tools: Director LLMs: GPT-4o, Qwen-VL-Max (low-temperature decoding). CXR tools: MedGemma-4B (Gemma3 with SigLIP encoder), LLaVA-Rad, CheXagent, LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-2, MedVLM-R1. ReAct framework. Hardware: two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Metrics toolkit for RaTEScore, GREEN and RadGraph-F1; GPT-4o for LLMScore and for ranking case complexity.
papers.gap: Confidence from EDV is a qualitative LLM judgement (High/Medium/Low), not a calibrated probability, and there is no formal deferral rule to a clinician. Only chest X-ray. Heavy compute and large LLM needs. No prospective or real-workflow validation.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), CXRAgent is the closest design to our planned orchestrator: a director agent that validates each tool hand-off (EDV), re-invokes alternative tools on low confidence, chooses a team mode by case difficulty, and issues a cautious interpretation that flags discrepancies for the radiologist. For brain-tumour MRI, we could reuse EDV as a hand-off check between segmentation, classification and surgical-planning agents, but replace the qualitative High/Medium/Low label with calibrated uncertainty and an explicit threshold for clinician deferral. The paper itself notes GPU and cost barriers in low-resource or rural hospitals, which supports our focus on lighter models for Sri Lanka.
papers.limitations: Multi-stage orchestration, iterative tool reasoning and EDV add computation and latency compared with single-loop agents; quantization may be needed. Needs a large multimodal LLM and several tools, with substantial GPU memory, which may not be available in low-resource or rural hospitals. Must meet regulatory needs for traceability, auditability, fail-safe mechanisms, physician oversight, privacy and stability. Failure case shows mislocalised pleural effusion and missed opacification due to overlapping appearance of pathologies. Future work: Not explicitly listed beyond these deployment challenges.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built an inference-only agent with a multimodal LLM as director (GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-Max, low temperature, on two RTX A6000 GPUs) and six existing CXR tools: MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Rad, CheXagent, LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-2 and MedVLM-R1. For each image and question, the director first runs a ReAct loop. It reasons over the image, question and a memory log, selects one or more tools, stores their outputs, and repeats until it has enough information. Every tool statement then passes through the Evidence-driven Validator. The director itself writes a short conclusion, lists image signs that support it and signs that refute it, and gives a High, Medium or Low confidence. A claim without visible support, or with clear contradiction, is marked Low and not used directly. On Low confidence the director calls a different tool with a similar job, compares tools, and, if doubt remains, writes a cautious note that flags the discrepancy for the radiologist. Next, the director plans the collaboration mode: Skip for clear cases, Relay for step-by-step refinement, Dispatch for parallel sub-tasks to role agents such as a cardiologist and pulmonologist, or Probe for targeted questions in ambiguous cases. It recruits k role agents, each with a role and mission, runs them, and synthesises a final answer from team output and memory. Evaluation used CheXbench (11 sub-tasks), 1,000 Medical-CXR-VQA questions (594 presence, 256 abnormality, 150 view) and the full MIMIC-CXR test split (3,858 reports) with RaTEScore, GREEN, RadGraph-F1 and a GPT-4o 1-5 LLMScore. Ablations removed tools, EDV, team and memory. A stress test fed 1 correct and 3 wrong tool answers. Five radiologists compared 100 blinded report pairs. CXRAgent reached 67.0% on CheXbench, 75.6% on Medical-CXR-VQA and RaTEScore 0.569. A PhD student could adapt this by using brain MRI tools and replacing the qualitative confidence label with calibrated scores and a deferral threshold.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective technical development and benchmark study with ablations plus a blinded pairwise reader study by five certified radiologists. Institutions: Hangzhou Dianzi University, Tsinghua University, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), China. Public datasets only; no prospective patients.
papers.datasets: 1) CheXbench (public): image perception and image-text reasoning tasks used: single disease identification (SDI) on MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert, multiple disease identification (MDI) on MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert, VQA on Rad-Restruct and SLAKE, fine-grained reasoning (FGR) on OpenI, binary disease classification (BDC) on CheXpert, SIIM and RSNA, view classification (VC) on MIMIC-CXR; per-task sample counts Not reported. 2) Medical-CXR-VQA: randomly sampled 594 Presence, 256 Abnormality and 150 View binary questions (1,000 total). 3) MIMIC-CXR: 377,110 CXRs with 227,835 reports; entire test split used for report generation (3,858 reports). Complexity subsets: 200 most complex and 200 simplest test cases, ranked by GPT-4o for ambiguity and complexity (complex = intricate anatomy, post-surgical hardware or ambiguous conclusions). Reader study: 100 randomly selected samples. EDV stress test: SDI task of CheXbench (MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert) with all candidate options treated as tool outputs (1 correct, 3 misleading).
papers.preprocessing: No model training, so no train/validation/test split; all data are used as test sets. Medical-CXR-VQA questions randomly sampled per official task type. Tool outputs are normalised by EDV into a common structure (conclusion, supportive evidence, refuting evidence, confidence). Image resolution and normalisation: Not reported (tools used as released). Answer extraction rules: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Stage 1, Tool invocation (ReAct): Thought_i = Plan(Log_{i-1}, I, q) decides whether more tools are needed; Action_i selects a set of tools from T (MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Rad, CheXagent, LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-2, MedVLM-R1); observations are added to the log (Log_i = Log_{i-1} U Obs_i); loop ends when enough information is gathered. Evidence-driven Validator (run by the director LLM itself, no extra vision model): for each tool statement it writes a conclusion, supportive evidence, refuting evidence and a confidence rating of High, Medium or Low. Evidence must be visible in the image, map clearly to the finding, have no clear contradiction, and be sufficient for downstream use; otherwise the statement is Low and not used directly. On Low confidence or strong refuting evidence the director (a) re-invokes an alternative tool with similar function but different architecture, (b) cross-checks tools to resolve conflict, and (c) if ambiguity remains, writes a cautious interpretation that flags discrepancies to the radiologist. Stage 2, Diagnostic planning: director chooses by in-context reasoning (no trained policy) one of Skip (clear case, no team), Relay (experts refine sequentially), Dispatch (parallel sub-tasks to domain experts, for example cardiologist and pulmonologist), Probe (targeted probing questions to each member for complex or ambiguous cases). Stage 3, Collaborative decision-making: Team = {(agent_i, role_i, mission_i)} for i = 1..k = R(I, q, s); Algorithm 1 runs the team by mode and concatenates outputs; final Diagnose(q, I, s, Memory, TeamOutput). Team size k chosen dynamically (value not fixed). Low-temperature decoding (exact value not reported).
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning; inference-only agent. Deployed on two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs with GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-Max as director via API. Low-temperature decoding to reduce run-to-run variation. Latency, cost and number of runs: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy for CheXbench tasks and Medical-CXR-VQA (average over all samples; overall = average over tasks). Report generation on the full MIMIC-CXR test split with RaTEScore (entity-level NER-based), LLMScore (GPT-4o rating 1-5 on ITU five-point scale), GREEN (LLM-based) and RadGraph-F1 (entities and relations), computed with a public toolkit. Subgroup analysis on 200 simple vs 200 complex reports. Ablations: None, Tools, Tools+EDV, Full model, for both directors; memory vs memory-less; EDV under simulated 3:1 misleading tool outputs; EDV on 200 complex cases. Significance: McNemar's test for accuracy (CheXbench, Medical-CXR-VQA) and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for report metrics. Reader study: 5 certified radiologists, 100 random samples, blinded randomised pairwise comparison of CXRAgent vs one of MedRAX, CheXagent, MedGemma or LLaVA-Rad, with image and reference report shown; judged on completeness, accuracy and clinical utility; win and tie rates reported.
papers.baselines: General multimodal LLMs: Qwen-VL-Max, GPT-4o, Janus-Pro-7B. Radiology-specialised models: LLaVA-Med, CheXagent, LLaVA-Rad, MedGemma, MAIRA-2, CXRMate, CXRMate-ED, CvT2DistilGPT2, MedVersa, IFCC, Libra. Agent: MedRAX with GPT-4o or Qwen director.
papers.results: CheXbench overall accuracy: LLaVA-Med 36.0, CheXagent 61.8, Janus-Pro-7B 42.3, GPT-4o 59.9, Qwen-VL-Max 60.3, MedGemma 55.5, MedRAX (GPT) 57.1, MedRAX (Qwen) 56.7, CXRAgent (GPT) 66.3, CXRAgent (Qwen) 67.0. Selected CXRAgent (GPT / Qwen) task scores: SDI MIMIC-CXR 39.3 / 42.9; SDI CheXpert 52.1 / 55.6; MDI MIMIC-CXR 64.6 / 61.3; MDI CheXpert 73.2 / 68.9; VQA Rad-Restruct 62.6 / 59.1 (MedRAX GPT best 68.7); VQA SLAKE 86.2 / 87.0; FGR OpenI 53.4 / 59.4; BDC CheXpert 64.8 / 60.5 (CheXagent best 76.0); BDC SIIM 77.0 / 72.0; BDC RSNA 83.0 / 83.0; VC MIMIC-CXR 74.0 / 87.7 (CheXagent 97.5). Medical-CXR-VQA overall: LLaVA-Med 44.1, CheXagent 62.1, Janus-Pro 51.4, GPT-4o 69.2, Qwen-VL-Max 70.8, MedGemma 71.5, MedRAX (GPT) 68.2, MedRAX (Qwen) 70.5, CXRAgent (GPT) 71.7, CXRAgent (Qwen) 75.6 (presence 68.0, abnormality 75.7, view 83.3). MIMIC-CXR report (LLMScore / RadGraph / GREEN / RaTEScore): CXRAgent (GPT) 3.267 / 0.251 / 0.359 / 0.569; CXRAgent (Qwen) 3.337 / 0.243 / 0.334 / 0.557; IFCC 2.723 / 0.265 / 0.356 / 0.568; LLaVA-Rad 3.172 / 0.235 / 0.330 / 0.538; CXRMate-ED 3.077 / 0.266 / 0.336 / 0.540; MedRAX (GPT) 2.388 / 0.122 / 0.201 / 0.486; GPT-4o alone 2.364 / 0.112 / 0.190 / 0.480. 200 complex cases: CXRAgent (GPT) LLMScore 3.208, RaTEScore 0.554 vs CXRMate-ED 0.549, LLaVA-Rad 0.534, IFCC 0.530. Ablation CheXbench overall (None / Tools / Tools+EDV / Full): Qwen 60.3 / 63.0 / 65.4 / 67.0; GPT 59.9 / 60.5 / 64.3 / 66.3. Medical-CXR-VQA ablation: Qwen 70.8 / 73.2 / 74.6 / 75.6; GPT 69.2 / 69.7 / 71.1 / 71.7. Report ablation RaTEScore: GPT 0.480 / 0.550 / 0.560 / 0.569; Qwen 0.473 / 0.521 / 0.553 / 0.557. EDV under misleading tools (w/o -> w/): MIMIC-CXR GPT 25.6 -> 27.7, Qwen 26.1 -> 31.8; CheXpert GPT 42.0 -> 46.2, Qwen 43.7 -> 45.6. Memory ablation RaTEScore: GPT 0.538 -> 0.569, Qwen 0.547 -> 0.557. Reader win/tie rates (%): vs CheXagent completeness 58.6/4.0, accuracy 52.8/1.2, usability 54.4/2.4; vs MedGemma 76.2/6.4, 80.8/1.8, 87.0/0.4; vs MedRAX 85.6/5.2, 84.2/2.8, 85.2/1.8; vs LLaVA-Rad 42.6/11.6, 50.8/6.4, 51.6/4.4; average 65.8/6.8, 67.2/3.1, 69.6/2.3.
papers.statistics: McNemar's test on overall accuracy for CheXbench and Medical-CXR-VQA: CXRAgent (GPT-4o or Qwen) better than all other methods, p < 0.05. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for report metrics: CXRAgent better than most baselines, p < 0.05 (not significant for GREEN against CheXagent, LLaVA-Rad, CXRMate and CXRMate-ED with the Qwen director). No confidence intervals. Inter-rater agreement among the five radiologists: Not reported.
papers.availability: Code and data: https://github.com/laojiahuo2003/CXRAgent/ (linked in the paper).

papers.title: VILA-M3: Enhancing Vision-Language Models with Medical Expert Knowledge
papers.authors: Nath V, Li W, Yang D, Myronenko A, Zheng M, Lu Y, Liu Z, Yin H, Tang Y, Guo P, Zhao C, Xu Z, He Y, Law YM, Simon B, Harmon S, Heinrich G, Aylward S, Edgar M, Zephyr M, Han S, Molchanov P, Turkbey B, Roth H, Xu D
papers.venue: CVPR 2025 (IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition); arXiv:2411.12915v2
papers.aim: To show that a medical vision-language model (VLM) becomes more accurate when it learns to call specialised medical expert models (segmentation and classification) on demand. They add a fourth training stage, expert-guided instruction fine-tuning, to the usual VLM training recipe.
papers.method: VILA-M3 is built on the open VILA framework (vision encoder + linear projector + LLM). It is fine-tuned on medical VQA, report, classification and expert-trigger conversations so that it learns to emit tokens such as <VISTA3D(hepatic tumor)> or <BRATS()>; the expert output (mask or yes/no list) is returned as a new user turn and the model then answers. Four sizes (3B, 8B, 13B, 40B) were trained and compared with Med-Gemini, task-specific SOTA models and GPT-4o.
papers.result: Average score over 8 metrics: VILA-M3-40B 64.3, 13B 63.4, 8B 63.0, 3B 61.5 vs Med-Gemini 55.7 and task-specific SOTA 58.6 (about 9% over Med-Gemini, 6% over task SOTA). VQA-RAD accuracy 90.4 (40B), PathVQA 92.7, MIMIC-CXR BLEU-4 21.6, ROUGE 32.2. Adding expert feedback raised CheXpert average F1 (e.g. 3B 57.4 to 60.7) and ChestX-ray14 average F1 (e.g. 3B 48.4 to 51.3). Dataset balancing gave about 4% average gain. General VILA benchmark dropped 7%, 11%, 4% and 23% for 3B, 8B, 13B, 40B.
papers.tools: VILA framework (NVIDIA, NVlabs/VILA); CLIP-L vision encoder (384x384; 448x448 for 40B); LLM backbones Vicuna/Llama-2 (3B, 13B), Llama-3 (8B), Yi-34B (40B); expert models MONAI VISTA3D (CT, 127 classes), MONAI BRATS SegResNet (brain MRI, BraTS 2018), TorchXRayVision CNN ensemble (CXR, 18 diseases); Llama-3.1-8B-instruct for report cleaning and instruction generation; bf16, gradient checkpointing; NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs (32 or 128 GPUs); GPT-4o API as comparator.
papers.gap: Brain MRI is only used through a 2D input plus a 3D BraTS expert; no quantitative brain-tumour segmentation or diagnosis results are reported for the VLM. There is no uncertainty estimate or rule for deferring to clinicians, no reader study, and no privacy or federated training. The expert call is learned from synthetic conversations, not from clinician workflow.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration) this is a concrete pattern for an imaging agent: a VLM that routes a brain-MRI query to a BraTS segmentation expert via model cards and tool tokens, then reasons over the returned mask. Our framework can reuse the model-card prompt, the expert-trigger token format and the feedback loop, but must add calibrated confidence so the orchestrator can defer to a neurosurgeon or radiologist when the VLM or expert is unsure.
papers.limitations: Benchmarks are mostly chest X-ray; segmentation benefit is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 3). The 40B model lost 23% on general VLM benchmarks (SQA-I fell to 0.0). Models over-fit at 3 epochs. GPT-4o refused over 50% of prompts when expert information was added, so that comparison was not done. Training validation sets were merged into training due to compute cost. Future work: retrieval-augmented generation and a multi-agent framework where expert models can consult other experts.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors start from pre-trained VILA checkpoints that already passed projector pre-training, vision-language pre-training and generic instruction tuning. They add a fourth stage: expert-guided instruction fine-tuning on medical data, with the CLIP-L vision encoder (384x384 input; 448x448 for 40B), linear projector and LLM all unfrozen. Four sizes are trained: 3B and 13B (Vicuna/Llama-2), 8B (Llama-3) and 40B (Yi-34B). The training set mixes eight sources, 819,456 samples in total: USMLE text (10,178), VQA-RAD (6,281), SLAKE (5,972), PathVQA (26,034), MIMIC-Diff-VQA (129,232), MIMIC-CXR reports (270,000), VISTA3D CT conversations (50,000) and BraTS brain-MRI conversations (15,000). MIMIC reports are cleaned first with the DCL text and then rewritten by Llama-3.1-8B-instruct against a pool of standard sentences. Expert conversations are made by running each expert on public data (VISTA3D on MSD and TotalSegmentatorV2 CT; MONAI SegResNet on BraTS 2018 four-sequence MRI; TorchXRayVision on MIMIC). Llama-3.1 writes varied user requests, and the target answer is a trigger such as 'Let me trigger <VISTA3D(hepatic tumor)>'. A system prompt lists model cards giving modality, task, accuracy and valid arguments. At run time the expert output comes back as a new user turn: a mask overlay with a colour legend, or yes/no answers for 18 chest diseases. The model then writes its final answer. Datasets are up-sampled by category (factors 1-16), which grows the data to 1,840,428 samples and raises expert segmentation from 7.9% to 34.8% of the mix. Training uses learning rate 2e-5 with a cosine schedule, warm-up 0.03, no weight decay, batch 16 per GPU, bf16 and gradient checkpointing, on 32 A100 GPUs (128 for 40B). Each size is trained for 1, 2 and 3 epochs; 2 epochs takes 5.5-21 hours. Evaluation uses official test splits: accuracy for VQA, F1 for classification, and BLEU-4, ROUGE and GREEN for reports. Results are compared with Med-Gemini, task-specific models and GPT-4o, with McNemar tests. To adapt this, a PhD student could swap in a local brain-MRI segmenter as the expert and add a confidence output before the final answer.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective model development and benchmarking study on public datasets. NVIDIA with SingHealth (Singapore) and NIH (USA). No prospective or clinical deployment.
papers.datasets: Training mixture (Supp. Table 7, original count -> balancing factor -> balanced count): USMLE medical text 10,178 x10 = 101,780; RadVQA 6,281 x16 = 100,496; SLAKE 5,972 x16 = 95,552; PathVQA 26,034 x4 = 104,136; MIMIC-Diff-VQA (expert) 129,232 x2 = 258,464; MIMIC report generation (expert) 270,000 x1 = 270,000; VISTA3D CT segmentation conversations 50,000 x8 = 400,000; BRATS brain-MRI segmentation conversations 15,000 x16 = 240,000; total 819,456 original, 1,840,428 balanced. SLAKE: 642 images (CXR, CT, MRI), 14,028 QA pairs; used 4,919 train, 1,053 val, 1,061 test. PathVQA: 4,289 pathology images, 32,632 QA pairs; 19,654 train, 6,259 val, 6,719 test. VQA-RAD used for VQA (counts in table above). Classification: ChestX-ray14 subset of 1,962 images adjudicated by 4 radiologists (fracture, pneumothorax, lung opacity); CheXpert subset by Saporta et al. (atelectasis, cardiomegaly, consolidation, edema, pleural effusion). Report generation: MIMIC-CXR-JPG v2.0.0/2.1.0, over 377,110 images, 227,827 reports, official train/val/test CSV splits. Expert datasets: CT from MSD (liver, spleen, pancreas) and TotalSegmentatorV2 run through VISTA3D; brain MRI from BraTS 2018 run through the MONAI BRATS SegResNet (T1, T1-Gd, T2, FLAIR). Inclusion/exclusion criteria: Not reported beyond official splits.
papers.preprocessing: Images resized to 384x384 for the CLIP-L encoder (448x448 for 40B). Images inserted as image tokens before, after or inside text. Text-only USMLE data added to keep language skills. MIMIC reports cleaned with the DCL enhanced text version, then standardised by Llama-3.1-8B-instruct using an extracted 'sentence pool' and a conversion prompt. Expert data built by running expert models on existing datasets and turning outputs into conversations (instruction variants generated with Llama-3.1); a subset of VQA and report samples got model cards and CXR-expert trigger statements added. Segmentation masks are re-tokenised as an overlay image with a text description of colours; classification results returned as yes/no for 18 diseases using a threshold (threshold value not reported). Dataset balancing by category-wise up-sampling (factors above): VQA share 24.9% -> 30.4%, language 1.2% -> 5.5%, expert segmentation 7.9% -> 34.8%, report generation 33.0% -> 14.7%. Train and validation sets of VQA datasets both used for training; official test splits used for evaluation. Augmentation: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Architecture: auto-regressive VLM (VILA). Image -> CLIP-L ViT -> linear projector -> visual tokens concatenated with text tokens -> LLM. Four-stage training: (0) projector pre-training, (1) vision-language pre-training, (2) instruction fine-tuning (IFT), (3) expert-guided IFT on medical data (this paper fine-tunes stage 3 starting from VILA checkpoints; vision encoder, projector and LLM all unfrozen). Backbones: 3B Vicuna/Llama-2 (Sheared LLaMa in Table 3), 8B Llama-3, 13B Vicuna, 40B Yi-34B. Expert triggering: a system prompt lists model cards (modality, task, overview, accuracy, valid arguments), e.g. <BRATS(args)>, <VISTA3D(args)> with args 'everything', 'hepatic tumor', 'pancreatic tumor', 'lung tumor', <VISTA2D(args)>, <CXR(args)>. The VLM predicts a keyword with argument; the expert runs (VISTA3D segments the full 3D volume even though the VLM sees 2D); its output returns as a conversational user turn (mask overlay + text, or 18-disease yes/no list); the VLM then gives the final answer. Loss: standard auto-regressive next-token loss (not separately reported). No uncertainty estimate or deferral threshold.
papers.training: Batch size 16 per GPU for training, 4 for evaluation; gradient accumulation adjusted to keep the same effective batch size across nodes. Learning rate 2e-5, cosine schedule, warm-up ratio 0.03, weight decay 0, bf16 mixed precision, gradient checkpointing. Optimizer: Not reported (VILA default). Epochs: models trained for 1, 2 and 3 epochs; 2 epochs reported in Table 2. Hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB; 3B/8B/13B on 4 nodes x 8 = 32 GPUs; 40B on 16 nodes = 128 GPUs. Training time (2 epochs): 3B about 5.5 h, 8B about 11.0 h, 13B about 19.5 h, 40B about 21 h. Inference memory: CXR expert about 1.5 GB; VISTA3D about 12 GB (higher peak for large volumes).
papers.evaluation: Held-out official test sets. Metrics: accuracy for closed-ended VQA (VQA-RAD, SLAKE, PathVQA, MIMIC-VQA); F1 for classification (ChestX-ray14 subset, CheXpert subset); BLEU-4, ROUGE and GREEN for MIMIC-CXR report generation. Total average across 8 metrics. With vs without expert feedback ablation. Balanced vs unbalanced data ablation. 1/2/3 epoch over-fitting analysis. General VILA benchmark (VQAv2, GQA, VizWiz, SQA-I, VQA-T, POPE, MME/20, MMB, MMB-CN, SEED, MM-Vet) to check loss of general skills. GPT-4o queried with the same prompts via API (10 retries). Per-finding report analysis on MIMIC test set for 40B. No reader study or clinician evaluation.
papers.baselines: Med-Gemini (1.5T); task-specific SOTA: LLaVA-Med (7B), LLaVA-Rad (7B), DCL (0.25B) for reports, TorchXRayVision ensemble for classification; GPT-4o; base VILA-1.5 checkpoints (3B, 8B, 13B, 40B) on general benchmarks.
papers.results: Table 1 (VQA-RAD / MIMIC-VQA / SLAKE / PathVQA accuracy; BLEU-4; ROUGE; ChestX-ray14 F1; CheXpert F1; total average): Med-Gemini 78.8 / 78.6 / 84.8 / 83.3 / 20.5 / 28.3 / 46.7 / 48.3 / 55.7. Task SOTA 84.2 / - / 86.8 / 91.7 / 15.4 / 30.6 / 50.0 / 51.5 / 58.6. VILA-M3-3B 78.2 / 82.4 / 79.8 / 87.9 / 20.2 / 31.7 / 51.3 / 60.8 / 61.5. 8B 84.7 / 82.1 / 82.7 / 91.0 / 21.1 / 32.0 / 48.9 / 61.6 / 63.0. 13B 80.5 / 86.4 / 83.2 / 91.0 / 21.6 / 32.1 / 51.2 / 61.5 / 63.4. 40B 90.4 / 81.9 / 84.0 / 92.7 / 21.6 / 32.2 / 51.3 / 61.0 / 64.3. Report generation without/with expert (BLEU-4, ROUGE, GREEN): 3B 19.7/31.4/39.4 vs 20.2/31.7/39.1; 8B 21.4/32.2/39.8 vs 21.2/32.1/39.7; 13B 21.4/32.1/39.3 vs 21.6/32.1/39.3; 40B 21.6/32.2/39.2 both. ChestX-ray14 average F1 without/with expert: GPT-4o 33.1/-; Med-Gemini 46.9/-; TorchXRayVision -/50.0; 3B 48.4/51.3; 8B 45.8/50.8; 13B 49.9/51.2; 40B 47.1/51.3. CheXpert average F1 without/with expert: GPT-4o 33.9; Med-Gemini 48.4; TorchXRayVision 51.5; 3B 57.4/60.7; 8B 61.4/60.5; 13B 55.8/61.5; 40B 59.4/61.0. General benchmark average VILA1.5 vs VILA-M3: 3B 63.2 vs 56.2; 8B 71.1 vs 60.5; 13B 70.0 vs 66.2; 40B 75.5 vs 52.2. Balancing: about 4% average gain (3B, 13B), about 2% (8B). Per-finding GREEN (40B, without -> with expert): atelectasis 35.93 -> 36.56, cardiomegaly 38.99 -> 39.79, no finding 45.60 -> 46.57. Brain-tumour segmentation: qualitative only. Confidence intervals: Not reported.
papers.statistics: McNemar chi-square tests of VILA-M3 (with expert) vs GPT-4o per class, significance at p < 0.05. ChestX-ray14: 3B fracture 5.5e-10, pneumothorax 3.2e-5, lung opacity 6.1e-41; 8B 1.3e-1, 3.1e-1 (not significant), 4.5e-14; 13B 5.9e-20, 5.0e-8, 1.0e-44; 40B 3.1e-12, 2.5e-8, 3.2e-49. CheXpert: all classes significant for all sizes (e.g. 3B atelectasis 2.3e-53). No confidence intervals.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/NVlabs/VILA (framework) and the MONAI VILA-M3 release linked from the paper; models: https://huggingface.co/MONAI; demo: https://vila-m3-demo.monai.ngc.nvidia.com/. Datasets are public (MIMIC-CXR requires PhysioNet credentialed access).

papers.title: Integrating Vision-Language Models and Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Clinical Reasoning in Brain Tumor Analysis
papers.authors: Slimene I, Zouari S, Masmoudi E, Marrakchi C, Khiari M, Rhimi N, Hechmi A, Ghribi HE
papers.aim: To build one multi-agent system that classifies brain MRI, retrieves similar past cases, segments the tumour, explains the prediction and writes a medical report. The goal is to add reasoning, case retrieval and report writing to deep learning models that usually work alone.
papers.method: A LangChain multi-agent pipeline uses a medical vision transformer (MedViT) to embed MRI scans, FAISS to retrieve the k most similar cases, and a Gemini agent to pre-write descriptions of all training scans stored in MongoDB. Further agents run a U-Net (ResNet-34 encoder) for segmentation and Grad-CAM for heatmaps. A LLaMA-70B agent refines the final report.
papers.result: MedViT reached 97.56% validation accuracy and 98% test accuracy on a four-class brain MRI dataset (glioma, meningioma, pituitary, no tumour). Segmentation, retrieval and report quality numbers: Not reported in the abstract.
papers.tools: LangChain (agent orchestration); MedViT (medical vision transformer); FAISS (vector index); MongoDB (case-description store); Google Gemini LLM (description agent); U-Net with ResNet-34 encoder (segmentation); Grad-CAM (heatmaps); LLaMA-70B (report refinement). Hardware: Not reported.
papers.gap: Based on the abstract, there is no uncertainty estimate, no deferral to clinicians, no clinician evaluation of reports, no external or multi-centre validation and no privacy-preserving training. Reliance on cloud LLMs (Gemini, LLaMA-70B) may not suit low-resource or privacy-sensitive hospitals.
papers.relation: For O1 this is the closest domain match: a multi-agent LLM system for brain-tumour MRI with separate classification, retrieval, segmentation, explanation and report agents. It gives a baseline agent decomposition for our orchestrator. Our work must add calibrated selective autonomy (deferral when confidence is low), clinician validation in Sri Lanka and federated training instead of central data and cloud LLMs.
papers.limitations: Only the abstract was available (publisher PDF behind a bot check). Reported results cover only MedViT classification accuracy on a four-class dataset. Dataset source, size and split, segmentation metrics, report evaluation and future work: Not reported in the abstract.
papers.methodologyDetail: Only the abstract and metadata could be read, so the walk-through is limited to what the abstract states. The authors build a clinical reasoning pipeline for brain-tumour MRI in LangChain, with each step handled by a separate agent. First, a medical vision transformer (MedViT) is trained on a four-class brain MRI dataset: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour and no tumour. MedViT does two jobs. It predicts the class, and it turns each scan into a high-dimensional embedding vector. The embeddings of the training scans are stored in a FAISS index, so that for a new scan the system can find the k most similar past cases. Second, before inference, a Gemini-based LLM agent writes a detailed text description of every training scan. These descriptions are saved in MongoDB and linked to the matching FAISS IDs, so a retrieved neighbour comes with its text. Third, a segmentation agent outlines the tumour with a U-Net that uses a ResNet-34 encoder. Fourth, an explainability agent makes Grad-CAM heatmaps to show which image regions drove the prediction. At inference the agents work together: they analyse the input scan, retrieve similar cases with their descriptions, add the segmentation and heatmap, and draft a full report. A LLaMA-70B agent then rewrites the summary in a medical style. The only reported numbers are MedViT's 97.56% validation accuracy and 98% test accuracy. Dataset size, class counts, split ratios, preprocessing, hyperparameters, value of k, prompts, segmentation metrics and report evaluation are not given in the abstract. To reproduce or adapt this, a student would need the full paper (open access under CC BY-NC-ND on ScienceDirect). For our framework, the same agent breakdown could be kept, with three changes: a calibrated confidence score on the MedViT output, a deferral rule that sends low-confidence cases to clinicians, and local or federated models instead of cloud LLMs.
papers.studyDesign: System development and retrospective evaluation on a brain MRI dataset. ESPRIT School of Engineering, Tunis, Tunisia. Not prospective; no clinical deployment reported.
papers.datasets: Four-class brain MRI dataset (glioma, meningioma, pituitary, no tumour). Name, source, number of images and class counts: Not reported in the abstract. Segmentation dataset: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Not reported in the abstract (train/validation/test split exists, since validation and test accuracy are given, but ratios are not reported).
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: MedViT encodes each MRI scan into a high-dimensional embedding and also gives the class prediction. Step 2: embeddings are indexed with FAISS so the k most similar cases can be retrieved (k value not reported). Step 3: a Gemini-based LLM agent writes a detailed description for every training scan; descriptions are stored in MongoDB and linked to FAISS IDs. Step 4: a segmentation agent runs a U-Net with ResNet-34 encoder. Step 5: an explainability agent produces Grad-CAM heatmaps. Step 6: at inference, agents combine the classification, retrieved similar cases and their descriptions, segmentation and heatmap into a report. Step 7: a LLaMA-70B agent refines the summary for medical writing. Prompts, losses, thresholds and any uncertainty rule: Not reported.
papers.training: Not reported in the abstract.
papers.evaluation: Validation and test accuracy for four-class classification. Other evaluation (segmentation, retrieval, report quality, clinician review): Not reported in the abstract.
papers.baselines: Not reported in the abstract.
papers.results: MedViT four-class classification: validation accuracy = 97.56%; test accuracy = 98%. No other quantitative results in the abstract. Confidence intervals: Not reported.
papers.statistics: Not reported
papers.availability: Not available (not stated in the abstract).

papers.title: Development, Evaluation, and Deployment of a Multi-Agent System for Thoracic Tumor Board
papers.authors: Ellis-Caleo T, Keyes T, Ambers N, Bekheet F, Yim W, Kotecha N, Shah NH, Neal J
papers.aim: To find which LLM system best writes short, tumour-board-ready patient summaries from the electronic health record, and then to deploy it and monitor it at the Stanford thoracic tumour board. The study also tests whether more agent autonomy helps.
papers.method: Five automated GPT-4.1 summarisers, from a single-note prompt to a high-autonomy multi-agent system, were compared with a physician reference and the existing manual SecureGPT workflow on 50 tumour-board cases. Completeness was scored against oncologist-written fact rubrics by a GPT-5 judge validated against two physicians, and two physicians rated quality on 1-5 scales. The best system (low-autonomy multi-agent) was deployed in January 2026 and 50 production summaries were rated.
papers.result: LLM judge agreed with physicians: exact agreement 89.3-89.4%, Cohen kappa 0.687-0.709, Gwet AC1 0.870-0.871; Fleiss kappa 0.731 (2 physicians) vs 0.708 (with LLM). Single-step, multi-step and low-autonomy multi-agent systems were more complete than SecureGPT (all p <= 0.001); the high-autonomy multi-agent system was not (p = 0.221). No automated method beat SecureGPT on physician ratings; single-step and multi-step had lower relevance. All 50 post-deployment summaries scored >= 3 in all four domains.
papers.tools: GPT-4.1 (OpenAI) at temperature 0 for all generators; GPT-5 (reasoning effort 'medium') as LLM judge via LiteLLM proxy and Azure Key Vault; ChatEHR (Stanford Health Care LLM-EHR platform); SecureGPT (HIPAA-compliant LLM environment); LangChain (single-note, single-step, multi-step); Microsoft Healthcare Agent Orchestrator (HAO) for multi-agent systems; FHIR API for note retrieval; Epic EHR (Smart Form, Smart Data Element); Pydantic; Python; R tidyverse.
papers.gap: Single centre, single cancer type, text notes only (no imaging or genomics attachments). No uncertainty or deferral mechanism; no 'single agent with all tools' baseline. Post-deployment monitoring was short (one month, 50 cases) and descriptive. Staging and molecular/NGS facts remained incomplete.
papers.relation: For O1 this is a strong deployment template for a tumour-board style multi-agent pipeline (Data Loader, FHIR, Curation, Summarisation agents with per-statement citations and auditable filtering). Its main finding, that low-autonomy, tightly specified agents beat high-autonomy agents, directly supports our calibrated selective autonomy design. Its rubric-based fact scoring, validated LLM judge and pre-set acceptability threshold (score >= 3) can be reused for clinician validation of neuro-oncology summaries in Sri Lanka.
papers.limitations: Single academic centre and one thoracic workflow; generalisability unclear. No single-agent-with-all-tools baseline. Task is short, structured summarisation, so higher autonomy may help in harder tasks. Genomic results stored in media tabs were not accessible. Rubrics written by one oncologist. Moderate inter-physician agreement on subjective ratings. Future work: cancer staging, clinical trial matching and treatment recommendation validated against clinicians.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study takes place at the weekly Stanford thoracic tumour board, which reviews 12-20 cases a week at about 3-5 minutes per case. Before the study, administrative staff pasted one chosen note into SecureGPT to get a summary of 999 characters or less. The team picked 50 random cases from April-June 2025. For each case a blinded oncologist wrote a reference summary, and the existing SecureGPT summary was retrieved. Five automated generators were built on GPT-4.1 (temperature 0), each limited to 999 characters with three headings (ID, Biomarkers/NGS, Prior therapy). They read raw EHR notes with no preprocessing. (1) Single-note uses only the latest oncology note. (2) Single-step joins all notes from the last 180 days in one call. (3) Multi-step writes extracts of up to 5 lines per note, then combines them. (4) A low-autonomy multi-agent system (Microsoft HAO) retrieves once from a fixed 180-day window and follows detailed cancer-specific instructions. (5) A high-autonomy multi-agent system picks its own window, can retrieve again, and gets only high-level guidance. Next, one oncologist wrote a fact rubric for each case: a median of 6 attributes and 3.5 subattributes, each typed by domain. A GPT-5 judge, given the rubric as Pydantic objects, labelled each item Yes, Partial or No, with an error type when not Yes. Before use, the judge was checked against two physicians on 250 pilot summaries (89% exact agreement, Cohen kappa about 0.70, AC1 0.87). Completeness was the share of rubric items present in each summary. Methods were compared with a Friedman test and Wilcoxon tests against SecureGPT, using Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Two physicians also rated all 350 summaries from 1 to 5 on four domains, with 3 or more counted as acceptable. The low-autonomy multi-agent system was the only one that improved completeness without losing relevance, so it was deployed in January 2026. It runs four sequential agents: Data Loader, FHIR retrieval, Curation (filters notes with auditable reasons) and Summarisation (writes per-statement citations into Epic). In the first month, 50 production summaries were rated, and all scored at least 3. This design can be copied for a neuro-oncology board.
papers.studyDesign: Quality-improvement study: retrospective comparative evaluation (cases April-June 2025) followed by prospective deployment with post-deployment monitoring (from January 2026). Stanford Health Care thoracic tumour board, Palo Alto, USA (Stanford University, Stanford Health Care, Microsoft AI).
papers.datasets: Randomly chosen 50 thoracic tumour-board cases from April to June 2025 (one academic quarter). Data: unstructured clinical notes in the Epic EHR, retrieved via FHIR, within a fixed 180-day look-back before the tumour-board date (unless the high-autonomy agent chose otherwise). Per case 7 summaries (physician reference, SecureGPT manual, 5 automated) = 350 summaries for physician rating. Pilot judge-validation set: 50 patients x 5 methods = 250 summaries. Rubrics: median 6 attributes per patient (IQR 5-7, range 2-12) and median 3.5 subattributes (IQR 2-6, range 0-16), typed as Demographics, Stage, Pathology, Molecular Findings, Medical, Surgical or Radiation Treatment. Post-deployment: 50 production summaries from the first month (weekly n = 10, 10, 5, 6, 19). Inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond random selection: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: No note preprocessing: no template stripping, deduplication or redaction. Notes restricted to a 180-day look-back window for longitudinal methods. Output constrained to 999 characters with headings 'ID', 'Biomarkers/NGS' and 'Prior therapy'. Rubrics serialised into Pydantic objects; rubric items scored at the finest level (subattributes if present, otherwise attribute). No train/test split (no model training; prompting only).
papers.modelDetails: All generators use GPT-4.1, temperature 0, via ChatEHR. (1) Single-note: summarise the most recent oncology note. (2) Single-step: concatenate all notes in 180 days chronologically, one LLM call. (3) Multi-step: per-note extracts of <= 5 lines (date + key fields), then a synthesis call. (4) Low-autonomy multi-agent: one retrieval from a fixed 180-day window, detailed thoracic-cancer-specific instructions on which notes and facts to include. (5) High-autonomy multi-agent: chooses the retrieval window per patient, can call the retrieval tool repeatedly, follows only high-level guidance. Deployed system (low-autonomy, HAO): four sequential agents. Data Loader Agent hands off to FHIR Agent; FHIR Agent calls one EHR tool (patient ID, time window, resource type) and writes notes as timestamped text files to an ephemeral workspace; Curation Agent filters out non-relevant notes in place with an auditable rationale; Summarisation Agent uses only charted information, writes the summary with per-statement citations; storage resolves cited notes, computes character offsets for quoted snippets and saves under a workflow-instance ID into Epic. Tool permissions are scoped per agent. Judge: GPT-5 labels each rubric item Yes / Partial / No, plus an error type (Missing, Incorrect, Ambiguous, Other) when not Yes; semantic equivalence allowed. Uncertainty-based deferral: none; humans review all summaries at the board.
papers.training: No model training; all systems use prompting of GPT-4.1 (temperature 0). Judge GPT-5 with reasoning effort 'medium', other parameters default. Hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Two prespecified axes. (1) Objective completeness: per-summary proportion of rubric items 'fully present' (Yes) and 'fully or partially present' (Yes or Partial), scored by the GPT-5 judge, overall and per attribute type. Judge validated on 250 pilot summaries against two physicians using exact agreement, Cohen kappa, Gwet AC1 and Fleiss kappa, with patient-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 replicates). (2) Subjective quality: two physicians rated each summary 1-5 for Overall, Writing Style, Relevance and Accuracy; final score = mean of the two, rounded down; >= 3 prespecified as acceptable. Deployment criterion: better completeness than SecureGPT without loss of relevance. Post-deployment: a board-certified medical oncologist and an internal medicine resident rated 50 production summaries; weekly means with bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 replicates).
papers.baselines: Physician-authored reference summary (board-certified medical oncologist, blinded); manual SecureGPT workflow (staff prompt with one chosen note, pre-specified comparator); and the five automated systems compared with each other.
papers.results: Judge validation: exact agreement 89.3-89.4%; Cohen kappa 0.687-0.709; Gwet AC1 0.870-0.871; Fleiss kappa 0.731 (95% CI 0.697-0.762) for 2 physicians and 0.708 (95% CI 0.684-0.734) with the LLM added. Completeness differed across methods: Friedman chi2(5) = 57.0 (fully present) and 50.7 (fully or partially), both p < 0.001. Versus SecureGPT (Wilcoxon V, BH-adjusted p): single-note fully V = 474, p = 0.169; partial V = 398, p = 0.052. Single-step fully V = 16.5, p < 0.001; partial V = 18, p < 0.001. Multi-step fully V = 17.5, p < 0.001; partial V = 23.5, p < 0.001. Low-autonomy multi-agent fully V = 40.5, p < 0.001; partial V = 50.0, p = 0.001. High-autonomy multi-agent fully V = 145, p = 0.221; partial V = 164, p = 0.380. Physician ratings vs SecureGPT: single-note worse for overall (V = 602, p = 0.001), relevance (V = 724, p < 0.001), writing style (V = 620, p = 0.005), accuracy (V = 410, p = 0.005); single-step lower relevance (V = 591, p = 0.005) and overall (V = 496, p = 0.022); multi-step lower relevance (V = 354, p = 0.024), overall not different (V = 232, p = 0.243); no difference for either multi-agent system. Inter-physician: exact agreement 62.4%, Spearman rho = 0.669, 77.4% of disagreements were 1 point. Cancer stage and molecular/NGS facts were least complete in all automated methods (exact percentages in Table 1 image, not extractable). Post-deployment: all 50 summaries and all weekly mean 95% CIs >= 3 in all four domains.
papers.statistics: Friedman rank-sum test across methods; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc tests vs SecureGPT with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction; Wilcoxon for ordinal Likert ratings; Cohen kappa, Gwet AC1, Fleiss kappa with patient-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 replicates); Spearman and Pearson correlations; bootstrap CIs for weekly post-deployment means.
papers.availability: Not available (code, prompts in appendices only; patient data not shared).

papers.title: TRiSM for Agentic AI: A review of Trust, Risk, and Security Management in LLM-based Agentic Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Raza S, Sapkota R, Karkee M, Emmanouilidis C
papers.aim: To review trust, risk and security management (TRiSM) for multi-agent systems built on large language models (AMAS). The review proposes a framework, a risk taxonomy and new metrics for coordination and tool use.
papers.method: Structured literature review guided by three research questions. The authors searched six digital libraries (2022-2025) with a two-block Boolean query, screened in two stages, rated quality with four reviewers and kept 180 primary studies. They then adapted the AI TRiSM pillars (explainability, ModelOps, security, privacy, lifecycle governance) to AMAS and proposed the Component Synergy Score (CSS) and Tool Utilization Efficacy (TUE) metrics.
papers.result: 250 papers shortlisted after title/abstract screening; 180 primary studies kept after full-text screening, plus standards and reports. Journal articles made up 61.2% of the corpus. Outputs: a TRiSM framework for AMAS; a risk taxonomy (autonomy abuse, persistent memory poisoning, orchestration compromise, goal misalignment, tool misuse, multi-agent collusion or drift, prompt injection); a five-dimension evaluation template with formulas for trust index, composite score, CSS and TUE; a governance-control table mapped to standards; and a research roadmap. No experiments.
papers.tools: Literature databases: IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, arXiv, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar. Frameworks discussed: AutoGen, CrewAI, LangChain/LangGraph, MetaGPT, ChatDev, OpenAI Swarm, Strands. Benchmarks discussed: HarmBench, ToolBench, API-Bank, AgentBench, GAIA, OpenXAI. Privacy techniques: differential privacy (DP-SGD, DP in federated learning), SMPC, homomorphic encryption, trusted execution environments. Standards: EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC, GDPR, HIPAA.
papers.gap: No empirical validation of the framework or of CSS/TUE on a real system; weights in the composite scores are left to the user. Few clinical examples. No concrete method for confidence-based deferral to humans in multi-agent pipelines. No standard benchmark for TRiSM in AMAS.
papers.relation: For O1 this review supplies the governance layer for our multi-agent clinical system: auditable logs of agent actions, tool calls and inter-agent messages, role separation and scoped tool permissions, guardian agents, human-in-the-loop escalation, and privacy controls including DP in federated learning. Its trust index includes calibration (ECE/Brier), which matches our calibrated selective autonomy aim. CSS and TUE could be adapted to measure how well our imaging, reasoning and planning agents work together.
papers.limitations: Review only; metrics are proposed, not tested. Human-centred evaluation is costly and does not scale; emergent coordination lacks ground truth; composite weights vary by domain; behavioural drift is hard to capture; metrics can be gamed (Goodhart's law). Many controls lack real-world validation. Future work: open benchmarks and red-teaming, longitudinal drift evaluation, deployment case studies with costs, extension to multimodal (vision-language) and embodied agents, human oversight dashboards and regulatory sandboxes.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a structured review, not an experiment, so the method is the review protocol and the frameworks it produces. The authors set three research questions. RQ1 asks which trust, risk and security problems are specific to LLM multi-agent systems. RQ2 asks which governance, explainability, security, privacy and lifecycle controls exist. RQ3 asks how these systems are evaluated and where the gaps are. They searched IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, arXiv, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar for January 2022 to December 2025. The query had two blocks joined by AND: agent terms (for example 'agentic AI', 'multi-agent LLMs', 'LLM-based agents') and TRiSM terms (for example trust, security, privacy, explainability, accountability, adversarial attacks). Screening had two stages, title and abstract first and then full text, with fixed inclusion and exclusion rules. Four reviewers rated each paper as low, medium or high on four quality criteria, and settled disagreements by discussion. This gave 250 shortlisted papers and 180 included studies, plus standards such as the EU AI Act, NIST and ISO. From these studies they built a risk taxonomy covering autonomy abuse, memory poisoning, orchestrator compromise, goal misalignment, tool misuse and collusion. They mapped each risk to controls: role separation, scoped permissions, sandboxing, audit logs, guardian agents, human-in-the-loop escalation, and privacy methods (differential privacy including DP in federated learning, secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption, trusted execution environments). They then set out an evaluation template with formulas. The trust index T combines calibrated accuracy, robustness and alignment and divides by a violation penalty. A composite score is a weighted sum of trust, explainability, user and coordination scores; the authors advise reporting the full vector and choosing systems by thresholds or Pareto optimality. CSS averages, over agent pairs, how much one agent improves another times the quality of the downstream output. TUE is a weighted sum of tool selection, argument validity, execution, outcome and efficiency scores. For our project, a student could adopt the audit and permission controls directly. They could also compute CSS and TUE on logs from our brain-tumour agents, with calibration (ECE) as part of T.
papers.studyDesign: Structured (systematic-style) literature review with bibliometric analysis. Vector Institute (Canada), Cornell University (USA), University of Groningen (Netherlands). Not applicable for prospective/retrospective.
papers.datasets: No patient data. Literature corpus: publications from January 2022 to December 2025 (plus earlier foundational works). 250 papers shortlisted, 180 primary studies included. Inclusion: 2022-2025 (plus influential earlier papers); focus on agentic, multi-agent or LLM-powered systems addressing at least one TRiSM aspect; peer-reviewed papers, widely cited preprints or reputable technical reports. Exclusion: rule-based or symbolic agents without LLM autonomy; papers only on low-level training or architecture without agentic or TRiSM relevance; non-English or incomplete bibliographic records. Publication types: articles 61.2%, misc 21.7%, proceedings 12.3%, book 1.9%, tech report 1.6%, collection 1.0%, PhD thesis 0.3%.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Two-stage screening: title/abstract, then full text. Quality assessment on four criteria (clear AMAS objectives; documented methods or architecture; engagement with at least one TRiSM aspect; relevant empirical, theoretical or normative contribution), each rated low, medium or high; studies rated low on more than two criteria excluded or flagged as context only.
papers.modelDetails: Framework: TRiSM pillars adapted to AMAS (explainability, ModelOps, application security, model privacy, lifecycle governance), with a reference architecture including orchestrator, memory, tools, a human-in-the-loop interface and a Trust and Audit module that records actions and rationales. Trust index T = (w_acc A + w_rob R + w_align L) / (1 + lambda V), with A calibrated task success, R robustness under shift, L alignment (1 - violation rate), V violation penalty, weights summing to 1, lambda >= 0. Composite M_comp = w_T M_T + w_E M_E + w_U M_U + w_Co M_Co, with the full vector reported and model selection by minimum thresholds (e.g. M_T >= tau_T) or Pareto optimality. CSS = (1/N_pairs) x sum over ordered agent pairs of Impact(a_i -> a_j) x Quality(a_j | a_i); worked example: planner speeds coder by 35% (Impact 0.35), tester coverage 92% (Quality 0.92), CSS for that link = 0.32. TUE_lin = a_s Sel + a_a Arg + a_e Exec + a_o Out + a_f Eff, each in [0,1], weights summing to 1 (selection, argument validity, execution success, outcome correctness, efficiency). Security metrics: attack success rate, robustness score, defence effectiveness rate, false positive and negative rates.
papers.training: Not applicable (review).
papers.evaluation: Not applicable as an experiment. The paper proposes a five-dimension evaluation template: trustworthiness (OOD success, violation rate, calibration ECE/Brier, fairness), explainability (coverage, faithfulness, stability, human ratings), user-centred performance (CSAT, goal fulfilment, clarification turns, NASA-TLX), coordination (team success, messages/tokens, rounds to consensus, plan consistency, deadlock rate, CSS, TUE), and composite reporting.
papers.baselines: Not applicable. Compared with prior surveys in a coverage table (Table 1) on whether they address TRiSM aspects.
papers.results: Screening: 250 shortlisted, 180 included. Corpus composition: journal articles 61.2%. Figure 1 cites more than 2,300 papers mentioning 'agentic AI' from January 2023 to April 2025. No quantitative system results; CSS example value 0.32 is illustrative only.
papers.statistics: Not reported
papers.availability: Not available (review; no code). arXiv version: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04133.

papers.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
papers.authors: Cemri M, Pan MZ, Yang S, Agrawal LA, Chopra B, Tiwari R, Keutzer K, Parameswaran A, Klein D, Ramchandran K, Zaharia M, Gonzalez JE, Stoica I
papers.aim: To find out why LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) fail. The authors build a failure taxonomy (MAST) and a large annotated dataset of failed and successful MAS runs (MAST-Data).
papers.method: Six experts used Grounded Theory to study 150 execution traces from 5 MAS frameworks and derived 14 failure modes in 3 categories. Definitions were refined in three inter-annotator agreement rounds (Cohen's kappa 0.88), then an OpenAI o1 LLM-as-a-judge was calibrated against human labels (kappa 0.77) and used to annotate 1642 traces from 7 frameworks. Two intervention case studies (AG2 MathChat, ChatDev) tested prompt and topology fixes.
papers.result: MAS failure rates were 41% to 86.7% on 7 open-source MAS. Failure categories across 1642 traces: system design issues 44.2%, inter-agent misalignment 32.3%, task verification 23.5%. Most common modes: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of termination conditions 12.4%, disobey task specification 11.8%. LLM annotator (o1 few-shot): accuracy 0.94, F1 0.80, kappa 0.77. ChatDev with new topology rose from 25.0% to 40.6% on ProgramDev-v0; AG2 with improved prompt rose from 84.75% to 89.75% on GSM-Plus (GPT-4).
papers.tools: MAS frameworks: ChatDev, MetaGPT, HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2 (MathChat), Magentic-One, OpenManus. LLMs: GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf. OpenAI o1 as LLM judge. Python library 'agentdash' (pip). Cohen's kappa, Wilcoxon test.
papers.gap: MAST is not claimed to be exhaustive. Simple prompt or topology fixes give only modest gains and task success stays low. Inter-agent misalignment needs agents that model other agents' information needs ('theory of mind'). Verification is often shallow (compile checks only). Closed-source MAS (e.g. Manus) cannot be analysed because traces are not available.
papers.relation: Directly relevant to O1 (multi-agent orchestration). The 14 failure modes give a checklist for the orchestrator: role adherence, explicit termination rules, clarification requests instead of guessing, no information withholding between pathway agents, and multi-level verification before a result is passed on. MAST failure modes such as 'fail to ask for clarification' and 'incorrect verification' map onto our deferral-to-clinician design. The LLM-annotator pipeline could be reused to audit traces of our brain-tumour agents.
papers.limitations: The taxonomy is derived from coding, math and general-agent tasks only, not from clinical tasks. Large-scale labels come from an LLM judge (kappa 0.77 with humans), so some labels may be wrong. Benchmarks differ across MAS, so failure profiles are not a fair performance comparison. Interventions were tested on only two systems. Future work: deeper structural MAS redesigns, better verification, and training models for inter-agent communication.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors wanted a shared vocabulary for why LLM multi-agent systems fail. They first ran five open-source MAS (HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2, ChatDev, MetaGPT) on programming and math tasks and collected over 150 execution traces, each averaging more than 15,000 lines. Six experts analysed these traces with Grounded Theory: open coding of failure behaviours, constant comparison across systems, memoing and theorising, until no new failure types appeared (over 20 hours per expert). This produced a draft taxonomy. To make the labels consistent, three annotators independently labelled 5 random traces per round, met to resolve disagreements, and changed, merged or added definitions. After three rounds (about 10 hours of discussion) Cohen's kappa reached 0.88. The final MAST has 14 failure modes in 3 categories: system design issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification, each linked to pre-execution, execution or post-execution stages. Because manual labelling of 1600+ traces was too costly, they built an LLM-as-a-judge: OpenAI o1 receives the trace, the MAST definitions and few-shot human-labelled examples, and returns the failure modes with reasons. On held-out human labels it scored accuracy 0.94, F1 0.80 and kappa 0.77 (zero-shot kappa was only 0.58). They then checked generalisation on two unseen systems (OpenManus, Magentic-One) and benchmarks (MMLU, GAIA), where human kappa was 0.79. With this pipeline they labelled 1642 traces from 7 MAS and several LLMs (GPT-4/4o/4o-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, CodeLlama-7B). System design failures were most common (44.2%), followed by misalignment (32.3%) and verification (23.5%). Finally, two case studies tested fixes. In AG2 MathChat on 200 GSM-Plus problems with 6 repetitions, a clearer prompt with a verification section raised GPT-4 accuracy from 84.75% to 89.75%; a Solver-Coder-Verifier topology helped GPT-4o (p = 0.03). In ChatDev, a cyclic topology that ends only when the CTO approves all reviews raised ProgramDev-v0 success from 25.0% to 40.6%. A PhD student can adapt this by logging every agent message in the clinical pipeline, labelling failures with MAST codes, and using an LLM judge calibrated against clinician labels.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical, qualitative-plus-quantitative study of MAS execution traces. Grounded Theory analysis (open coding, constant comparison, memoing, theorising) by 6 expert annotators, followed by inter-annotator agreement studies and an LLM-as-a-judge annotation pipeline. Retrospective analysis of collected traces plus two prospective intervention experiments. Institutions: UC Berkeley (USA) and Intesa Sanpaolo (Italy).
papers.datasets: MAST-Data: 1642 annotated execution traces from 7 MAS frameworks. Human-evaluated/human-annotated/LLM-annotated sets of 30 traces each for ChatDev (ProgramDev, GPT-4o), MetaGPT (ProgramDev, GPT-4o), HyperAgent (SWE-Bench Lite, Claude-3.7-Sonnet), AppWorld (Test-C, GPT-4o), AG2 MathChat (GSM-Plus, GPT-4), Magentic-One (GAIA, GPT-4o), OpenManus (ProgramDev, GPT-4o). LLM-annotated only: 100 traces each for ChatDev and MetaGPT on ProgramDev-v2 with GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (MetaGPT only), Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf. Human-evaluated plus LLM-annotated: AG2 on OlympiadBench (GPT-4o, 206), GSMPlus (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, 193), MMLU (GPT-4o-mini, 168), Magentic-One on GAIA (GPT-4o, 165). MAST-Data-human: 21 traces each annotated by 3 experts. Taxonomy development set: 150+ traces from 5 MAS (HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2, ChatDev, MetaGPT), each over 15,000 lines of text on average. ProgramDev: 30 coding tasks (e.g. Tic-Tac-Toe, Chess, Sudoku); ProgramDev-v2: 100 tasks; ProgramDev-v0: 32 tasks used in the ChatDev case study. AG2 case study: 200 randomly selected GSM-Plus problems. Failure defined as the MAS not achieving the intended task objective.
papers.preprocessing: Traces were collected by running each MAS on its benchmark. Theoretical sampling was used to select the 5 initial frameworks and 2 task categories (programming, math). Annotators labelled traces with failure modes plus textual justifications. In each IAA round, 3 annotators independently labelled 5 randomly selected traces. Held-out human-annotated traces were used to validate the LLM annotator. No train/test split in the machine-learning sense; few-shot examples for the LLM judge came from human-annotated data.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: collect 150 traces from 5 MAS and analyse them with Grounded Theory until theoretical saturation (over 20 hours of annotation per expert). Step 2: build a preliminary taxonomy and refine it in 3 IAA rounds (about 10 hours spent resolving disagreements) until Cohen's kappa = 0.88. Final MAST: 14 failure modes in 3 categories mapped to pre-execution, execution and post-execution stages. FC1 System design issues: 1.1 disobey task specification (11.8%), 1.2 disobey role specification (1.5%), 1.3 step repetition (15.7%), 1.4 loss of conversation history (2.8%), 1.5 unaware of termination conditions (12.4%). FC2 Inter-agent misalignment: 2.1 conversation reset (2.2%), 2.2 fail to ask for clarification (6.8%), 2.3 task derailment (7.4%), 2.4 information withholding (0.85%), 2.5 ignored other agent's input (1.9%), 2.6 reasoning-action mismatch (13.2%). FC3 Task verification: 3.1 premature termination (6.2%), 3.2 no or incomplete verification (8.2%), 3.3 incorrect verification (9.1%). Step 3: LLM annotator = OpenAI o1 prompted with the trace, MAST definitions and few-shot human-annotated examples; it outputs detected failure modes with reasons. Step 4: test generalisation on 2 unseen MAS (OpenManus, Magentic-One) and 2 new benchmarks (MMLU, GAIA): human IAA kappa = 0.79. Step 5: annotate all 1642 traces. Interventions: AG2 (i) improved prompt with a verification section, (ii) new topology with Problem Solver, Coder and Verifier roles where only the Verifier can end the conversation; ChatDev (i) role-specific prompts so only superior agents can finalise conversations and verifier focuses on edge cases, (ii) topology changed from DAG to cyclic graph that ends only when the CTO confirms all reviews are satisfied, with a maximum iteration cut-off.
papers.training: No model training. LLM annotator is prompt-based (OpenAI o1, few-shot). AG2 case study run with GPT-4 and GPT-4o, 6 repetitions per configuration. ChatDev case study run with GPT-4o. Hardware, temperature and run times not reported.
papers.evaluation: Taxonomy reliability: Cohen's kappa between 3 expert annotators over 3 IAA rounds, plus one out-of-domain round. LLM annotator: accuracy, recall, precision, F1 and Cohen's kappa against held-out human labels. MAS task success checked by humans (HE) where marked. Failure distributions compared across MAS and across LLMs (e.g. GPT-4o vs Claude-3.7-Sonnet in MetaGPT; MetaGPT vs ChatDev on ProgramDev). Interventions: task accuracy (%) on GSM-Plus (AG2), ProgramDev-v0 and HumanEval (ChatDev), with Wilcoxon tests for AG2, plus MAST failure-mode counts before and after.
papers.baselines: LLM annotator: o1 zero-shot vs o1 few-shot. Interventions: baseline AG2 MathChat and baseline ChatDev vs improved-prompt and new-topology versions. Manus (closed source) checked only for task success (60% on ProgramDev).
papers.results: LLM annotator: o1 zero-shot accuracy 0.89, recall 0.62, precision 0.68, F1 0.64, kappa 0.58; o1 few-shot accuracy 0.94, recall 0.77, precision 0.833, F1 0.80, kappa 0.77. Human IAA kappa = 0.88 (in-domain), 0.79 (out-of-domain). Category share over 1642 traces: FC1 44.2%, FC2 32.3%, FC3 23.5% (over the first 210 traces: 41.8%, 36.9%, 21.3%). Failure rate of 7 SOTA open-source MAS: 41% to 86.7%. MetaGPT with GPT-4o had 39% fewer FC1 failures than with Claude-3.7-Sonnet. MetaGPT had 60-68% fewer FC1 and FC2 failures than ChatDev but 1.56x more FC3 failures. AG2 GSM-Plus GPT-4: baseline 84.75 +/- 1.94, improved prompt 89.75 +/- 1.44, new topology 85.50 +/- 1.18. AG2 GSM-Plus GPT-4o: baseline 84.25 +/- 1.86, improved prompt 89.00 +/- 1.38, new topology 88.83 +/- 1.51. ChatDev ProgramDev-v0: baseline 25.0, improved prompt 34.4, new topology 40.6. ChatDev HumanEval: 89.6, 90.3, 91.5. Role specification fix: +9.4% success; high-level objective verification step: +15.6% on ProgramDev. Topology changes reduced more failure modes than prompt changes. Inter-category correlations were low (0.17-0.32).
papers.statistics: Cohen's kappa for inter-annotator agreement (0.88; 0.79 out-of-domain) and LLM-human agreement (0.77). Wilcoxon test for AG2 interventions: GPT-4 new topology vs baseline p = 0.4 (not significant); GPT-4o baseline vs improved prompt and vs new topology p = 0.03. Results reported as mean +/- spread over 6 repetitions. Correlation analysis between failure categories (0.17-0.32).
papers.availability: Code and taxonomy: https://github.com/multi-agent-systems-failure-taxonomy/MAST. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mcemri/MAST-Data. Python package: pip install agentdash.

papers.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
papers.authors: Hong S, Zhuge M, Chen J, Zheng X, Cheng Y, Zhang C, Wang J, Wang Z, Yau SKS, Lin Z, Zhou L, Ran C, Xiao L, Wu C, Schmidhuber J
papers.aim: To reduce cascading hallucinations and logic errors in LLM multi-agent systems by encoding human Standardised Operating Procedures (SOPs) into agent roles, structured hand-off documents and a shared message pool.
papers.method: MetaGPT models a software company with five agents (Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer, QA Engineer) that work in a fixed SOP sequence and pass structured documents (PRD, system design, task list, code, tests) instead of free chat. Agents publish to and subscribe from a shared message pool, and the Engineer uses executable feedback (run unit tests, debug, up to 3 retries). It was evaluated on HumanEval, MBPP and a new 70-task SoftwareDev benchmark.
papers.result: Pass@1: HumanEval 85.9% and MBPP 87.7% (vs GPT-4 67.0% on HumanEval). On SoftwareDev (7 tasks) MetaGPT executability 3.75/4 vs ChatDev 2.25; running time 541 s vs 762 s; human revision cost 0.83 vs 2.5; 124.3 tokens per code line vs 248.9. Executable feedback added +4.2% (HumanEval) and +5.4% (MBPP) Pass@1.
papers.tools: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613; GPT-4 32K for SoftwareDev averages), GPT-3.5-Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), Deepseek Coder 33B as alternative backends. ReAct-style agent behaviour. Web search tool for Product Manager, code execution for Engineer. Open-source Python framework MetaGPT.
papers.gap: No UI/front-end or multimodal agents yet. Hard to meet complex real-world requirements. Users cannot easily interrupt agents or set checkpoints. Self-improvement of constraints across projects is only explored in an appendix.
papers.relation: Relevant to O1. MetaGPT shows how to make agent hand-offs explicit and auditable: each agent produces a structured artefact with a fixed schema, agents only act once their prerequisite documents exist, and a shared publish-subscribe pool stores all messages. For our brain-tumour system, the same idea can define structured hand-off records between imaging, pathology/report and surgical-planning agents, which also gives a log for clinician review and audit. The executable-feedback loop with a retry cap is a model for bounded self-checking before deferring to a clinician.
papers.limitations: Software engineering domain only. SoftwareDev main comparison uses only 7 tasks and human scoring of executability. Performance depends strongly on the backend (GPT-4 much better than GPT-3.5 or Deepseek Coder 33B). Higher token use than ChatDev. Future work: UI/front-end agents, multimodal tools, human checkpoints, and self-improving SOPs.
papers.methodologyDetail: MetaGPT treats a multi-agent LLM system like a small software company that follows written Standard Operating Procedures. The user gives a one-line requirement. Five role agents then work in a fixed order. The Product Manager (allowed to web-search) writes a Product Requirement Document with user stories and a requirement pool. The Architect turns this into a system design: file list, data structures, interface definitions and a sequence diagram. The Project Manager splits the design into tasks. The Engineer writes the classes and functions, and the QA Engineer writes test cases. Each role has a profile (name, goal, constraints) and uses ReAct-style reasoning. Instead of chatting, agents exchange structured documents with a fixed schema, which avoids information loss like in a 'telephone game'. All documents go into a shared message pool. Each agent subscribes only to the document types it needs (for example the Architect follows PRDs), and an agent starts only when all of its prerequisite inputs are available. After writing code, the Engineer runs unit tests, reads the errors, debugs using its memory of past runs and tries again, up to 3 retries. Evaluation used HumanEval (164 tasks) and MBPP (427 tasks) with Pass@1, and a new SoftwareDev set of 70 tasks, of which 7 were used for head-to-head comparison. For SoftwareDev, humans scored executability from 1 to 4 and counted manual fixes; time, tokens, cost and code size were also logged. Using GPT-4, MetaGPT reached 85.9% Pass@1 on HumanEval and 87.7% on MBPP, against 67.0% for GPT-4 alone. On SoftwareDev it scored 3.75 executability versus 2.25 for ChatDev and needed 0.83 human revisions versus 2.5. Ablations showed that adding roles beyond the Engineer raised executability from 1.0 to 4.0 and cut revisions from 10 to 2.5, at a cost rise from $0.915 to $1.385. Removing executable feedback lowered Pass@1 by 4.2 and 5.4 points. To adapt this, a PhD student can define a fixed clinical SOP, a schema for each agent's output document, a subscription map, and a capped self-check loop before hand-off.
papers.studyDesign: Framework design paper with benchmark experiments and ablation studies. Computer-science laboratory study (no human participants except evaluators). Institutions: DeepWisdom, KAUST (Saudi Arabia), Xiamen University, CUHK-Shenzhen, Nanjing University (China), University of Pennsylvania, UC Berkeley (USA), IDSIA (Switzerland).
papers.datasets: HumanEval: 164 handwritten Python programming tasks with specifications, reference code and tests. MBPP: 427 Python tasks with descriptions, reference code and automated tests. SoftwareDev (new): 70 software development tasks (mini-games, image processing, data visualisation etc.), each with its own prompt; 7 representative tasks randomly chosen for main comparisons (Flappy bird, Tank battle game, 2048 game, Snake game, Brick breaker game, Excel data process, CRUD manage); 11 tasks listed in the appendix; 5 tasks used for backend-LLM and instruction-level experiments.
papers.preprocessing: Prompts for HumanEval and MBPP were slightly modified to match response format requirements. For SoftwareDev, high-level prompts were used (average 13.2 words); a detailed-prompt variant averaged 42.2 words. No train/test split because no model training was done.
papers.modelDetails: Roles: Product Manager (writes PRD with user stories and requirement pool; can use web search), Architect (system design: file list, data structures, interface definitions, sequence flow diagram), Project Manager (task distribution), Engineer (writes code; can execute code), QA Engineer (writes test cases). Each role has a profile with name, goal and constraints. All agents follow ReAct-style behaviour and watch the environment (message pool). Workflow: sequential SOP from user requirement to PRD to design to tasks to code to tests. Structured communication: each role outputs documents and diagrams following a fixed schema, not free dialogue. Publish-subscribe: a global shared message pool; agents subscribe by role interests and an agent acts only after all prerequisite dependencies are received. Executable feedback: after first code generation the Engineer writes and runs unit tests, reads results, debugs using its own execution and debug memory, and repeats until tests pass or a maximum of 3 retries is reached. Appendix: a self-improvement mechanism that updates role constraints from summaries of past projects.
papers.training: No model training; all agents are prompted LLMs (mainly GPT-4). HumanEval prompt-sensitivity experiments were repeated five times with gpt-4-0613 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0613. Temperature, hardware and other run settings not reported. Cost measured: SoftwareDev running time 541 s and 31,255 tokens per task on average (7 tasks); ablation expense from $0.915 (1 agent) to $1.385 (4 agents).
papers.evaluation: HumanEval and MBPP: unbiased Pass@k (k = 1, single attempt). SoftwareDev: (A) executability scored by humans from 1 (non-functional) to 4 (flawless); (B) cost: running time, token usage, money; (C) code statistics: number of code files, lines per file, total lines; (D) productivity = tokens per line of code (lower is better); (E) human revision cost = number of manual corrections (each up to 3 lines). Ablations on roles (adding Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager to Engineer) and on executable feedback; backend LLM comparison; high-level vs detailed instructions.
papers.baselines: Code LLMs: AlphaCode (1.1B), Incoder (6.7B), CodeGeeX (13B), CodeGeeX-Mono (16.1B), CodeGen, PaLM Coder (540B), Codex (175B), Codex + CodeT, GPT-4. Agent frameworks on SoftwareDev: AutoGPT, LangChain with Python REPL tool, AgentVerse, ChatDev. MetaGPT without executable feedback.
papers.results: Pass@1 HumanEval / MBPP: MetaGPT 85.9 / 87.7; MetaGPT w/o feedback 81.7 / 82.3; GPT-4 67.0 / not reported; Codex + CodeT 65.8 / 67.7; Codex 47.0 / 58.1; PaLM Coder 36.0 / 47.0; CodeGeeX-Mono 32.9 / 38.6; CodeGeeX 18.9 / 26.9; Incoder 15.2 / 17.6; AlphaCode 17.1 / not reported. SoftwareDev (ChatDev / MetaGPT w/o feedback / MetaGPT): executability 2.25 / 3.67 / 3.75; running time 762 / 503 / 541 s; tokens 19,292 / 24,613 / 31,255; code files 1.9 / 4.6 / 5.1; lines per file 40.8 / 42.3 / 49.3; total lines 77.5 / 194.6 / 251.4; productivity 248.9 / 126.5 / 124.3; human revision cost 2.5 / 2.25 / 0.83. Executability on 7 tasks: AutoGPT, LangChain, AgentVerse 1.0 each, ChatDev 2.1, MetaGPT 3.9. Role ablation (agents, lines, expense, revisions, executability): Engineer only 1, 83.0, $0.915, 10, 1.0; +Product 2, 112.0, $1.059, 6.5, 2.0; +Product+Architect 3, 143.0, $1.204, 4.0, 2.5; +Product+Project 3, 205.0, $1.251, 3.5, 2.0; all four 4, 191.0, $1.385, 2.5, 4.0. Backends on 5 tasks (time s, lines, executability, revisions): GPT-3.5 75.18, 161.6, 2.8, 2.4; GPT-4 552.94, 178.2, 3.8, 1.2; Deepseek Coder 33B 1186.20, 120.2, 1.4, 2.6. Instruction level: high-level executability 3.8, revisions 1.2; detailed 4.0, revisions 1.6.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals; values are averages).
