For a PhD orchestrator, the most useful items are: calibrated per-patient uncertainty and implausible-output checks (traceability 3), full logging of inputs, outputs and clinician decisions with anonymised IDs in encrypted logs (traceability 5), human override (usability 2), local validity and recalibration in low-resource settings (universality 1 and 4), and federated learning or differential privacy (general 2). A student can score their system against all 30 items as a compliance table.
papers.studyDesign: International expert consensus study (modified Delphi), 24 months, started 2021. FUTURE-AI Consortium led from Universitat de Barcelona (BCN-AIM) with experts from 50 countries on all continents; origin in five EU projects (EuCanImage, ProCAncer-I, CHAIMELEON, PRIMAGE, INCISIVE; AI4HI network). Funded by EU Horizon 2020 grant 952103 (EuCanImage). Not a patient study.
papers.datasets: No patient data. Participants: round 1, six working groups of 3 experts each (18 experts); rounds 2-5, 72 experts (AI scientists, clinicians, ethicists, social scientists, legal and industry experts); round 6, 44 additional external experts (patient advocates, social scientists, regulators, more from Africa, Latin America and Asia); round 8, final consortium of 117 experts from 50 countries. Literature review of trustworthy AI, reporting guidelines (TRIPOD+AI, CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, PROBAST-AI, CLEAR) and EU, FDA and WHO documents.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable. Consensus process steps: literature review and thematic clustering of trustworthy AI requirements into 6 principles (Table 1); round 1 working groups proposed 6-10 best practices per principle, merged to 55 after removing overlap; round 2 survey kept items with >90% high agreement and discarded those with strong negative feedback (mostly method-specific ones), giving 22 items and 16 contentious points, plus a new general category; round 3 broadened scope from medical imaging to healthcare, giving 30 items; round 4 rated each item for research vs deployable tools; round 5 manuscript feedback; round 6 external feedback from 44 experts; round 7 four online meetings in June 2023; round 8 final online vote.
papers.modelDetails: Not an AI model. The framework structure: Fairness (define bias sources; collect individual and data attributes; evaluate fairness and correct bias). Universality (define clinical settings including low vs high resource; use standards such as SNOMED CT, OMOP, DICOM, FHIR/HL7, IEEE, ISO; evaluate on external/multisite data; evaluate local clinical validity with recalibration or fine-tuning). Traceability (risk management file; documentation such as AI information leaflet, model cards, AI passport; quality control of inputs and outputs with out-of-distribution detection, sanity checks and calibrated uncertainty per patient; periodic auditing, e.g. biannual or annual, with drift detection; logging of user actions, AI inputs, AI outputs, clinical decisions, timestamp, user ID, anonymised patient ID, in encrypted logs; governance with assigned roles and liability). Usability (user requirements; human-AI interaction and oversight with human-in-the-loop checks and ability to overrule AI; training materials; usability evaluation including automation bias; clinical utility and safety, e.g. randomised trial). Robustness (define data variations; train with representative real-world data; stress and repeatability tests). Explainability (define needs with users; evaluate explanations quantitatively and with users). General (stakeholder engagement; privacy and security incl. federated learning, differential privacy, encryption; risk mitigation; evaluation plan; regulatory compliance such as EU AI Act, MDR, FDA SaMD; ethical issues; social and environmental issues). Compliance levels: + recommended, ++ highly recommended, separately for research and deployable tools.
papers.training: Not applicable (no model training). Consensus process lasted 24 months over 8 rounds.
papers.evaluation: Quantitative analysis of voting patterns (consensus and disagreement levels) and qualitative synthesis of free-text feedback by recurring themes. Round 2 voting options: absolutely essential, very important, of average importance, of little importance, not important at all; plus keep/refine wording. Round 6 options: agree, disagree, neutral, did not understand, no opinion. Consensus threshold in round 2: >90% high agreement. Final approval: less than 5% disagreement.
papers.baselines: Compared conceptually with existing guidelines: FAIR data principles, TRIPOD+AI, CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, PROBAST-AI, CLEAR, WHO ethics report, EU High-Level Expert Group checklist.
papers.results: Round 1: 55 preliminary recommendations from 6 groups of 3 experts. Round 2: 72 experts; 22 recommendations retained and 16 contentious points identified; seventh 'general' category added. Round 3: 30 recommendations (6 new general items). Round 6: 44 external experts gave feedback; most non-agreement due to unclear wording. Round 7: 4 online meetings, June 2023; adversarial-attack testing was merged into cybersecurity, and mandatory third-party clinical evaluation was dropped as impractical in resource-limited settings. Round 8: 117 experts, all 30 recommendations approved with <5% disagreement; remaining disagreement was mainly about 'recommended' vs 'highly recommended'. From Table 2, 26 of 30 items are highly recommended (++) for deployable tools and 13 of 30 for research tools.
papers.statistics: Descriptive consensus percentages only (>90% agreement threshold in round 2; <5% disagreement in final vote). No statistical tests.
papers.availability: Guideline and self-assessment checklist at www.future-ai.eu; appendix tables (glossary, stakeholders) online with the BMJ article. No code or data.

papers.title: Intricacies of human-AI interaction in dynamic decision-making for precision oncology
papers.authors: Niraula D, Cuneo KC, Dinov ID, et al.
papers.aim: To study how clinicians change their radiotherapy dose decisions when they see recommendations, outcome estimates and uncertainty from an AI decision-support tool (ARCliDS). The study looks at model-agnostic and model-specific collaborative behaviour.
papers.method: A two-phase within-subject reader study. Clinicians first chose a mid-treatment dose without AI (Unassisted) and then re-chose it after seeing ARCliDS recommendations (AI-assisted), and gave confidence (0-5) and an AI trust score (0-5). Decisions were analysed with matched-pair randomization t-tests, Spearman correlations and intraclass correlation coefficients.
papers.result: 144 evaluations (NSCLC 72 = 9 evaluators x 8 patients; HCC 72 = 8 evaluators x 9 patients). AI changed 41 (57%) NSCLC and 34 (47%) HCC decisions, but distribution-level tests were mostly not significant. Decision adjustment correlated with dissimilarity to AI (NSCLC rho=0.53, HCC rho=0.60, p<0.001). Agreement with AI correlated with AI trust (NSCLC rho=0.59, HCC rho=0.70, p<0.001). Inter-evaluator ICC rose with AI, e.g. NSCLC ICC(C,1) 0.135 to 0.216, HCC ICC(C,1) 0.163 to 0.264.
papers.tools: ARCliDS (model-based deep reinforcement learning, graph neural network radiotherapy environment, ensemble of 5 models for uncertainty); R Shiny, Plotly, reticulate, googlesheets4, shinyapps.io (Standard plan, max 5 instances, 8 GB each), Google Sheets storage; Python with pydicom, dicompylercore, NumPy (float16 arrays), scipy.ndimage.zoom; irr R package for ICC; randomization test code from David C Howell.
papers.gap: No ground truth for the continuous dose decisions; no external validation dataset; small sample; retrospective, simulated setting; no subgroup analysis by experience or specialty; effect of faulty AI not tested.
papers.relation: Studies how clinicians accept or override AI recommendations in oncology depending on AI confidence, which is relevant to logging and using clinician validations.
papers.limitations: Adaptive radiotherapy is not standard practice; patients came from the AI training data, not an external set; 144 evaluations give low inferential power; retrospective setting may differ from prospective behaviour; remarks were optional and uneven (48 total). Future work: prospective randomized study, larger sample, faulty-AI arms, varying explainability, time pressure, stratification by clinician characteristics, per-user online fine-tuning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors tested how clinicians work with ARCliDS, a reinforcement-learning tool that recommends a mid-treatment daily radiotherapy dose. ARCliDS was trained earlier on two retrospective trial cohorts: NSCLC patients from trial NCT01190527 (30 fractions, 13 multi-omics features chosen from 297) and HCC patients from three adaptive SBRT trials (3+2 fractions, 13 features chosen from 110). Its environment predicts TCP and NTCP, and its agent maximises a reward r = tcp(1-ntcp) with bonus points (+2 when tcp>0.70 and ntcp<0.172 for NSCLC, or tcp>0.90 and ntcp<0.25 for HCC; +1 when tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50). An ensemble of 5 models gives mean +/- SEM for the dose and outcomes. Cross-validated AUROC was 0.73 (TCP) and 0.79 (NTCP) for NSCLC and 0.74 and 0.68 for HCC. For the study, 8 NSCLC and 9 HCC patients were randomly picked. DICOM CT, structures and dose were converted to float16 NumPy arrays and shown as 2D slices in an R Shiny web app with Plotly viewers, auto-saving to Google Sheets. Each evaluator watched a 10-minute tutorial, then for each patient (random order) entered an unassisted dose (NSCLC 1.5-4 Gy/fx, HCC 1-15 Gy/fx) and confidence 0-5. Next they saw the AI dose, a TCP-NTCP outcome space with error bars and feature distribution plots, then re-entered dose and confidence and answered 4 items that sum to an AI trust score 0-5. They could not go back to the unassisted page. Thirteen clinicians from Moffitt and Michigan completed 17 evaluations, giving 144 paired decisions. Analysis used matched-pair randomization t-tests, Spearman correlations of derived values (adjustment aia-un, dissimilarity ai-un, agreement -|aia-ai|, closeness to standard of care), and McGraw-Wong ICC for inter-reader agreement. A PhD student can reuse this paired design, the 0-5 confidence and trust scales, and the derived quantities to measure clinician validation of a deferring AI.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, two-phase sequential Human-AI interaction reader study (within-subject, each case: Unassisted then AI-assisted). Two institutions in the USA: Moffitt Cancer Center (Tampa, FL) and Michigan Medicine (University of Michigan). IRB Moffitt MCC# 20750. Two disease modules: NSCLC adaptive radiotherapy and HCC adaptive SBRT.
papers.datasets: (1) NSCLC: UMCC 2007-123 phase II dose-escalation trial NCT01190527; inoperable or unresectable NSCLC, 30 daily fractions (about 50 Gy EQD2 in evaluation phase, up to 92 Gy EQD2 total); endpoints local control (LC) and radiation pneumonitis grade >=2 (RP2); 297 multi-omics features reduced to 13 (cytokines pre-IL4, pre-IL15, slope-IP10; PET radiomics pre-MTV, RD-GLSZM-LZLGE, RD-GLSZM-ZSV; dosimetry tumour gEUD, lung gEUD; SNPs Cxcr1-Rs2234671, Ercc2-Rs238406, Ercc5-Rs1047768; miR-191-5p, miR-20a-5p). Training cohort size: Not reported in this paper (see Niraula et al. 2023). (2) HCC: adaptive arm of trials NCT01519219, NCT01522937, NCT02460835; adaptive SBRT 3+2 fractions with 1-month break; endpoints LC and liver toxicity (>=2 point Child-Pugh rise); 110 features reduced to 13 (sex, age, pre-cirrhosis, pre-ECOG-PS, active lesions, pre-albumin, GTV, Liver-GTV, GTV gEUD, Liver-GTV volume, RD-TGF-beta, RD-CD40L, RD-HGF); 95 of 99 HCC patients had local control. Reader study cases: 8 NSCLC and 9 HCC patients randomly selected from the training data based on imaging availability. Imaging shown: CT, RT structures, 3D dose, cumulative DVH; pre/mid PET for NSCLC; pre-treatment MRI and liver function for HCC. Readers: 20 volunteers, 13 completed, 4 did both modules, 17 completed evaluations (9 NSCLC, 8 HCC); physicians and residents of various specialties.
papers.preprocessing: DICOM CT, RT structure and 3D dose files converted with pydicom and dicompylercore: pixel-to-coordinate transform; select overlapping region between CT and dose; enlarge and interpolate dose to CT resolution with scipy.ndimage.zoom; merge all RT structures into one 3D grid using unique integer values; save as compressed float16 3D NumPy arrays. PET and MRI registered onto CT and RT structures with the same procedure. Cumulative DVH extracted. 2D axial, coronal and sagittal slices shown to reduce rendering time. AI recommendations and outcome estimates precomputed. ARTE validation used 80-20 split, 10-fold stratified shuffle cross-validation.
papers.modelDetails: ARCliDS has two parts. ARTE (artificial radiotherapy environment): radiobiologically constrained transition functions for patient state (graph of multi-omics features, graph neural network based), an RT outcome estimator (TCP and NTCP) and a reward function. ODM (optimal decision maker): agent trained with model-based deep reinforcement learning. Base reward r = tcp(1-ntcp). NSCLC reward: r+2 if tcp>0.70 and ntcp<0.172; r+1 if tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50; else r. HCC reward: r+2 if tcp>0.90 and ntcp<0.25; r+1 if tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50; else r. Dose range: NSCLC 1.5-4 Gy/fx; HCC 1-15 Gy/fx. Uncertainty: ensemble of 5 models, recommendation shown as mean +/- SEM daily dose plus EQD2; outcome space TCP vs NTCP with SEM error bars, colored by reward, green diamond for recommendation; population feature distribution plots. AI trust score (0-5) from 4 multiple-choice items: outcome reasonableness 1 pt, outcome uncertainty 1 pt, agreement with recommended dose range 2 pts, dose uncertainty 1 pt; only 'Reasonable' or 'Agree' scores points. No automatic deferral rule; the clinician always makes the final decision.
papers.training: ARCliDS modules were trained earlier on the retrospective trial cohorts (details in Niraula et al. 2023, Sci Rep); optimizer, learning rate, epochs and batch size: Not reported in this paper. Reader training: two 10-minute tutorial videos (one per disease), a pre-evaluation information session with demo and Q&A; evaluation designed to take under one hour; study ran a little over five months. Cyber security clearance took about 2 weeks (over 4 months total to reach the application).
papers.evaluation: Each evaluator saw patients in a randomized order; Unassisted phase locked once AI was seen and unassisted decision hidden on the AI page. Outcomes: unassisted decision (un), AI-assisted decision (aia), AI recommendation (ai), confidence (0-5) before and after, AI trust (0-5), free-text remarks. Derived: decision adjustment frequency, adjustment level (aia-un), dissimilarity (ai-un), agreement -|aia-ai|, closeness to standard of care -|d-SOC| with SOC 2 Gy/fx NSCLC and 10 Gy/fx HCC. Two-sided matched-pair randomization t-test on un-aia; Spearman correlations; Pearson for un vs aia; ICC (McGraw and Wong, two-way random effects, Consistency and Absolute agreement, single and average) via irr; toxicity-free local control score TCP(1-NTCP). AI model itself: 80-20 split 10-fold stratified shuffle CV, AUROC for TCP and NTCP; radiobiological self-evaluation of ODM. No external validation.
papers.baselines: Unassisted clinician decisions (Human only) versus AI-assisted decisions (Human + AI); standard of care dose (NSCLC 2 Gy/fx, HCC 10 Gy/fx); retrospective clinical decisions for the ODM self-evaluation.
papers.results: Adjusted decisions: NSCLC 41/72 (57%), HCC 34/72 (47%); 15/17 evaluations (88%) had at least 2 adjustments; NSCLC evaluators #7 and #8 made zero. Adjustment range: NSCLC 0-100% by evaluator, 44-78% by patient; HCC 22-67% by evaluator, 25-75% by patient. Adjustment vs dissimilarity: NSCLC rho=0.53, NSCLC excluding zero-adjusters rho=0.58, HCC rho=0.60 (all p<0.001). Trust vs agreement: 0.59, 0.69, 0.70 (p<0.001). aia confidence vs trust: NSCLC rho=0.14 (p=0.26), NSCLC excl. rho=0.34 (p=0.0094), HCC rho=0.47 (p<0.001). Change in confidence vs trust: HCC rho=0.32 (p=0.0055), NSCLC 0.11 (p=0.37), NSCLC excl. 0.19 (p=0.17). Change in confidence vs adjustment level: NSCLC rho=-0.24 (p=0.045), excl. -0.29 (p=0.028), HCC 0.28 (p=0.017). Confidence vs closeness to SOC: un NSCLC 0.15 (p=0.21), excl. 0.25 (p=0.059), HCC 0.32 (p=0.0056); aia NSCLC 0.092 (p=0.44), excl. 0.29 (p=0.029), HCC 0.48 (p<0.001). ICC unassisted to AI-assisted: NSCLC ICC(C,1) 0.135 [-0.005,0.507] to 0.216 [0.04,0.606]; ICC(A,1) 0.102 to 0.201; ICC(C,9) 0.584 to 0.713; ICC(A,9) 0.504 to 0.694; HCC ICC(C,1) 0.163 to 0.264; ICC(A,1) 0.117 to 0.195; ICC(C,8) 0.608 to 0.742; ICC(A,8) 0.515 to 0.659. NSCLC: 76% of adjustments raised TCP and NTCP; HCC: 74% (25/34) lowered TCP and NTCP. Score change aia-un: NSCLC mean 0.0011 (SD 0.0058); HCC mean 0.0059 (SD 0.0144), median 0.0034. ARTE AUROC: NSCLC TCP 0.73+/-0.15, NTCP 0.79+/-0.17; HCC TCP 0.74+/-0.27, NTCP 0.68+/-0.24. ODM reproduced 36% good / improved 74% bad decisions (NSCLC) and 50% / 30% (HCC). Remarks: 48 total (14, 14, 9, 11).
papers.statistics: Two-sided matched-pair randomization t-test (H0: un-aia=0), mostly not significant; Spearman rank correlation with two-sided p-values and 95% covariance ellipses; Pearson correlation for un vs aia (significant positive but not near 1); ICC with 95% CI and one-sided F-test p-values (e.g. NSCLC ICC(C,1) AI-assisted p=0.004; HCC ICC(C,1) AI-assisted p=0.001).
papers.availability: Evaluator decision source data provided with the paper. Patient clinical data restricted (University of Michigan data sharing application). ARCliDS code is proprietary (Moffitt and University of Michigan). Online tools: https://arclids.shinyapps.io/ARCliDS/, https://arclids.shinyapps.io/Eval_NSCLC_v2/, https://arclids.shinyapps.io/Eval_HCC_v2/.

papers.title: Human-AI interaction and collaboration in radiology: from conceptual frameworks to responsible implementation
papers.authors: Kocak B, Cuocolo R
papers.aim: To give a clear overview of how radiologists and AI interact and collaborate, where collaboration adds value or causes harm, and what is needed for responsible implementation.
papers.method: Narrative review based on targeted, topic-driven literature searches, expert knowledge and backward and forward reference chaining, without a formal systematic search. It builds conceptual models, a workflow taxonomy along an autonomy spectrum and design principles, and summarises evidence on cognitive effects, governance and emerging systems.
papers.result: The review proposes an eight-model workflow taxonomy from human-only reading to standalone AI, including an 'uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering' model where AI auto-finalises normal cases and escalates uncertain or positive ones. It summarises evidence such as 'AI as supporting reader' cutting second human reads by up to 87% in more than 280,000 mammograms, prostate MRI AUC rising from 0.882 to 0.916 with AI (61 readers, 360 exams), trainee accuracy falling from about 80% to 20% with incorrect AI, and biased AI lowering clinician accuracy by about 9.1-11.3 percentage points.
papers.tools: Not applicable (review). Mentions vision-language models (e.g. Flamingo-CXR), saliency maps, NLP report-image discrepancy checking, active learning, FDA Predetermined Change Control Plan; figures made in Canva.com; language edited with ChatGPT 5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro.
papers.gap: Most studies evaluate algorithms alone, not the human-AI team in real workflows. Few prospective, multi-institutional studies of team performance, workload, equity and long-term learning. Explanation tools (saliency maps) are unstable; calibrated uncertainty for role arbitration is not yet well tested.
papers.relation: Reviews frameworks for dividing work between radiologists and AI, which guides where the orchestrator should hand control to clinicians.
papers.limitations: Narrative, non-systematic review, so study selection may be biased; no pooled quantitative analysis; workflow diagrams are simplified and focus on narrow task-specific AI. Future work: prospective multi-institutional studies of team performance, workload, equity and training outcomes; uncertainty-aware role arbitration; usable explanations; AI literacy.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review, so there is no dataset or model to reproduce. The authors ran targeted, topic-driven literature searches, used their own expert knowledge, and followed references backward and forward. They did not use a formal systematic protocol, quality scoring or meta-analysis. They organised the material in five steps. First, they defined core terms (human-AI interaction, collaboration, team performance, diagnostic complementarity, automation bias, algorithmic aversion, cognitive offloading, trust calibration, physician-in-the-loop) in a table. Second, they built a workflow taxonomy of eight models along an autonomy spectrum, from human-only reading to standalone AI. For each model they listed the human role, the AI role, the output and the autonomy level. The 'uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering' model lets the AI auto-finalise normal cases and escalate uncertain or positive ones, while the radiologist audits a sample of auto-finalised cases. Third, they gave six design principles (task allocation, workflow placement, interaction mode, trust calibration, learning and feedback, training and supervision) and a table of advantages and risks for five interaction setups. Fourth, they summarised evidence on cognitive effects using numbers from cited studies, for example trainee accuracy falling from about 80% to 20% with wrong AI, and biased AI lowering accuracy by 9.1-11.3 points. Fifth, they described governance (liability stays with the clinician, interdisciplinary committees, shadow then pilot deployment, drift monitoring, FDA change-control plans, EU AI Act literacy) and a five-step physician-in-the-loop active learning loop. For this PhD, the taxonomy and active learning loop can be used as the design template for when the orchestrator acts alone, when it defers, and how clinician corrections feed recalibration.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (review article) by authors from Basaksehir Cam and Sakura City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkiye and University of Salerno, Italy. No primary data; not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset used. Cited evidence includes: Lee et al. reader study, 30 radiologists and residents, 120 chest radiographs (60 with malignant nodules); Ng et al. simulation, more than 280,000 mammograms from two countries; prospective 'AI as additional reader' study, tens of thousands of screening exams; Zajac et al. qualitative study, 18 radiologists at 9 sites in Denmark and Kenya; PI-CAI consortium, 61 readers from 53 centres in 17 countries, 360 MRI exams; EuroAIM/EuSoMII survey of 572 ESR members; international survey of 1,041 radiologists; Chinese survey of 6,726 radiologists from 1,143 hospitals; prospective study of 18,680 chest radiographs.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual frameworks, not a model. Diagnostic complementarity: human and AI errors only partly overlap, so the team can beat either alone. Autonomy spectrum with 8 workflow models: standard of care (human only); concurrent decision support (low); second reader and quality assurance (low to moderate); AI as supporting reader (moderate, AI acts as second reader only when it agrees with reader 1, discordant cases go to human reader 2); AI as additional reader (moderate, safety net on negative-consensus cases, arbitrator reviews flags); AI triage and worklist prioritisation (moderate to high); uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering (high, AI auto-finalises normal cases, escalates uncertain or positive cases, radiologist audits a sample of auto-finalised normals); standalone AI reporting (autonomous, not clinically viable). Six design principles: task allocation, workflow placement, mode of interaction, trust calibration, learning and feedback, training and supervision. Physician-in-the-loop active learning loop in 5 steps: use in routine reporting; flag a subset (uncertain or discordant) for feedback; store in feedback set; periodic review, recalibration or retraining; redeploy and monitor drift and safety. No numeric thresholds given.
papers.training: Not applicable (review). Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable; no formal search protocol, quality appraisal or synthesis method reported. The review recommends phased deployment (shadow deployment, then scoped pilot, then full rollout), continuous post-market surveillance for drift, and evaluation frameworks such as Park et al., ECLAIR and RADAR.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (review).
papers.results: Reported evidence from cited studies: AI supporting reader reduced second human reads by up to 87% while maintaining screening performance; AI additional reader added 0.7-1.6 cancers per 1,000 women screened (83.3% invasive, 47.0% <=10 mm); prostate MRI with AI: AUC 0.882 to 0.916, sensitivity 94.3% to 96.8%, specificity 46.7% to 50.1% at PI-RADS >=3 (3 more true positives, 10 fewer false positives); AI triage cut critical chest radiograph reporting delay from 11.2 to 2.7 days and pneumothorax turnaround from 80.1 to 35.6 min; CTPA pulmonary embolism turnaround 59.9 to 47.6 min; trainee mammography accuracy about 80% with correct AI vs 20% with incorrect AI; biased AI reduced clinician accuracy by about 9.1-11.3 percentage points; saliency map localisation AUPRC 0.024-0.16; reading time 13.3 s vs 14.8 s overall, 10.8 s vs 13.1 s for normal-flag studies, 18.6 s vs 18.4 s for abnormal-flag studies; survey: 47.2% expected more workload, costs 49.5%, legal 43.7%, lack of validation 35.5%; 37% cited lack of trust (aOR 1.77, 95% CI 1.24-2.53, P=0.002 outside Europe); 98% said radiology teams should join AI development, 45% said radiologists should keep full responsibility; 64.8% of Singapore residents and faculty were AI novices, 59.2% said teaching was inadequate.
papers.statistics: No own statistical analysis. Cited: adjusted odds ratio 1.77 (95% CI 1.24-2.53; P=0.002) for lack-of-trust view outside Europe.
papers.availability: Not available (review; no code or data). Open-access article under CC BY-NC 4.0 at dirjournal.org.

heading: O2 - Calibrated uncertainty and escalation (when to defer to the clinician)

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.authors: Guo C, Pleiss G, Sun Y, Weinberger KQ
papers.aim: To check if the confidence scores of modern deep networks match their real accuracy.
papers.method: Measured calibration with ECE and reliability diagrams on many networks and datasets. Compared post-hoc fixes.
papers.result: Modern deep networks are over-confident. Depth, width, batch norm and less weight decay make it worse. Temperature scaling (one parameter) fixes most of it.
papers.tools: ResNet, DenseNet, Wide-ResNet; CIFAR, ImageNet, text datasets
papers.gap: Only tested on the same distribution as training.
papers.relation: Every agent in our system must be calibrated before we use its confidence for escalation. Temperature scaling is our first baseline.
papers.limitations: Calibration breaks when data shifts (new hospital). Future: shift-robust calibration.

papers.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
papers.authors: Gal Y, Ghahramani Z
papers.aim: To get model uncertainty from normal deep networks without changing them much.
papers.method: Showed dropout training is approximate Bayesian inference. Keep dropout on at test time and run many forward passes (MC dropout).
papers.result: Better predictive log-likelihood and RMSE on regression tasks, and useful uncertainty in classification and RL.
papers.tools: Dropout networks, Bayesian approximation
papers.gap: Uncertainty quality depends on dropout rate, and is often still too low.
papers.relation: Cheap way to get epistemic uncertainty for our MRI segmentation and classification agents on modest hardware.
papers.limitations: Several forward passes needed, so slower at inference. Future: better approximations.

papers.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
papers.authors: Lakshminarayanan B, Pritzel A, Blundell C
papers.aim: To give a simple, non-Bayesian way to estimate predictive uncertainty.
papers.method: Train several networks with different random starts, using proper scoring rules (and optional adversarial training), then average.
papers.result: Well-calibrated predictions and higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution samples, often better than MC dropout.
papers.tools: Deep ensembles, MNIST, SVHN, ImageNet
papers.gap: Training and running many models costs a lot.
papers.relation: Strong UQ baseline to compare with MC dropout for our agents. Cost matters in low-resource hospitals.
papers.limitations: Compute and memory cost. Future: lighter ensembles.

papers.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Geifman Y, El-Yaniv R
papers.aim: To let a network refuse to predict on uncertain inputs while guaranteeing a chosen error rate.
papers.method: Selection with Guaranteed Risk (SGR): pick a confidence threshold on held-out data so the error on accepted cases stays under a target, with high probability. Tested softmax response and MC dropout.
papers.result: On ImageNet they could guarantee 2% top-5 error while still covering about 60% of images.
papers.tools: VGG / ResNet, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet
papers.gap: Single model, single decision, same cost for every mistake.
papers.relation: The risk-coverage trade-off is basically our escalation threshold. We need to extend it to asymmetric error cost and to a chain of agents.
papers.limitations: Guarantee assumes test data like calibration data. Future: training models for selection.

papers.title: Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
papers.authors: Mozannar H, Sontag D
papers.aim: To train a classifier and a 'defer to the expert' decision together, with a sound loss.
papers.method: Adds an extra 'defer' class and a consistent surrogate loss based on cross-entropy, taking expert accuracy into account.
papers.result: Beat confidence-based and earlier L2D baselines on CIFAR-10 with synthetic experts, CIFAR-100, CheXpert and hate-speech data.
papers.tools: Surrogate loss, WideResNet, CheXpert
papers.gap: Needs expert labels on training data. Does not limit how many cases go to the expert.
papers.relation: Core method for O2. We need to add the limit of clinician review time and the clinical cost of each error type.
papers.limitations: One expert, one decision. Future: multiple experts and budget constraints.

papers.title: Predict Responsibly: Improving Fairness and Accuracy by Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Madras D, Pitassi T, Zemel R
papers.aim: To show that a model should defer by thinking about who will receive the case, not only its own confidence.
papers.method: Learning-to-defer model that is trained with the downstream decision maker in mind, compared with simple reject option.
papers.result: Better accuracy and fairness of the whole system on COMPAS and Heritage Health data.
papers.tools: Neural networks, fairness metrics
papers.gap: Decision makers were simulated.
papers.relation: Supports our idea that deferral depends on the clinician (radiologist, pathologist, neurosurgeon) who will review it.
papers.limitations: Not tested in medicine. Future: real human decision makers.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
papers.authors: Raghu M, Blumer K, Corrado G, Kleinberg J, Obermeyer Z, Mullainathan S
papers.aim: To decide which cases an algorithm should handle and which should go to humans, to use human effort well.
papers.method: Triage using predicted human error / disagreement plus model uncertainty. Tested on medical data like diabetic retinopathy grading.
papers.result: Mixing algorithm and human by triage did better than full automation or full human review.
papers.tools: Deep learning, uncertainty estimation, triage
papers.gap: Workflow and time cost of humans not modelled in detail.
papers.relation: Our case: specialist time is the scarcest thing. This paper frames the problem in the same way.
papers.limitations: Preprint, retrospective only. Future: prospective test.

papers.title: Enhancing the reliability and accuracy of AI-enabled diagnosis via complementarity-driven deferral to clinicians (CoDoC)
papers.authors: Dvijotham K, Winkens J, Barsbey M, et al., Karthikesalingam A
papers.aim: To learn when to trust a predictive AI and when to defer to the clinician, in real screening.
papers.method: CoDoC uses only the AI confidence score, the clinician's read and ground truth from past data to learn deferral regions. Does not need access to the model inside.
papers.result: In breast cancer screening data it cut false positives (around 25% in the UK set) at the same false negatives and reduced clinician workload a lot. Also tested on TB screening.
papers.tools: Density estimation on confidence scores, mammography and chest X-ray AI
papers.gap: Single AI model and single decision. Retrospective.
papers.relation: The closest prior work to our O2. Our difference: a chain of agents, brain MRI + pathology, and small Sri Lankan data.
papers.limitations: Needs enough labelled past cases with clinician opinion. Future: prospective use.
papers.notes: Same paper as O1-P46 (CoDoC); PDF and methodology under O1-P46

papers.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Bates S
papers.aim: To explain conformal prediction in a practical way.
papers.method: Tutorial with code: split conformal, adaptive sets, conformal risk control, examples on images and medicine.
papers.result: Shows how to turn any model output into prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage.
papers.tools: Conformal prediction, Python examples
papers.gap: Guarantee needs exchangeable data, which is not true across hospitals.
papers.relation: For tumour type we can give a set of likely classes with a coverage guarantee. A large set = escalate. Works with small calibration sets.
papers.limitations: Coverage only on average, not per patient. Future: shift-aware conformal.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
papers.authors: Ovadia Y, Fertig E, Ren J, Nado Z, Sculley D, Nowozin S, Dillon JV, Lakshminarayanan B, Snoek J
papers.aim: To compare uncertainty methods when test data is shifted from training data.
papers.method: Large benchmark of methods (vanilla, temperature scaling, dropout, ensembles, SVI, last-layer) under increasing shift and OOD data.
papers.result: Calibration gets worse as shift grows. Temperature scaling on clean validation does not hold. Deep ensembles were the most robust.
papers.tools: Images, text, genomics; ResNet, LSTM
papers.gap: No method was good under strong shift.
papers.relation: Sri Lankan scanners and protocols are a dataset shift from BraTS. We must test calibration on local data, not just public data.
papers.limitations: Not medical imaging. Future: shift-robust methods.

papers.title: Confidence Calibration and Predictive Uncertainty Estimation for Deep Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Mehrtash A, Wells WM, Tempany CM, Abolmaesumi P, Kapur T
papers.aim: To study calibration and uncertainty of segmentation networks in medical images.
papers.method: Compared Dice vs cross-entropy loss, model ensembles, and proposed segment-level uncertainty. Datasets incl. prostate, heart and brain tumour MRI.
papers.result: Dice-trained models are badly calibrated. Ensembles improve calibration. Segment-level uncertainty relates to how good the Dice is, so it can flag bad segmentations.
papers.tools: FCN / U-Net style models, ensembles, MRI
papers.gap: Ensembles are costly, and no link to a decision (accept or refer).
papers.relation: Direct use in our MRI agent: give a per-tumour uncertainty that is passed to the next agent and used for escalation.
papers.limitations: Few datasets. Future: cheaper UQ.

papers.title: QU-BraTS: MICCAI BraTS 2020 Challenge on Quantifying Uncertainty in Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Mehta R, Filos A, Baid U, Sako C, McKinley R, Rebsamen M, et al., Arbel T
papers.aim: To create a fair way to score uncertainty maps in brain tumour segmentation and compare methods.
papers.method: New score that rewards confidence on correct voxels and uncertainty on wrong ones, and penalises throwing away too many correct voxels. Used to rank challenge teams.
papers.result: Ranked many teams. Ensemble and test-time augmentation methods were common among top teams.
papers.tools: BraTS 2020 multi-parametric MRI, 3D CNNs, ensembles, TTA
papers.gap: Voxel-level score only, not linked to clinical decisions.
papers.relation: Ready-made metric to evaluate our MRI agent uncertainty in a brain tumour setting.
papers.limitations: Only BraTS (adult glioma) data. Future: link uncertainty to clinical use.

papers.title: Second opinion needed: communicating uncertainty in medical machine learning
papers.authors: Kompa B, Snoek J, Beam AL
papers.aim: To argue why medical ML must show uncertainty and be able to say 'I don't know'.
papers.method: Perspective paper with examples and overview of UQ methods.
papers.result: Recommends that models abstain when uncertain and that uncertainty is reported in medical ML studies.
papers.tools: Perspective / review
papers.gap: No new method or experiment.
papers.relation: Good motivation reference for our problem statement and O2.
papers.limitations: Opinion piece. Future: standards for reporting uncertainty.

papers.title: Calibrated Learning to Defer with One-vs-All Classifiers
papers.authors: Rajeev Verma, Eric Nalisnick
papers.relation: Gives a consistent learning-to-defer loss whose deferral probabilities are calibrated, directly supporting a calibrated defer-to-clinician rule.

papers.title: Sample Efficient Learning of Predictors that Complement Humans
papers.authors: Mohammad-Amin Charusaie, Hussein Mozannar, David Sontag, Samira Samadi
papers.relation: Studies learning deferral policies when expert (clinician) labels are scarce, which fits a low-resource setting.

papers.title: Learning to Defer to a Population: A Meta-Learning Approach
papers.authors: Dharmesh Tailor, Aditya Patra, Rajeev Verma, Putra Manggala, Eric Nalisnick
papers.relation: Lets a deferral system adapt to new or changing clinicians at test time, which matters when the pool of available specialists varies.

papers.title: Post-Hoc Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
papers.authors: Harikrishna Narasimhan, Wittawat Jitkrittum, Aditya Krishna Menon, Ankit Singh Rawat, Sanjiv Kumar
papers.relation: Shows how to add deferral to an already-trained classifier after training, a practical route for adding escalation to existing diagnostic agents.

papers.title: Principled Approaches for Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Anqi Mao, Mehryar Mohri, Yutao Zhong
papers.venue: ISAIM 2024 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer)
papers.relation: Gives consistent surrogate losses for routing a case to one of several experts, such as a radiologist or neurosurgeon, with costs included.

papers.title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Anqi Mao, Christopher Mohri, Mehryar Mohri, Yutao Zhong
papers.relation: Learns a deferral rule on top of a fixed pretrained predictor using cost-sensitive losses, which fits a modular multi-agent pipeline.

papers.title: Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts: Consistent Surrogate Losses, Confidence Calibration, and Conformal Ensembles
papers.authors: Rajeev Verma, Daniel Barrejon, Eric Nalisnick
papers.relation: Combines calibration and conformal sets for deferral among several experts, linking uncertainty calibration directly to escalation.

papers.title: Cost-Sensitive Learning to Defer to Multiple Experts with Workload Constraints
papers.authors: Jean V. Alves, Diogo Leitao, Sergio Jesus, Marco O. P. Sampaio, Javier Liebana, Pedro Saleiro, Mario A. T. Figueiredo, Pedro Bizarro
papers.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (arXiv preprint)
papers.relation: Builds error costs and limited expert capacity into deferral, which matters where specialist time is scarce.

papers.title: Towards Unbiased and Accurate Deferral to Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Vijay Keswani, Matthew Lease, Krishnaram Kenthapadi
papers.venue: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2021)
papers.relation: Optimises a classifier and a deferral system together for accuracy and fairness across a set of human experts.

papers.title: Differentiable Learning Under Triage
papers.authors: Nastaran Okati, Abir De, Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez
papers.relation: Learns a triage policy that splits cases between the model and humans, the core decision O2 must make.

papers.title: Combining Human Predictions with Model Probabilities via Confusion Matrices and Calibration
papers.authors: Gavin Kerrigan, Padhraic Smyth, Mark Steyvers
papers.relation: Shows how calibrated model probabilities can be combined with clinician labels, an alternative to full deferral.

papers.authors: Shalmali Joshi, Sonali Parbhoo, Finale Doshi-Velez
papers.relation: Extends learning to defer to multi-step clinical decisions, which resemble staged diagnosis and surgical planning.

papers.relation: Gives clinical-scale evidence that confidence-based referral of uncertain cases to radiologists beats both the AI alone and the radiologist alone.

papers.authors: Paul F. Jaeger, Carsten T. Luth, Lukas Klein, Till J. Bungert

papers.authors: Till J. Bungert, Levin Kobelke, Paul F. Jaeger

papers.title: Failure Detection in Medical Image Classification: A Reality Check and Benchmarking Testbed

papers.title: Rethinking Confidence Calibration for Failure Prediction
papers.authors: Fei Zhu, Zhen Cheng, Xu-Yao Zhang, Cheng-Lin Liu

papers.title: Revisiting the Calibration of Modern Neural Networks

papers.relation: Covers uncertainty quantification together with federated learning in radiology, linking the escalation objective to the PhD's privacy-preserving setting.

papers.title: Clinical AI tools must convey predictive uncertainty for each individual patient
papers.authors: Banerji CRS, Chakraborti T, Harbron C, MacArthur BD
papers.relation: Argues that clinical AI must report per-patient uncertainty so clinicians know when not to rely on it, which is the rationale for uncertainty-aware escalation.

papers.title: Bridging the clinical gap: Confidence informed IDH prediction in brain gliomas using MRI and deep learning
papers.authors: Bangalore Yogananda CG, Truong NCD, Wagner BC, et al.
papers.relation: Uses confidence to decide when MRI-based IDH predictions in glioma are reliable enough for clinical use and when to fall back to tissue testing.

papers.title: CONSeg: Voxelwise Uncertainty Quantification for Glioma Segmentation Using Conformal Prediction
papers.authors: Elyassirad D, Gheiji B, Vatanparast M, Ahmadzadeh AM, et al.
papers.relation: Applies conformal prediction to glioma MRI segmentation so that uncertain cases can be flagged for neuroradiologist review.

papers.title: Quantifying U-Net uncertainty in multi-parametric MRI-based glioma segmentation by spherical image projection
papers.authors: Yang Z, Lafata K, Vaios E, Hu Z, Mullikin T, Yin FF, et al.
papers.relation: Estimates segmentation uncertainty for glioma on multi-parametric MRI to support clinician review of contours.

papers.title: Method to Minimize the Errors of AI: Quantifying and Exploiting Uncertainty of Deep Learning in Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Lee J, Shin D, Oh SH, Kim H
papers.relation: Uses uncertainty to find and reduce errors in brain-tumour segmentation, supporting the idea of sending uncertain outputs to a human.

papers.title: Post-operative glioblastoma multiforme segmentation with uncertainty estimation
papers.authors: Holtzman Gazit M, Faran R, Stepovoy K, Peles O, Shamir RR
papers.relation: Adds uncertainty estimates to post-operative glioblastoma segmentation to flag unreliable results in a neurosurgical workflow.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Classification of Adamantinomatous Craniopharyngioma from Preoperative MRI
papers.authors: Prince EW, Ghosh D, Gorg C, Hankinson TC
papers.relation: Classifies a brain tumour from preoperative MRI with an uncertainty measure that indicates when a prediction should not be trusted.

papers.title: Uncertainty quantification in the radiogenomics modeling of EGFR amplification in glioblastoma
papers.authors: Hu LS, Wang L, Hawkins-Daarud A, Eschbacher JM, et al.
papers.relation: Shows that restricting glioblastoma radiogenomic predictions to low-uncertainty cases raises accuracy, a form of selective prediction in neuro-oncology.

papers.title: Uncertainty quantification in multi-parametric MRI-based meningioma radiotherapy target segmentation
papers.authors: Wang L, Yang Z, LaBella D, Reitman Z, Ginn J, et al.
papers.relation: Uncertainty maps for brain-tumour (meningioma) target delineation that point clinicians to regions needing manual review in treatment planning.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Selective Prediction in Brain-Tumour MRI Classification: Selective Risk Reduction and Component-Wise Reliability Findings
papers.authors: Alshamlan H
papers.relation: Applies selective prediction with abstention directly to brain-tumour MRI classification and evaluates risk-coverage trade-offs.

papers.title: Conformal selective prediction with cost aware deferral for safe clinical triage under distribution shift
papers.authors: Kwon H, Kim DJ
papers.relation: Combines conformal selective prediction with cost-aware deferral to clinicians under distribution shift, closely matching the O2 escalation design.

papers.title: Conformal Triage for Medical Imaging AI Deployment
papers.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Pomerantz S, Do S, Bates S, et al.
papers.relation: From a strong conformal-prediction group: uses conformal risk control to triage imaging cases between autonomous AI output and radiologist review, with statistical guarantees.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction in Clinical Medical Sciences
papers.authors: Vazquez J, Facelli JC
papers.relation: Reviews clinical uses of conformal prediction as a distribution-free way to decide when a model's output is reliable enough to act on.

papers.title: Impact of uncertainty quantification through conformal prediction on volume assessment from deep learning-based MRI prostate segmentation
papers.authors: Gade M, Nguyen KM, Gedde S, Fernandez-Quilez A
papers.relation: Shows that conformal uncertainty on MRI segmentation can screen out unreliable volume estimates before they reach clinical use.

papers.title: Predictive uncertainty estimation for out-of-distribution detection in digital pathology
papers.authors: Linmans J, Elfwing S, van der Laak J, Litjens G
papers.relation: Tests whether uncertainty estimates can catch out-of-distribution pathology slides that should be referred rather than auto-classified.

papers.title: Benchmarking common uncertainty estimation methods with histopathological images under domain shift and label noise
papers.authors: Mehrtens HA, Kurz A, Bucher TC, Brinker TJ
papers.relation: Benchmarks uncertainty methods for selective classification on pathology images under domain shift, which matters for multi-site deployment in low-resource settings.

papers.title: Generalisation effects of predictive uncertainty estimation in deep learning for digital pathology
papers.authors: Poceviciute M, Eilertsen G, Jarkman S, Lundstrom C
papers.relation: Evaluates whether uncertainty-based filtering of pathology predictions still works on external data, which bears on dependable escalation at new hospitals.

papers.title: Statistical uncertainty quantification to augment clinical decision support: a first implementation in sleep medicine
papers.authors: Kang DY, DeYoung PN, Tantiongloc J, Coleman TP, Owens RL
papers.relation: An implemented clinical decision-support system that shows uncertainty to clinicians so they can judge when to override automated output.

papers.title: Identifying normal mammograms in a large screening population using artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Lang K, Dustler M, Dahlblom V, Akesson A, Andersson I, Zackrisson S
papers.relation: Studies AI confidence thresholds for autonomously clearing normal exams while sending the rest to radiologists, a real-world selective autonomy design.

papers.title: Class imbalance on medical image classification: towards better evaluation practices for discrimination and calibration performance
papers.authors: Mosquera C, Ferrer L, Milone DH, Luna D, Ferrante E
papers.relation: Gives radiology-specific guidance on evaluating calibration under class imbalance, needed to validate the confidence scores behind escalation for rare tumour types.

heading: O3 - Data-efficient MRI and pathology models, fusion and federated learning

papers.title: nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation
papers.authors: Isensee F, Jaeger PF, Kohl SAA, Petersen J, Maier-Hein KH
papers.aim: To make segmentation work out-of-the-box on any new medical dataset without manual tuning.
papers.method: Rules that set preprocessing, network (2D/3D U-Net), training and post-processing automatically from dataset properties.
papers.result: Beat most specialised methods on 23 public datasets and many challenges.
papers.tools: U-Net, PyTorch, 3D CNN
papers.gap: Needs strong GPU and no uncertainty output by default.
papers.relation: Our main baseline for tumour segmentation on Sri Lankan MRI.
papers.limitations: Heavy compute, still needs good labels. Future: lighter and label-efficient versions.

papers.title: The RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS 2021 Benchmark on Brain Tumor Segmentation and Radiogenomic Classification
papers.authors: Baid U, Ghodasara S, Mohan S, Bilello M, Calabrese E, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To describe the BraTS 2021 dataset and tasks.
papers.method: Large multi-institution multi-parametric MRI (T1, T1Gd, T2, FLAIR) with expert labels for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour. Also MGMT prediction task.
papers.result: Around 2,000 glioma cases, the biggest public brain tumour MRI set at that time.
papers.tools: Multi-parametric MRI, standard preprocessing (skull strip, co-registration)
papers.gap: Mostly gliomas from Western centres, pre-processed and standardised.
papers.relation: Public pre-training and benchmark set before we use local data. Also shows the gap: our data is not standardised.
papers.limitations: Population and scanner bias. Future: more tumour types and regions.

papers.title: Swin UNETR: Swin Transformers for Semantic Segmentation of Brain Tumors in MRI Images
papers.authors: Hatamizadeh A, Nath V, Tang Y, Yang D, Roth HR, Xu D
papers.aim: To use a Swin transformer encoder for 3D brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: Swin transformer encoder with shifted windows, CNN decoder, skip connections. Trained on BraTS 2021.
papers.result: Among the top methods in BraTS 2021 validation.
papers.tools: Swin Transformer, MONAI, PyTorch
papers.gap: Transformers usually need lots of data.
papers.relation: Candidate model for our MRI agent, compared with nnU-Net.
papers.limitations: Heavy model, small data risk. Future: pretraining.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Pre-Training of Swin Transformers for 3D Medical Image Analysis
papers.authors: Tang Y, Yang D, Li W, Roth HR, Landman B, Xu D, Nath V, Hatamizadeh A
papers.aim: To pretrain 3D models on unlabelled scans so less labelled data is needed later.
papers.method: Self-supervised tasks: masked volume inpainting, rotation prediction and contrastive coding, on about 5,000 unlabelled CT scans.
papers.result: State-of-the-art results on BTCV and Medical Segmentation Decathlon after fine-tuning.
papers.tools: Swin UNETR, self-supervised learning, MONAI
papers.gap: Pretrained on CT, transfer to brain MRI not shown well.
papers.relation: Our labelled Sri Lankan data will be small. Self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled local MRI is a key option.
papers.limitations: Big compute for pretraining. Future: pretraining on MRI.

papers.title: Segment Anything in Medical Images (MedSAM)
papers.authors: Ma J, He Y, Li F, Han L, You C, Wang B
papers.aim: To build one promptable segmentation model for many medical image types.
papers.method: Fine-tuned Segment Anything on over 1.5 million medical image-mask pairs across 10 modalities. User gives a bounding box.
papers.result: Better than SAM and comparable or better than specialist models on many internal and external tests.
papers.tools: SAM, ViT, box prompts
papers.gap: 2D slices, needs a box prompt, weaker on very small or unclear edges.
papers.relation: Clinician can draw a box and correct the result. Good for human-in-the-loop correction and fast labelling of local data.
papers.limitations: Not 3D native. Future: 3D and text prompts.

papers.title: Attention-based Deep Multiple Instance Learning
papers.authors: Ilse M, Tomczak JM, Welling M
papers.aim: To learn from bag-level labels only (e.g. one label per slide) and still find important instances.
papers.method: Attention pooling over instance features, trained end-to-end.
papers.result: Matched or beat other MIL methods and gives attention maps showing important patches (tested on histopathology data).
papers.tools: CNN, attention pooling
papers.gap: Assumes instances are independent.
papers.relation: Biopsy slides will have only slide-level diagnosis. This is the basic method for our pathology agent.
papers.limitations: Small datasets in paper. Future: larger WSI.

papers.title: Data-efficient and weakly supervised computational pathology on whole-slide images (CLAM)
papers.authors: Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Chen TY, Chen RJ, Barbieri M, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To classify whole slides using only slide labels and small datasets.
papers.method: Attention MIL with clustering constraint on top of frozen pretrained features. Tested on renal cancer subtyping, lung cancer subtyping and lymph node metastasis.
papers.result: High AUC with limited labels, worked on independent test sets and even on smartphone microscopy images. Gives interpretable heatmaps.
papers.tools: ResNet-50 features, attention MIL, PyTorch, OpenSlide
papers.gap: Not tested on brain tumours. Feature extractor from ImageNet.
papers.relation: Strong baseline for our pathology agent on small Sri Lankan biopsy sets.
papers.limitations: Scanner/stain differences. Future: better features.

papers.title: Towards a general-purpose foundation model for computational pathology (UNI)
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Ding T, Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Jaume G, et al., Mahmood F
papers.aim: To pretrain one strong pathology feature model useful for many tasks.
papers.method: Self-supervised (DINOv2) training on over 100 million tissue patches from about 100,000 slides, tested on 34 tasks.
papers.result: Better than earlier pathology encoders on most tasks, including rare cancer classification and few-shot learning.
papers.tools: ViT-Large, DINOv2, self-supervised learning
papers.gap: Trained on US hospital data. Licence and compute limits.
papers.relation: Feature extractor for our pathology agent so we need fewer local labels.
papers.limitations: Bias to source data, big model. Future: multimodal.

papers.title: Pathomic Fusion: An Integrated Framework for Fusing Histopathology and Genomic Features for Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Lu MY, Wang J, Williamson DFK, Rodig SJ, Lindeman NI, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To combine histology images and molecular data for glioma grading and survival.
papers.method: CNN and graph network features from histology fused with genomic features using gated attention and Kronecker product.
papers.result: Fusion did better than single-source models and the WHO 2016 grading on TCGA glioma and kidney cancer.
papers.tools: CNN, GCN, SNN, Kronecker fusion
papers.gap: Assumes all data sources are present for every patient.
papers.relation: Our combined diagnosis agent fuses imaging, pathology and lab markers. We need it to work when markers are missing.
papers.limitations: TCGA data only. Future: handle missing modalities.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data (FedAvg)
papers.authors: McMahan HB, Moore E, Ramage D, Hampson S, Aguera y Arcas B
papers.aim: To train a shared model without collecting raw data in one place.
papers.method: Federated Averaging: each client trains locally for some steps, server averages the weights.
papers.result: Needed far fewer communication rounds than synchronised SGD, and worked with non-IID data in their tests.
papers.tools: CNN, LSTM, MNIST, Shakespeare
papers.gap: Performance drops with strong data differences between clients.
papers.relation: The basic federation method we start with across hospitals.
papers.limitations: No privacy guarantee alone. Future: heterogeneity handling.

papers.title: Federated Optimization in Heterogeneous Networks (FedProx)
papers.authors: Li T, Sahu AK, Zaheer M, Sanjabi M, Talwalkar A, Smith V
papers.aim: To make federated training stable when clients have very different data and compute.
papers.method: Adds a proximal term so local models do not drift too far from the global model, and allows partial work from clients.
papers.result: More stable convergence and better accuracy than FedAvg in heterogeneous settings (around 22% average absolute gain in very heterogeneous settings).
papers.tools: Federated optimisation, LEAF benchmarks
papers.gap: Extra hyper-parameter to tune.
papers.relation: Our case is a few hospitals with small and very different cohorts. FedProx is a must-try baseline.
papers.limitations: Not medical data. Future: personalisation.

papers.title: FedBN: Federated Learning on Non-IID Features via Local Batch Normalization
papers.authors: Li X, Jiang M, Zhang X, Kamp M, Dou Q
papers.aim: To handle feature shift between clients, like different scanners.
papers.method: Keep batch normalisation layers local at each client and only average the other weights.
papers.result: Better than FedAvg and FedProx on feature-shift benchmarks, including a medical imaging one.
papers.tools: CNN, batch normalisation, federated learning
papers.gap: Only for models with BN, and a new site needs some local data.
papers.relation: Scanner and protocol differences between Sri Lankan hospitals are exactly this feature shift.
papers.limitations: Small number of clients tested. Future: other normalisation types.

papers.title: Federated learning in medicine: facilitating multi-institutional collaborations without sharing patient data
papers.authors: Sheller MJ, Edwards B, Reina GA, Martin J, Pati S, Kotrotsou A, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To check if federated learning can match central training for brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: BraTS data split by institution, compared federated learning with institutional incremental and cyclic training, and with data-sharing.
papers.result: Federated model reached about 99% of the quality of the centrally trained model, better than the other collaborative methods.
papers.tools: U-Net, BraTS, federated averaging
papers.gap: Simulated federation on public data, not real hospitals.
papers.relation: Direct proof that FL works for brain tumour MRI. Our job is to show it with a few small real Sri Lankan sites.
papers.limitations: Simulated sites. Future: real deployment.

papers.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
papers.authors: Pati S, Baid U, Edwards B, Sheller M, Wang SH, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To run a real worldwide federated study for glioblastoma boundary detection.
papers.method: 71 sites on 6 continents trained a segmentation model together with FL, data never left the site.
papers.result: Big improvement over the model trained on public data for both surgically targetable tumour and whole tumour boundaries.
papers.tools: 3D U-Net, OpenFL, federated learning
papers.gap: Large sites with good IT. Little on what happens with a handful of small sites.
papers.relation: Biggest real FL proof in brain tumours. Our gap is small low-resource sites, which they did not study.
papers.limitations: Heterogeneity across sites not fully solved. Future: smaller sites, more tumour types.

papers.title: Towards fair decentralized benchmarking of healthcare AI algorithms with the Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge
papers.authors: Zenk M, Baid U, Pati S, et al.
papers.relation: Benchmarks federated aggregation and generalisation of brain-tumour segmentation across real hospitals, the core setting for federated training across Sri Lankan hospitals.

papers.title: The MICCAI Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) Challenge 2024: Efficient and Robust Aggregation Methods
papers.authors: Linardos A, Pati S, Baid U, et al.
papers.relation: Compares efficient and robust federated aggregation strategies for glioma segmentation, guiding the choice of aggregation for a small hospital network.

papers.title: Federated brain tumor segmentation: An extensive benchmark
papers.authors: Manthe M, Duffner S, Lartizien C
papers.relation: Systematically benchmarks global, personalised and hybrid federated methods for brain-tumour segmentation on heterogeneous partitions.

papers.title: Federated Modality-Specific Encoders and Multimodal Anchors for Personalized Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Dai Q, Wei D, Liu H, et al.
papers.relation: Handles hospitals that acquire different MRI sequence sets in federated brain-tumour segmentation, a realistic heterogeneity in low-resource sites.

papers.title: A review on brain tumor segmentation based on deep learning methods with federated learning techniques
papers.authors: Ahamed MF, Hossain MM, Nahiduzzaman M, et al.
papers.relation: Surveys deep-learning and federated approaches specifically for brain-tumour segmentation, framing the method space for O3.

papers.title: HarmoFL: Harmonizing Local and Global Drifts in Federated Learning on Heterogeneous Medical Images
papers.authors: Jiang M, Wang Z, Dou Q
papers.relation: Addresses scanner/site feature shift in federated medical imaging, relevant to heterogeneous MRI across Sri Lankan hospitals.

papers.title: FedDG: Federated Domain Generalization on Medical Image Segmentation via Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space
papers.authors: Liu Q, Chen C, Qin J, Dou Q, Heng PA
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.relation: Federated domain generalisation lets a model trained on some hospitals generalise to unseen sites, important for new Sri Lankan centres.

papers.title: IOP-FL: Inside-Outside Personalization for Federated Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Jiang M, Yang H, Cheng C, Dou Q
papers.relation: Personalised federated segmentation that serves both participating and unseen clients, suited to small heterogeneous hospital data.

papers.title: FedDP: Dual Personalization in Federated Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Wang J, Jin Y, Stoyanov D, Wang L
papers.relation: Personalises both feature and prediction levels in federated segmentation to cope with non-IID multi-hospital data.

papers.title: Personalizing Federated Medical Image Segmentation via Local Calibration
papers.authors: Wang J, Jin Y, Wang L
papers.relation: Local calibration of federated segmentation models for site-specific shifts, relevant to per-hospital adaptation.

papers.title: FedLPPA: Learning Personalized Prompt and Aggregation for Federated Weakly-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Lin L, Liu Y, Wu J, et al.
papers.relation: Combines federated learning with weak/sparse annotations, matching the limited expert labelling available in local hospitals.

papers.title: Think Twice Before Selection: Federated Evidential Active Learning for Medical Image Analysis with Domain Shifts
papers.authors: Chen J, Ma B, Cui H, Xia Y
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.relation: Uses evidential uncertainty to choose which cases clinicians should annotate in a federated setting, linking data efficiency with calibrated uncertainty.

papers.title: Robust Learning Protocol for Federated Tumor Segmentation Challenge
papers.authors: Rawat A, Zizzo G, Kadhe S, et al.
papers.relation: Proposes robust aggregation and training protocols for federated brain-tumour segmentation under heterogeneous institutions.

papers.title: The BraTS-Africa Dataset: Expanding the Brain Tumor Segmentation Data to Capture African Populations
papers.authors: Adewole M, Rudie JD, Gbadamosi A, et al.
papers.relation: Provides a low-resource-setting glioma MRI dataset with lower-quality scans, a close analogue for Sri Lankan data and domain shift.

papers.title: Brain tumor segmentation in Sub-Saharan Africa patient population: The BraTS-Africa challenge
papers.authors: Adewole M, Rudie JD, Gbadamosi A, et al.
papers.relation: Reports how segmentation models transfer to low-resource MRI cohorts, directly informing adaptation to small Sri Lankan datasets.

papers.title: Optimizing Brain Tumor Segmentation with MedNeXt: BraTS 2024 SSA and Pediatrics
papers.authors: Hashmi S, Lugo J, Elsayed A, et al.
papers.relation: Shows how to fine-tune modern architectures on small low-resource (Sub-Saharan) glioma cohorts with distribution shift.

papers.title: How We Won BraTS-SSA 2025: Brain Tumor Segmentation in the Sub-Saharan African Population Using Segmentation-Aware Data Augmentation and Model Ensembling
papers.authors: Ankomah CT, Ayivor LE, Nyame I, et al.
papers.relation: Winning recipe of augmentation and ensembling for data-scarce, low-quality MRI in a low-resource population.

papers.title: MedNeXt: Transformer-Driven Scaling of ConvNets for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Roy S, Koehler G, Ulrich C, et al.
papers.relation: Strong data-efficient 3D ConvNeXt segmentation backbone that performs well on limited medical data including brain tumours.

papers.title: nnU-Net Revisited: A Call for Rigorous Validation in 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Isensee F, Wald T, Ulrich C, et al.
papers.relation: Shows well-configured CNN baselines still beat newer architectures, guiding rigorous baseline choice for small local MRI data.

papers.title: TransBTS: Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Using Transformer
papers.authors: Wang W, Chen C, Ding M, et al.
papers.relation: Hybrid CNN-transformer architecture for multimodal MRI brain-tumour segmentation, a key candidate model family.

papers.title: NestedFormer: Nested Modality-Aware Transformer for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Xing Z, Yu L, Wan L, Han T, Zhu L
papers.relation: Modality-aware fusion of multi-sequence MRI for brain-tumour segmentation, relevant to multi-source fusion.

papers.title: CKD-TransBTS: Clinical Knowledge-Driven Hybrid Transformer With Modality-Correlated Cross-Attention for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Lin J, Lin J, Lu C, et al.
papers.relation: Injects radiological clinical knowledge into modality grouping for brain-tumour segmentation, a data-efficient design prior.

papers.title: mmFormer: Multimodal Medical Transformer for Incomplete Multimodal Learning of Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Zhang Y, He N, Yang J, et al.
papers.relation: Robust segmentation when some MRI sequences are missing, common in low-resource hospital protocols.

papers.title: M3AE: Multimodal Representation Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing Modalities
papers.authors: Liu H, Wei D, Lu D, et al.
papers.relation: Self-supervised masked-autoencoder pretraining that handles missing MRI sequences, combining data efficiency with incomplete inputs.

papers.title: D2-Net: Dual Disentanglement Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation With Missing Modalities
papers.authors: Yang Q, Guo X, Chen Z, Woo PYM, Yuan Y
papers.relation: Disentangles modality and tumour-region features for segmentation with incomplete MRI protocols.

papers.title: Latent Correlation Representation Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation With Missing MRI Modalities
papers.authors: Zhou T, Canu S, Vera P, Ruan S
papers.relation: Models inter-modality correlations to segment brain tumours when sequences are unavailable.

papers.title: ACN: Adversarial Co-training Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing Modalities
papers.authors: Wang Y, Zhang Y, Liu Y, et al.
papers.relation: Knowledge transfer from full-modality to missing-modality models for brain-tumour segmentation on incomplete local scans.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Distillation to Improve MRI-Based Brain Tumor Segmentation With Missing MRI Sequences
papers.authors: Rahimpour M, Bertels J, Radwan A, et al.
papers.relation: Distils multi-sequence knowledge into models that run on reduced MRI protocols typical of resource-limited hospitals.

papers.title: BrainSegFounder: Towards 3D Foundation Models for Neuroimage Segmentation
papers.authors: Cox J, Liu P, Stolte SE, et al.
papers.relation: Self-supervised 3D neuroimaging foundation model that fine-tunes to brain-tumour segmentation with few labels.

papers.title: MedSAM2: Segment Anything in 3D Medical Images and Videos
papers.authors: Ma J, Yang Z, Kim S, et al.
papers.relation: Promptable 3D foundation segmentation model that enables label-efficient, clinician-in-the-loop tumour delineation and volume reconstruction.

papers.title: TransMIL: Transformer based Correlated Multiple Instance Learning for Whole Slide Image Classification
papers.authors: Shao Z, Bian H, Chen Y, et al.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.relation: Weakly supervised slide-level classification needing only slide labels, suited to biopsy-slide analysis with limited annotation.

papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers to Gigapixel Images via Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Chen C, Li Y, et al.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.relation: Hierarchical self-supervised WSI representations that reduce label needs for histopathology classification and grading.

papers.title: A visual-language foundation model for computational pathology
papers.authors: Lu MY, Chen B, Williamson DFK, et al.
papers.relation: CONCH pathology foundation model supports few-shot and zero-shot slide classification, relevant to small local biopsy cohorts.

papers.title: Neuropathologist-level integrated classification of adult-type diffuse gliomas using deep learning from whole-slide pathological images
papers.authors: Wang W, Zhao Y, Teng L, et al.
papers.relation: Deep learning on glioma whole-slide images for WHO CNS5 integrated classification, directly matching biopsy-slide analysis and grading.

papers.title: Mutual Contrastive Low-rank Learning to Disentangle Whole Slide Image Representations for Glioma Grading
papers.authors: Zhang L, Wei Y, Fu Y, Price S, Schonlieb CB, Li C
papers.relation: Contrastive WSI representation learning for glioma grading from histopathology with limited labels.

papers.title: MGMT promoter methylation status prediction using MRI scans? An extensive experimental evaluation of deep learning models
papers.authors: Saeed N, Ridzuan M, Alasmawi H, Sobirov I, Yaqub M
papers.relation: Rigorously tests whether MRI deep learning can predict a key molecular marker, informing realistic expectations for imaging-marker fusion.

papers.title: An international study presenting a federated learning AI platform for pediatric brain tumors
papers.authors: Lee EH, Han M, Wright J, Kuwabara M, Mevorach J, et al.
papers.relation: Shows real-world multi-hospital federated training for brain tumour MRI on small, rare-disease cohorts, directly mirroring the federated Sri Lankan hospital setting.

papers.title: The federated tumor segmentation (FeTS) tool: an open-source solution to further solid tumor research
papers.authors: Pati S, Baid U, Edwards B, Sheller MJ, Foley P, et al.
papers.relation: Provides an open-source clinical tool for federated brain tumour segmentation that could be deployed across local hospitals.

papers.title: Federated benchmarking of medical artificial intelligence with MedPerf
papers.authors: Karargyris A, Umeton R, Sheller MJ, Aristizabal A, et al.
papers.relation: Offers a privacy-preserving federated evaluation framework (piloted on brain tumour segmentation) for validating models on local hospital data without sharing it.

papers.title: Swarm learning for decentralized artificial intelligence in cancer histopathology
papers.authors: Saldanha OL, Quirke P, West NP, James JA, Loughrey MB, et al.
papers.relation: Demonstrates decentralised privacy-preserving training of whole-slide pathology models across centres, applicable to federated biopsy-slide analysis.

papers.title: Gradient Matching Federated Domain Adaptation for Brain Image Classification
papers.authors: Zeng LL, Fan Z, Su J, Gan M, Peng L, Shen H, Hu D
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
papers.relation: Addresses site heterogeneity in federated brain MRI classification through federated domain adaptation, a core problem for multi-hospital local data.

papers.title: Integrated approach of federated learning with transfer learning for classification and diagnosis of brain tumor
papers.authors: Albalawi E, T R M, Thakur A, Kumar VV, Gupta M, et al.
papers.relation: Combines transfer learning with federated training for brain tumour MRI classification, matching the data-efficient federated approach of O3.

papers.title: Stepwise Transfer Learning for Expert-level Pediatric Brain Tumor MRI Segmentation in a Limited Data Scenario
papers.authors: Boyd A, Ye Z, Prabhu SP, Tjong MC, Zha Y, et al.
papers.relation: Shows clinically validated expert-level segmentation from very small datasets via stepwise transfer learning, a key data-efficient strategy.

papers.title: Multi-class glioma segmentation on real-world data with missing MRI sequences: comparison of three deep learning algorithms
papers.authors: Pemberton HG, Wu J, Kommers I, Muller DMJ, Hu Y, et al.
papers.relation: Evaluates glioma segmentation on real-world clinical scans with missing sequences, typical of low-resource hospital protocols.
